**D-142 (2026-09-25) — A gate over this month's launches, computed from existing cases, added to the runner's summary and JSON report; not a new case.** The question: given the objects launched in the last 30 days, as a provider serves them, does the parser return them with the right identity? Inputs already in the corpus: the CelesTrak CSV capture of the last-30-days group (256 objects, ids 100404-100789, captured 2026-09-21) and the corpus's Alpha-5 rendering of those records, the form Space-Track's TLE output carries; the CSV case also records that CelesTrak's TLE request for the group answers HTTP 404. Per format the parser reads, records count as loaded (returned with the expected integer id), misidentified (returned with an id that is absent, not an integer, or not the expected one: 0, NaN, a raw string) or dropped (no record came back, whether refused or silently skipped); the eight Batch G runs showed all three shapes. Mechanics: `compare_values` now records structured counts on every values item (`expected`, `returned`, `loaded`, `misidentified`, `dropped`, `non_integer_id`), so the gate reads numbers rather than sentences; `gpconf/gates.py` holds the gate's definition and reads the snapshot's date, count, id range and leading letters from the case data; the CLI prints `gate this month's launches: ...` below the case table and the JSON report carries `gates`. Wording, on the owner's instruction, names the behaviour and never grades the project, since the site's table says a count is not a verdict: "reads this month's launches in every format it reads here", "only via CSV", "not in any format it reads", and for a TLE-only parser "nothing to load from this feed", with Space-Track's Alpha-5 form reported alongside; a parser that raises on the file counts as dropping every record; a format the parser does not read says "not read", a file not on disk "file absent". Every headline carries the snapshot facts and the caveat that a decoder wrong from J upward is not caught by a snapshot whose ids all begin with A. Computed from the Batch G records without re-running, the eight libraries read: PyEphem, satellite.js, Gpredict, tle.js: nothing to load from the CelesTrak TLE feed, 256 misidentified as Space-Track serves them; gods-eye-view: 1 misidentified, 255 dropped; SatDump 1.2.2: 256 dropped, master: only via CSV; libsgp4 master: only via CSV, PR #42: reads them in TLE; astroz: reads them in TLE, with the letter caveat. Tests: the four wordings, the no-grade rule, the snapshot facts from data, and the reference and naive adapters through a run (132 tests). Alternatives: a new case (rejected: the inputs and checks exist, and a case would double-count in the seventeen-case table); grading words LOADS/PARTLY/NO (rejected by the owner: a verdict on the project). Stage two, a separate decision: JSON, XML and KVN renderings of the same snapshot, so readers of those formats get a measured value.

**D-143 (2026-09-25) — The provider's recorded empty answer is handed to the parser under test as its own check, `empty-answer-yields-no-records`: zero records and no error is the pass, an exception or an invented record fails, a parser without the format skips.** Reason (the second of the four ideas under review, fail-closed semantics): a parser must keep three outcomes apart, a value it cannot represent, a file it cannot read, and an endpoint with no data; the corpus tested the first as a required refusal (the writer case, the vectors) and applied all three to itself in Batch A, but the third was never presented to a parser, because `load_source` recognised the 404 body and returned an empty result without calling the parser. Now, in the four cases that hold such a body (`analyst-objects`, `nine-digit-supgp-launch-nominals`, `six-digit-omm-saramago`, `tle-omits-six-digit-objects`; six files, five `No GP data found` and one `No SupGP data found`), the body goes to the parser first; the runner's own empty-404 handling then continues as before. Declared once in `tools/cases.py` and attached to the four cases' check lists; manifest and the four case docs regenerated; the frozen `expected.json` files embed their check lists from the last expected-value regeneration and gain the id at the next one, which does not affect the runner (it reads the manifest). Counts: the reference, naive and python-sgp4 adapters each return an empty list for the body, so each gains pass items and no failing count moves; the per-case rows of `docs/FAILURES.md` are unchanged. In CI's offline runs the raw files are absent, so the check does not run there. Tests: the four cases declare the check; the reference and naive adapters pass it on every body on disk; a parser that raises fails with "not an error" in the detail; a parser that returns a record fails; a parser without the format skips. Not done, held for their own decisions: a per-record refusal channel (item 2 of the idea) and a corrupt-input case (item 3, synthetic-derived).

**D-144 (2026-09-25) — A refusal channel in the adapter protocol, so that a record the library refuses with an error is kept apart from one it drops silently; the built-in python-sgp4 adapter adopts it; the eight Batch G runs are not re-run and the site's table carries a footnote.** Form (owner-approved as proposed): an entry in the list the adapter already returns, carrying `_refused` with the library's reason as a non-empty string, optionally `_field` (the catalog field as the input carried it) and `_input` (up to 80 characters of the line); and an optional first entry `{"_adapter": {"refusals": true}}` declaring that every record dropped with an error is reported, which is what makes "dropped" honest: with the declaration zero refusals means dropped silently, without it the report says refusals were not reported. Owner's addition: the reason is required and non-empty; a refusal without one is counted as a drop and fails the file's `refusals` item, since a refusal that gives no reason is no better than a drop for the thing this change separates. Runner: refusals are split out at the one normalisation point before any check sees them; `compare_values` credits a refusal whose field decodes to an expected id (digits or Alpha-5, decoded by the corpus) and writes "N expected record(s) not returned: R refused with a reason (e.g. ...), S silently"; the counts gain `refused`, `refused_matched`, `refused_without_reason`, `refusals_reported` and `top_refusal_reason`, and `dropped` excludes matched refusals; a per-file `refusals` item lists reasons with counts (info, or fail when a reason is missing); the empty-answer check (D-143) fails a refusal of the 404 body, since an empty answer is not an unreadable one; the gate reports "R refused (reason)" and "D dropped silently" or "D dropped (refusals not reported by this adapter)". Adoption: one line in a harness's catch block; the python-sgp4 adapter now catches `ValueError` from `twoline2rv` and from `omm.initialize` per record and declares the channel, so its nine-digit result reads as a refusal with the library's own message rather than a whole-file parse failure; no failing case count moves. Not re-run, on the owner's instruction: the eight Batch G harnesses, whose recorded "dropped" counts may include refusals (libsgp4 master's `TleException`, astroz's `InvalidCharacter`, Gpredict's rejected sets); the site's hand-run table says so in a footnote (S-043). Where the library returns a value rather than an error (satellite.js, tle.js, PyEphem's 0) or drops inside itself with no signal (SatDump's registry, gods-eye-view's dedupe) there is nothing to adopt, and misidentified or dropped is the finding. Tests: the split and the reason rule, field decoding, refusals credited and named through a run, the undeclared adapter not credited with silence, the reasonless refusal counted as a drop, the reference reporting none, the refused 404 body failing, and the python-sgp4 adapter's nine-digit refusal (144 tests). Fail-closed rule added when the first regeneration showed the hole: with the adapter refusing the one record in `csv-json-omitted-mandatory-fields`' two SupGP files instead of failing the file, the parser returned zero records and every per-file check passed on nothing, flipping the case to pass; now a file the reference reads records from, for which the parser returned none, gets a failing `records-returned` item that names the refusals or the silent drops, with the same counts the gate reads, and no other check runs on it (the same discipline as D-113 for the reference reader). With it the failing case counts are unchanged: reference none, naive 14, python-sgp4 7. One item count moves and is meant to: python-sgp4's nine-digit case has five failing items instead of four, because `starlink-all.csv` now loads its five-digit records around the 27 refused ones and the classification-C check runs on it and finds C not preserved, a result the whole-file failure had hidden. Held for its own decision: item 3, a corrupt-input case.

**D-145 (2026-09-25) — v0.3.0 planned as the fail-closed release; the plan is a private note at `docs/handoff/v0.3.0-plan.md`, outside the export allowlist; nothing built, no date.** Shape: D-142 to D-144 are already on main (the gate and structured counts, the provider's empty answer handed to the parser, the refusal channel with a required reason and fail-closed on a file returned empty); the release's remaining new work is one case, corrupt input, as a fourth input class feeding the same four counts, loaded, misidentified, refused, dropped, rather than a new concept, and the case count moves from seventeen to eighteen in the same release, because the protocol additions already call for a minor bump under the README's rule and the count change then costs one rebuild of everything that carries it instead of two. The case tests the parser under test on input the corpus has never fed it, where D-113 and D-117 hardened the corpus's own readers; it checks behaviours the Batch G reports recorded as documented but unverified on corrupt input. It needs the owner's provenance approval for synthetic-derived inputs under the D-096 precedent, each a frozen real record with one stated edit, placed between valid records so that resynchronisation is measured. Downstream: the version constants, the site's count sentences and data files, release notes, the Zenodo description, the failures table, and eight Batch G re-runs against the new shape producing a second round of findings and second contacts with the maintainers, which the note argues are the point of the release. The note marks every unverified claim. Alternatives: a corrupt-input case as its own concept with its own vocabulary (rejected: the D-144 counts already describe every outcome it can produce); adding the case before or after the protocol release (rejected: two rebuilds of the count).

**D-146 (2026-09-25) — Identity over time stated as an open question in the coverage gaps, not answered and not a new section (the fourth of the four ideas under review, documentation only).** A nine-digit SupGP id is a launch nominal CelesTrak serves for the days between launch and 18 SDS's first GP data, after which the object is expected under a catalog number of 100000 or above; what a tracker keeps as its stable key across that change, and how the nominal's history merges into the catalogued object's, is a question the corpus cannot answer. Checked first, so the text extends what was there: the nine-digit and classification-C cases already call their files perishable, the research note holds the two CelesTrak quotations the inference rests on, and it recorded, without interpreting, that 72000 and 799501621 share OBJECT_ID 2026-219A. Two facts checked for the text from the frozen records: the corpus holds no object in both forms (the 27 nominals are launch 2026-219; the same day's last-30-days group lists launches 2026-156 to 2026-220 but not 2026-219), and the shared designator is not one-to-one (72000 and 72001 carry 2026-219A and 2026-219B, as do two per-satellite nominals). Placed where the other gaps live: a gap entry on the nine-digit case, a one-sentence cross-reference on the classification-C case, both in `tools/cases.py` with the case docs and manifest regenerated, and the README's existing nine-digit bullet extended. The text says what the corpus covers (both forms parse; the nine-digit case is perishable and tied to a launch window), what it does not (correlation, merging, key stability), and why that is out of scope rather than missing: a data-relationship question for the provider's documentation, not a parsing property a fixture can freeze. Every claim in it is marked tested or inferred; the "no way to map" sentence in CelesTrak's text is about the TLE field width and is not used. No code changed.

**D-147 (2026-09-25) — Propagation-equivalence grading (grading two TLE renderings by whether they propagate to the same TEME position within a tolerance) is not built; an optional information-only figure in metres is left as a stated possibility. The fourth of the four ideas under review, closed.** Premise corrected in review: the idea as put said the writer case grades bytes. It does not. `tle-writer-round-trip` reads the written lines back through the corpus's own reference reader and accepts each field at its own resolution, quantised by truncation or by rounding half up (D-070, D-071), and `tle-writer-matches-provider-rendering` reports byte-identity for information only. The "two writers, different but equally valid TLEs" problem the idea addressed is therefore already handled for every freedom the format is known to allow. That correction came from the agent's review of the proposal, not from the owner. What settles the decision, measured on 2026-09-25 with python-sgp4 2.27 (WGS72, mode `i`) on the corpus's frozen ISS record (25544, epoch 2026-09-20T12:42:37.141056), no network: each TLE field moved by one unit in its last printed digit, position difference against the unmoved record at the same instant, in metres:

| field, one unit in its last digit | epoch | +1 h | +1 day | +7 days |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| mean anomaly (1e-4 deg) | 11.861 | 11.856 | 11.872 | 11.870 |
| argument of perigee (1e-4 deg) | 11.872 | 11.852 | 11.861 | 11.859 |
| RA of ascending node (1e-4 deg) | 11.870 | 9.274 | 11.858 | 11.800 |
| inclination (1e-4 deg) | 0.020 | 9.426 | 3.298 | 23.179 |
| epoch (1e-8 day) | 6.616 | 6.613 | 6.622 | 6.621 |
| eccentricity (1e-7) | 0.769 | 1.299 | 0.745 | 0.678 |
| mean motion (1e-8 rev/day) | 0.003 | 0.018 | 0.428 | 2.999 |
| BSTAR (1e-8, last mantissa digit of 0.15975e-3) | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.237 | 11.661 |
| first and second derivatives of mean motion | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

(1) A tolerance that accepts every valid writer must admit one unit in an angle's last digit, about 12 m at every horizon and up to 23 m at a week: a floor of roughly 12 m, derivable per record from its own resolution, not a guess. (2) The three precision defects the corpus has found are all smaller than that floor: satellite.js's millisecond epoch truncation, 6.19 m at 30 minutes for an 808 µs loss (D-132); Gpredict's dropped mean-motion digit, 0.04 m at 1 h, 0.86 m at 24 h and 6.0 m at 7 days (D-133); libsgp4's epoch rounding, 8 µs, about 6 cm along track (D-138, reported in dnwrnr/sgp4#45). A propagation grade wide enough for valid writers passes all three; the field-resolution checks catch them. (3) Propagation is blind by construction to identity and to both derivatives: in python-sgp4 at 8126f77, `sgp4()` in `sgp4/propagation.py` never reads `ndot` or `nddot` and `sgp4init` only stores them (the zero row above confirms it), and no identity field (catalog number, international designator, classification, element set number, name) enters the propagation at all. The eight Batch G findings were identity and epoch bugs; propagation grading would have missed every identity finding and, by (2), the epoch findings too. Also weighed: the runner is standard-library only (README), so the dependency would be required (breaking that for every user and CI), optional (reports differing by machine) or vendored (numerical code to maintain); and python-sgp4 is under test here, so using its propagator would put code from a tested project into the oracle, although for a relative comparison of two renderings a shared propagator error largely cancels, and an absolute claim would need a second implementation or published SGP4 verification vectors, whose terms are unread [untested]. Stated possibility, not built: an information-only figure in metres (the propagated position difference at epoch, +1 day and +7 days) on the writer case and on `tle-vs-omm-precision-loss`, skipping visibly when SGP4 is not installed, never passed or failed; worth doing only if the site wants to show metres. Alternatives: propagation grading replacing field-resolution grading (rejected by (1) to (3)); alongside it as pass/fail (rejected: at the tolerance valid writers require it can fail nothing the existing checks pass).

**D-148 (2026-09-26) — Statuses the runner reported without having earned them, in the spirit of Batch A: a provider file that is not on disk reports `not-fetched`, never `skip`; the count line says how many cases need fetched data and names a case that ran on part of its files; the fetch command names a script that exists; and the gate's headline claims nothing about a format it never tried, dates its snapshot from the frozen capture, and judges a freshly fetched CSV against its own count. The last of these is the one to remember: the gate would have shown the corpus's own reference reader as unable to read CSV on the first fresh fetch by any public user. No published count moved.** Found while measuring what a pip-installed runner would show before fetching (the v0.3 packaging proposal): the public export, which carries no provider data, run offline with the three built-in adapters. Five faults, all reproduced before the change. (1) A case whose provider files were absent reported `skip`, the status the site's library page defines as meaning "the library has no reader for the case's format"; python-sgp4's offline run printed 14 skips, one of them a real missing KVN reader and 13 missing data under the same word. D-119 had moved these cases from `not-exercised` to `skip` for the same reason, that the word claimed something about the data; `skip` in turn claimed something about the parser. (2) A case that ran on part of its files passed without a word: after a first fetch the three re-capture files are not yet on disk, and `analyst-objects`, `bstar-and-derivative-forms` and `tle-omits-six-digit-objects` reported `pass` with the gap visible only as a skip count in a column the default output does not explain. (3) The missing-file detail and the drift messages said "run tools/fetch.py", a path relative to a clone's root, which a user outside the root or with an installed runner does not have. (4) The gate headline said "reads this month's launches in every format it reads here" when the CSV capture was absent, and for a parser that misread the TLE lines it said "nothing to load from this feed", a claim that the parser reads TLE only, when its CSV reading had never been tried; a run selected with `--case` did the same, since the CSV case was not run. CI's offline naive run printed that TLE-only headline on every push. (5) Two faults in the gate found while fixing (4), not in the proposal: its snapshot date came from the local fetch's metadata, falling back to `expected.json`'s generation date, so an offline run printed 2026-09-23 for a capture of 2026-09-21 and a fresh fetch would print the user's fetch date beside the frozen count; and every format was judged against the frozen 256, so a CSV fetched on a later day was misjudged. Simulated in a scratch copy with ten rows removed from the CSV (246 records, live tier): the reference reader loaded 246 of 246 and the headline said "only via TLE". The last-30-days group is a rolling window, and the site's tracker, which fetches it daily, recorded 256 records at the frozen capture and then 231 later on 2026-09-21, 203 on 2026-09-23, 228 on 2026-09-24 and 204 on 2026-09-25 (its fetch of 2026-09-22 failed): never 256 again. So on the first fresh fetch by any public user the gate would have shown the corpus's own reference reader, the control every other result is read against, as unable to read CSV. The published results never showed it only because they are run on the original capture. Changes: `runner.py` gains the status `not-fetched`, ranked above `skip` and below `not-exercised` in a case's status, a `not-fetched` key in every case's counts, `CaseResult.missing()`, `fetch_hint(root)` (the clone's own script by a path that works from the working directory, quoted when it holds a space, or the repository URL when the root has no script), `is_provider_data(path)` (a file under `fixtures/<case>/raw/`) and `CorpusIncomplete`: a missing file that ships with the corpus (`derived/`, `vectors/`) cannot be fetched, so "need fetched data" would be false; the run stops with exit status 2 instead, and the per-case handler lets the error through rather than recording it as a parser failure. `__main__.py` adds the `n/f` column, "N need fetched data" in the count line, a line naming cases with no provider files, a line naming cases that ran on part of theirs (with the re-capture timing when one is missing) and the fetch command. `gates.py`: the states `not fetched` and `not run` limit the claim to "every format measured here", "only via X of the formats measured here" or "not in any format measured here", with the format left out named before the numbers, and forbid the TLE-only headline; `not read`, a format the parser declared unsupported, is a fact about the parser and keeps the old wording; the snapshot date is the source's `retrieved_at` in `expected.json`; each format is judged against its own values item's expected count, and a live capture is labelled "live capture fetched <date>, N objects, not the snapshot", or "every record dropped" when the parser raised on it. Two judgement calls, confirmed by the owner on 2026-09-26: a case that ran on part of its files keeps the result of those files and is named below the count line, rather than reporting `not-fetched` over its passes, because the passes are real results on the files present and a failure among them must still show; and a missing file that ships with the corpus stops the run with exit status 2. Alternatives: keeping `skip` and changing only the detail text (rejected: the site's tables read the status, not the detail); reporting a missing shipped file as `not-fetched` or as a parser failure (rejected: the first gives a false instruction, the second charges the parser for a broken copy). What moved, measured: in the full-data runs of reference, naive and python-sgp4 every case status, count, item and gate headline is identical before and after (compared field by field); `docs/FAILURES.md` differs only in its generation time; each case's JSON counts gain `"not-fetched": 0`. The site: its findings table is built from those full-data runs and does not move; its hand-run table's skips were checked against the pattern a missing-data case leaves, a skip count equal to the case's source count, and the 27 rows that match it are TLE-only libraries facing the all-XML `omm-xml-schema` or the all-CSV-and-JSON `csv-json-omitted-mandatory-fields`, whose 20 files were on disk from 2026-09-21, three days before the hand runs, so every skip there is a missing reader and the site's definition holds. Offline, the public export: reference 4 pass and 13 skip becomes 4 pass and 13 need fetched data; naive 4 fail and 13 skip becomes 4 fail and 13 need fetched data; python-sgp4 1 within tolerance, 2 fail and 14 skip becomes the same with 1 skip and 13 need fetched data; the naive gate headline changes from "nothing to load from this feed" to "not in any format measured here (CSV not measured: not fetched)". Tests: `tests/test_not_fetched.py` (new: the status, the JSON counts, the count line and table header, skip kept for a parser without hooks, a partly fetched case run from a scratch root without its re-capture, the fetch command in a clone, with a space and without the script, and exit 2 for a missing shipped file); `tests/test_gates.py` (every-format and not-in-any-format headlines with a format not fetched or not run, no TLE-only claim then, the not-read wording unchanged, only-via with an unknown third format, a live capture judged on its own count, no borrowed count when the parser raised on a live file, and the snapshot date read from `expected.json` with and without the local metadata); `tests/test_runner.py` (the D-119 tests now expect `not-fetched`). 162 tests pass in the private repository; in a copy of the public export with the new code, 160 run, 150 pass and 10 skip for want of provider data, and CI's two offline commands exit 0 and 1 as before. README ("Tolerances" and the gate paragraph), CHANGELOG and the CI comment updated.

**D-149 (2026-09-26) — v0.3.0 re-planned as the packaging release and the corrupt-input case moved to v0.4.0 (owner decision); the plan split into two private notes; two corrections recorded, one to D-145's argument and one to the proposal's own count.** After an outside review concluded that the corpus's ceiling is adoption friction, not missing cases, the agent proposed packaging on 2026-09-26 and the owner accepted it. v0.3.0 is: a PyPI package, `gpconf`, whose runner stays standard-library only, with optional extras; a `--preset` flag with four presets pip can complete (reference, naive, sgp4, pyephem) and two that need Node (satellite.js, tle.js); the five compiled and application harnesses (libsgp4, Gpredict, SatDump, astroz, gods-eye-view) kept out of the wheel as recipes; and an offline, report-only GitHub Action that exits 0 and carries no badge. The case count stays at seventeen. The corrupt-input case moves to v0.4.0 with D-145's decisions 2 to 4; decision 1, the README rule's added words "or an additive protocol change", stays with v0.3.0, which carries the protocol change it covers. The note D-145 names, `docs/handoff/v0.3.0-plan.md`, is renamed `v0.4.0-plan.md` and revised; a new `v0.3.0-plan.md` holds the packaging plan: the wheel's contents and exclusions (no raw provider data, D-019; no SupGP values, D-049; built from the public export, never from the private repository, whose `expected.json` files carry the values the export scrubs); the runner's root taken from its own file path, which points at site-packages once installed and is to be split into a read-only corpus root and a writable data root; a per-user cache folder for fetched data; the Node resolution problem, marked inferred and untested; and the Action's reason for staying offline, a fetch pattern from shared runner addresses that CelesTrak has not agreed to. Both notes stay private. Corrections, both from the agent: D-145's note argued that adding the case after a protocol-only 0.3.0 would force the rebuild of everything that carries the count twice; it does not, because v0.3.0 keeps seventeen cases and those surfaces change only when the count does, so the cost of landing later is one more release cycle, not a second rebuild. And the packaging proposal said four of the eight Batch G re-runs would become preset commands; three will (PyEphem, satellite.js, tle.js), since python-sgp4, the fourth pip preset, is a built-in adapter and not one of the eight. Alternatives: packaging and the case in one v0.3.0 (rejected: the case is unbuilt and needs its own provenance approval, and packaging should not wait for it); packaging as a 0.2.x patch (rejected: main already carries an additive protocol change, which makes the next release a minor).

**D-150 (2026-09-26) — v0.3.0 packaging, stage 1: the runner works when installed, not only from a clone. Two roots, a per-user cache folder for provider data with a `--data` flag and a `GPCONF_DATA` variable, and the fetch script as the `gpconf fetch` subcommand; no packaging metadata, build, upload or Action (owner instruction). A correction to D-148's re-capture sentence.** The problem, from the plan (`docs/handoff/v0.3.0-plan.md`, section 4): `__main__.py` and `runner.py` took the corpus root as the folder above the package, which is the repository in a clone and site-packages once installed; and the fetch script existed only as `tools/fetch.py`, a path an installed copy does not have. Changes. `gpconf/locate.py` (new) resolves two roots. The corpus root, read-only, holds what ships (manifest, every `expected.json` and `case.md`, `derived/`, `vectors/`, `tools/fetchlist.json`); first match of `--root`, a clone (the folder above the package holds `manifest.json` and `fixtures/`), and the corpus bundled as package data in `gpconf/corpus/`, found through `importlib.resources` so that an import from an archive is refused with a reason rather than failing on a missing file. The data root holds the provider files in the clone's layout, `fixtures/<case>/raw/`; first match of `--data`, `GPCONF_DATA`, the corpus root itself when that is a clone or came from `--root` (every clone and every test keeps its layout), and a per-user cache folder, one per corpus version: `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/gpconf/<version>` or `~/.cache/gpconf/<version>` (a relative `XDG_CACHE_HOME` is ignored, as the XDG specification says), `~/Library/Caches/gpconf/<version>` on macOS, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\gpconf\Cache\<version>` on Windows. The runner takes both roots and reads provider files from the data root and everything else from the corpus root; the gate reads a live capture's metadata from the data root. `gpconf/fetch.py` is `tools/fetch.py` moved into the package with its one root split in two (the fetch list and manifest from the corpus root, the files to and from the data root) and `--root` and `--data` options; its request logic is unchanged. `tools/fetch.py` is now a shim that runs the same code in a clone and, when imported, replaces itself in `sys.modules` with the package module, so the tests' `import fetch` and any patch reach the same code. `gpconf fetch` hands its arguments to that module, so it takes exactly the options `tools/fetch.py` always took. `gpconf run` prints `provider data: <folder> (<why>)` above the case table when the data root is not the corpus root, so a clone's output is unchanged; a missing corpus exits 2 with a reason; `check-tle` runs before any corpus lookup, since it checks the user's own file. D-148's fetch command now names the clone's `tools/fetch.py` where one exists and `python3 -m gpconf fetch` elsewhere, adding `--data DIR` when the data folder came from that flag and `--root DIR` for a bare corpus copy, and nothing for `GPCONF_DATA`, which reaches the fetch by itself. The fetch's dry-run summary, found while showing the installed copy, said "done: 0 request(s) made, 61 entries skipped" of the 61 requests it plans; it now says "dry run: no request made; a run would make 61 request(s) and leave 0 entries as they are". Alternatives: duplicating the fetch code in the package (rejected: two copies of the request logic under CelesTrak's policy is one too many); an environment switch to mark an installed copy (rejected: a clone must keep working with no setup, and the files beside the package already say which it is); one cache folder shared by all versions (rejected for now: a version's frozen values belong with the files it was built against; reusing matching files across versions is an open item in the plan note); printing the data folder on every run (rejected: it would change every clone's output for no information). Correction to D-148: its runner line and README sentence said a missing re-capture file "is fetched on a later run, once its original is at least two hours old". It is not: the fetch list marks the three re-capture entries as re-captures, and the fetch selects them only with `--include-recaptures`, whose help calls them maintainer-only (`tools/fetch.py` as committed at D-148, the selection filter and the flag's help text); a dry run of an installed copy plans 61 of the 64 entries. A normal fetch therefore always leaves `analyst-objects`, `bstar-and-derivative-forms` and `tle-omits-six-digit-objects` without their re-capture, and the runner's line and the README now say so; the fetch command below it is printed only when a file a normal fetch would bring is missing, since for a missing re-capture it would make no request. The error was the agent's, found while moving the fetch code. What moved: in the full-data runs of reference, naive and python-sgp4, every case, count, item and gate headline is identical to D-148's reports, compared field by field; `docs/FAILURES.md` is not regenerated. Scope, as instructed: no change to `pyproject.toml`, no build, no upload, no Action. The bundled corpus folder is assembled by the tests, which copy the shipped files into a scratch copy of the package, standing in for the build step of a later stage. Tests: `tests/test_install_layout.py` (new, 16): the cache folder on each platform, the precedence of the two roots, a clone printing no data line, and a copy outside the repository run in subprocesses with only that copy on `PYTHONPATH` and a scratch `HOME` (the copy, not the repository, is imported; an offline run finds the bundled corpus, names the cache and creates nothing; `list`; a fetch dry run plans every normal entry into the cache and writes nothing; `--data` and `GPCONF_DATA` redirect both run and fetch; with provider files copied into a data folder the copy runs every case; without a corpus, `run` exits 2 and `check-tle` still works), and `gpconf fetch` in-process with a stub where the request would be, writing to the data root and reading the list from the corpus root; `tools/fetch.py` and `gpconf.fetch` are the same module. No test makes a request. `tests/test_not_fetched.py`: the fetch command and the re-capture line updated. 178 tests pass in the private repository; a fresh public export (160 files, three new) runs 176 with 11 skipped for want of provider data, and CI's two offline commands exit 0 and 1 as before. README ("Fetching responsibly" and the not-fetched paragraph) and CHANGELOG updated.

**D-151 (2026-09-26) — v0.3.0 packaging, stage 2: the adapters move into the package and `--preset` arrives. Four presets, reference, naive, sgp4 and pyephem; each library preset records the version it was tested against and the report prints the version it found; naive is labelled a demonstration of failure. No packaging metadata, build, upload, Action or Node preset (owner instruction). No published count moved.** The three built-in adapters moved with `git mv` from `tests/adapters/` to `gpconf/adapters/` (`reference.py`, `naive.py`, `sgp4_adapter.py`), their code unchanged apart from docstrings and the python-sgp4 import message; the old files are shims that replace themselves in `sys.modules` with the package modules, so `--adapter tests.adapters.reference:Parser`, the tests, CI and the published documents that cite those names keep working and reach the same code. PyEphem's adapter came from the hand run's harness (`docs/handoff/batch-g/pyephem/adapter_pyephem.py`, corpus D-128, reported as pyephem#296) as `gpconf/adapters/pyephem_adapter.py`, its parsing unchanged; the harness's module-level list of refusals and its one stderr line per refused element set were for the findings note and are dropped, which changes no result; counted over a full run of the corpus, `readtle()` refuses no element set, so neither ever fired. It does not yet use the refusal channel (D-144), which the v0.4.0 plan gives every re-run; adopting it now would change its gate reading against the published row. `gpconf/presets.py` (new) names each preset's module, the library it exposes, the pip requirement, the optional extra and the tested version (python-sgp4 2.27, PyEphem 4.2.1). `gpconf run --preset NAME` loads it; `gpconf presets` lists the four with the installed version or the install command; the report's parser line reads, for example, "preset sgp4 (python-sgp4 2.27, the version it was tested with)", or names both versions and says results may differ from the published ones when they differ; the JSON report carries a `preset` block; a missing library is refused with exit status 2 and `pip install sgp4` or `pip install ephem`; `--preset` combined with another parser option is an error. The naive preset's line reads "preset naive (a demonstration of failure, not a parser anyone should use)". CI's two offline runs now use `--preset reference` and `--preset naive`. A conflict in the instruction, recorded rather than worked around: optional extras are declared in `pyproject.toml`, which this stage leaves alone; the registry records each extra (`sgp4`, `pyephem`) and its requirement, the install message names the library's own pip package, which is true today, and the extras go into `pyproject.toml` at the packaging stage. An export-allowlist gap, found while verifying the export and recorded for whoever adds the next folder: `PUBLIC_ALLOWLIST.txt` lists `gpconf/*.py`, a rule that was correct for as long as the package was one flat folder, and stopped being correct the moment this stage put `gpconf/adapters/` under it, because the allowlist's patterns do not recurse. Nothing failed: the private suite passed, since the private repository has every file, and the export dry run only reports a count. An export would have shipped the `tests/adapters/` shims without the modules they load, and public CI would have failed on the next push. It showed only as an export count five short of the files added (162 against 167). `gpconf/adapters/*.py` is added and the export now copies 167 files. So that the next folder cannot slip through the same way, the allowlist carries a comment above the package lines saying that patterns do not recurse and a new folder under `gpconf/` or `tests/` needs its own line, and `tests/test_export.py` now fails if any Python file under `gpconf/` or `tests/` is missing from an export. The check to make when adding a folder anywhere: does an existing allowlist pattern reach it? What moved in the published counts: nothing. The three built-in presets on full data in this repository give, for every case, count, item and gate, exactly the results of the D-148 reports behind `docs/FAILURES.md`, compared field by field; only the report's parser label differs, and `docs/FAILURES.md` is not regenerated. The PyEphem preset, run from a copy installed outside the repository (the corpus from a fresh public export, python-sgp4 2.27 and PyEphem 4.2.1 installed from PyPI into a scratch environment, the provider files of this repository as its data folder), fails the same six cases as the published hand-run row (PyEphem 4.2.1, 2026-09-24, 6 of 17); its other differences are all accounted for: D-143's empty-answer check turns three skipped cases into passes and adds a pass to `analyst-objects`; D-129 makes the SATCAT case not exercised; and the public export's scrub of SupGP values (D-049) drops the two Starlink G15-27 pairs from the pair lists of `mean-motion-derivative-convention` and `tle-vs-omm-precision-loss` (304 pairs to 302), so the installed copy never loads that CSV there and each case shows one skip fewer. The hand-run row stays as run. Alternatives: keeping the adapters in `tests/` (rejected: `tests/` is not part of an installed package); registering presets through package entry points (rejected for now: a standard-library table is enough for four, and entry points need the packaging metadata this stage leaves alone). Tests: `tests/test_presets.py` (new: the four presets and their descriptions, the naive label, the version label for a match and a mismatch, an unknown preset and a missing library refused with the install command, `--preset` not combinable, the old names being the package modules, a preset giving the adapter's results over the offline cases, the JSON block, the version printed by each installed library preset) a class in `tests/test_install_layout.py` running every preset from a copy outside the repository, and the export check in `tests/test_export.py`. 191 tests pass in this repository with one skip (PyEphem is not installed here); a fresh public export (167 files) runs 189 with 12 skipped; CI's two commands exit 0 and 1 as before. The export check fails when the `gpconf/adapters/` line is removed and passes with it.

**D-152 (2026-09-26) — The SatDump link stand-ins stay out of the MIT repository and its Zenodo archives, on the cautious reading of GPL-3.0; the public SatDump recipe will ship the harness and the list of symbol names the link needs, with the instruction to define each as an empty function or a default-constructed object; the harness's dead call to a predict function, and its redeclaration, are removed. Owner decision on the agent's analysis; analysis, not legal advice.** What the files are: `stubs.cpp` (20 lines, SatDump master f3d82ad) and `stubs-rel.cpp` (17 lines, release 1.2.2), kept with the hand run in `docs/handoff/batch-g/satdump/`, contain no line of SatDump. They include SatDump headers and define nine and seven SatDump symbols that SatDump's own compiled `tle.cpp` references and the harness never calls: the configuration object, the database pointer, a version string set to "harness", the member function `DBHandler::get_meta`, two HTTP helpers, the global logger and `Logger::logf`, an explicit specialisation of SatDump's `format_notated` template, and in the release file `main_cfg`, `saveUserConfig` and `eventBus`. Every body is empty or returns a constant. The permissive reading, which is genuinely strong: nothing expressive is copied, since the names and type signatures are dictated by the linker; names are not protected by copyright in the US under the Copyright Office's rule on words and short phrases; the Court of Justice of the EU held in SAS Institute v World Programming (2012) that a program's functionality and interfaces are not protected expression; the US Supreme Court held in Google v Oracle (2021) that reimplementing about 11,500 lines of declarations was fair use, and these are sixteen short definitions for non-commercial interoperability testing; GPL-3.0 counts as modifying only copying or adapting that needs copyright permission; the combined program is only built on the user's machine, and GPL-3.0 section 2 lets anyone make and run covered works they do not convey; MIT is GPL-compatible. On that reading the files could be published under MIT. The cautious reading: the stand-ins are not client code but replacements for parts of SatDump, defining SatDump's own objects and functions, including a member function of its `DBHandler` class and a specialisation of its template, and adapting part of a work is within GPL-3.0's definition of modifying; their selection, namespaces and types are dictated wholly by SatDump's internal structure at two commits; the US Federal Circuit held in 2014 that the structure and organisation of declarations can be protected, and the Supreme Court did not overturn that but decided fair use, a defence argued after an accusation. The deciding reasons: first, the asymmetry of the costs. Withholding the files costs a SatDump user the same sixteen empty definitions, written from the linker's errors. Publishing them wrongly would put GPL-derived material under MIT in a public repository, and every release of that repository is archived by Zenodo, where it cannot be withdrawn. Second, the corpus's policy to interpret licences strictly, never permissively (`CLAUDE.md`). The permissive reading is strong; it is not the standard the corpus sets. Consequences: the stand-in files stay private; the public SatDump recipe, in a later stage's harnesses folder, ships `harness.cpp` and `harness-rel.cpp`, which both readings accept as client code, since they call SatDump's functions the way any program uses a library and the FSF accepts GPL-compatible licences for such modules, together with the list of symbol names, which are not expression under either reading. The two harnesses redeclared `Julian_Date_of_Epoch` from SatDump's bundled predict fork and called it, but the result was discarded (`(void)jd`) and the ISO epoch was already built from a year computed locally with the fork's pivot, so the call and the redeclaration were dead code; both are removed, and the predict header stays because the harness calls `predict_parse_tle`. Verified by compiling the epoch helper on its own with clang, before and after: identical output over 63 year and day inputs. The full harness was not rebuilt, since no SatDump tree is on this machine. Open, not decided: publishing the stand-ins under GPL-3.0 in a separate repository, which would satisfy both readings; and asking SatDump's copyright holders, the one way to settle the question outright, which is the owner's contact to make.

**D-153 (2026-09-26) — The v0.3.0 plan's other five open items decided (owner decision on the agent's proposals).** (2) The Action, when a preset's library will not import, fails as a setup error with exit status 2 and a message saying that nothing ran and that this says nothing about the library. Results never fail a job, which is report-only with exit 0 for failed cases, but a run that tested nothing must not show green: that is the fault D-148 corrected in the runner, an unearned status. A library version other than the tested one is not a setup error; it runs and the report names both versions. The command line already exits 2 for a missing Python library (D-151), and its message gains the same two statements. Consequence for stage 3: a Node preset runs through the command protocol, one process per file, so a missing Node or library would otherwise show as a parse failure in every case, blamed on the library; stage 3 adds a preflight that checks both before any case runs. (3) tle.js: the preset `tle.js` reads the epoch from the raw year and day fields, reproducing the published row's 2 of 17, and `tle.js-api` reads it through `getEpochTimestamp()`, whose flooring to the millisecond (finding F3, a design choice) alone fails every TLE case in the hand run, 7 of 17. One harness serves both. (4) The `crosscheck` extra (python-sgp4, Skyfield, xmlschema, lxml) serves `tools/crosscheck.py` and `tools/validate_xml.py`, which the wheel does not carry; it is dropped from the published metadata, and maintainers install the pinned `tools/crosscheck-requirements.lock.txt`, to which the README's build paragraph will point. It was never published, so nothing breaks. It lands with the packaging metadata. (5) Fetched files are reused across corpus versions only in the stable tier and only on a SHA-256 match with the new version's manifest, copied with their metadata and marked as reused; live files are never reused, so an upgrade brings current data. Measured on the current fetch list: 22 of the 61 normal entries are stable, about 10 KB in all, and the other 39 are about 12.5 MB, so the saving is 22 requests per upgrade, a courtesy to CelesTrak rather than a gain in speed. Upstream drift is caught by the site's weekly check of the stable sources, not by a user's upgrade. It lands in the fetch code at a later stage. (6) The wheel is built by a staging script whose only input is a public export folder: it refuses a folder that holds any provider file or lacks `EXPORT-MANIFEST.txt`, walks the `gpconf` package recursively, copies the shipped corpus files into `gpconf/corpus/`, builds with plain setuptools package data and audits the wheel, every corpus file of which must match the export manifest's SHA-256. Rejected: hatchling's force-include, which maps whole folders, so a build run from the private tree would sweep in provider files, prevented only by procedure; and moving the data into `gpconf/` in the repository, which would break every published path, including the site's links and the Zenodo archives. Found while answering it: `pyproject.toml`'s `packages = ["gpconf"]` has omitted `gpconf/adapters` since D-151 and would have dropped it from a wheel, the allowlist fault of D-151 in another file; it is fixed with the staging script, at the packaging stage. The plan note records all six and the new open items.

**D-154 (2026-09-26) — v0.3.0 packaging, stage 3: the Node presets `satellite.js`, `tle.js` and `tle.js-api`, run from the working directory through `node --eval`, with a preflight that refuses a missing Node or library as a setup error, and `--module PATH`. No published result changed.** Resolution, tested before building on 2026-09-26 with Node 26.5.0 and satellite.js 7.1.0 and tle.js 5.0.3 installed in a scratch project: a harness file outside the user's project cannot import the library by bare name, even when run from inside the project (`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`), which the plan had only inferred; `createRequire`, which the plan proposed, is the wrong tool, since satellite.js 7.1.0 exports only an `import` condition, which `require` resolution does not take; code passed to `node --input-type=module --eval` resolves bare imports from the working directory, like a script in the project, and `import.meta.resolve` there gives the entry file. So each preset runs its harness as `node --input-type=module --eval <source> -- <arguments>` with the working directory as its current directory, and `--module PATH` (the environment variable `GPCONF_NODE_MODULE` inside the harness) names the library's entry file for a checkout that cannot import itself by name. The harnesses moved into the package as `gpconf/adapters/satellitejs.mjs`, `tlejs.mjs` and `tlejs_vectors.mjs` from the hand runs (D-132, D-139); their parsing bodies are byte-identical to the hand runs' (compared with `diff`), and only how each finds its library and reads its arguments changed. `tle.js` passes `fields` and `tle.js-api` passes `api` to the one harness, and both use the vector-hook harness, as the hand run did (D-153). `gpconf/adapters/node_preflight.mjs` imports the library before any case runs and reports the Node version, the entry file and the library's version, read from the nearest `package.json` above the entry that names the library; a missing Node or a library the working directory cannot import is refused with exit 2 and a message naming the folder, the `npm install` command and `--module`, and saying that nothing ran and that this says nothing about the library (D-153). Without the preflight the command protocol would have turned a missing library into a parse failure in every case, charged to the library. The Python presets' refusal gained the same two statements. `CommandParser` takes an argument list besides a shell string: a list runs without a shell, in a given working directory with a given environment, and only an element that is exactly `{fmt}` is substituted, so the harness source passed as an argument is never altered. `gpconf presets` shows, for each Node preset, whether the library imports from the working directory, with its version and Node's; the JSON report's `preset` block adds the runtime. `PUBLIC_ALLOWLIST.txt` gains `gpconf/adapters/*.mjs`, the check D-151 asked for when adding files, here a new file type in an existing folder; `tests/test_export.py` now checks every file of the package, not only Python files. **D-157 (2026-09-26) — v0.3.0 packaging, stage 6: stable-tier files are reused across corpus versions on a hash match, as D-153 set it; live files are never reused; the fetch and the run report say which files were reused rather than fetched.** Where: only in the per-user cache, where each corpus version has its own folder (D-150); a data folder named by `--data` or `GPCONF_DATA`, or a clone, holds one set of files and is not searched. What: when `gpconf fetch` fills a version's folder, `gpconf/fetch.py` looks in the other version folders beside it, newest first, for each stable-tier entry the folder lacks, and reuses a copy only when its bytes hash to the SHA-256 this version's manifest records and its metadata is present; the file and its `.meta.json` are copied, the metadata keeping the original `retrieved_at`, so the two-hour rule and the provenance still describe the one request that was made, and gaining `reused_from` (the version and the source path) and `reused_at`. A stable file whose bytes differ, or one without metadata, is requested; a live file is requested even when its bytes match, so that an upgrade brings current data. How it reads: a dry run prints `REUSE <url> (stable tier: the copy in corpus <version>'s cache holds the bytes this version's manifest records; copied, not requested)` and sums up "a run would make N request(s), reuse M file(s) from an earlier corpus version's cache"; a run prints `reused from <version>` against each file and "done: N request(s) made, M file(s) reused from an earlier corpus version's cache"; the runner reads `reused_from` from each provider file's metadata, lists the reused files per case in the JSON report under `reused`, and prints below the count line "N provider file(s) were reused from corpus <version>'s cache rather than fetched: stable tier, bytes matching this version's recorded SHA-256". Measured on the current fetch list, as D-153 expected: of the 61 normal entries, 22 are stable and 39 live. Shown from a copy installed outside the repository with a scratch home, whose per-user cache held an earlier version's folder, `0.2.0`, filled with this repository's 61 fetched files: the dry run planned 22 reuses and 39 requests and wrote nothing; a real run with a stand-in in place of the request function, which copied the file this repository already holds so that no request was made, reused the 22 stable files, called the stand-in 39 times, and its drift check found all 61 files matching the tested snapshot; the run report then said that 22 provider files were reused from corpus 0.2.0's cache. Tests: `tests/test_fetch_reuse.py` (new, 7): the version folders found newest first and non-version folders ignored; a stable file with matching bytes and metadata reused, a live file with matching bytes requested, a stable file with other bytes requested, one without metadata requested; the dry run's lines and summary with no request and no folder created; a run copying and marking the reused file, keeping `retrieved_at`, and caching it on the next run; reuse not attempted outside a per-user cache; and, where this repository's provider files exist, 22 reused and 39 requested over the real fetch list and the run report naming the reused files.

**D-158 (2026-09-26) — v0.3.0 packaging, stage 7: the GitHub Action, `action.yml` with `tools/action_report.py`, built as D-153 set it; it runs the corpus from its own checkout at the tag a workflow names, not from PyPI; tested locally and then live on the owner's scratch repository, seven jobs on macOS, Ubuntu and Windows, all green, with the three platforms' summaries character-identical; the live test found one fault, fixed here: the runner's advice to fetch into the Action's data folder, which is thrown away with the job.** The owner's question first: the plan had the Action install gpconf from PyPI, which does not exist yet; can it be built and tested now, or should it wait for the package? It can be built now, and without PyPI at all. A composite action runs from GitHub's download of the whole repository at the tag the workflow names, found in `github.action_path`, and that checkout already holds the runner and the corpus at exactly that tag. So the Action runs `gpconf` from it: nothing is installed, the tag pins code and corpus together, no step needs a package index, and there is nothing to swap in at release. The plan's `pip install gpconf==<version>` is replaced (plan note, section 6). Rejected: waiting for PyPI (it tests nothing more, and adds a dependency and a version to keep in step with the tag); installing the built wheel inside the Action (it would need the wheel published somewhere the Action can reach). `action.yml` is a composite action with the inputs `preset` (required), `python` (default `python3`, the interpreter the maintainer's library is installed in), `module` (Node presets) and `working-directory` (where a Node preset resolves its library), and the outputs `report`, `failed` and `exercised`. Its one step runs `tools/action_report.py` with the inputs in the environment, never in the shell text, so an input cannot inject a command. The script runs `gpconf run --preset <name>` against the Action's checkout with an empty data folder and `GPCONF_DATA` removed, so it is offline whatever the job sets. Failed cases exit 0: a result never becomes a verdict in someone else's CI. A preset that cannot run exits 2, and the summary says "Setup error: nothing was run.", gives the runner's message, which ends "Nothing was run; this says nothing about <library>.", and adds that this is a problem with the job's setup, not a result about the library. Any other runner failure is passed on and summarised as not a result. The job summary carries the parser line with the library version found and tested, how many of the seventeen cases were exercised offline and how many need provider data, which the Action does not fetch, the case table, the gate line, and the site's sentence "A count is a result against that version on that date, not a verdict on the project.", with the site's address. No badge. Local test, the composite step's own command run by bash with GitHub's environment and a fresh public export as the action's folder: python-sgp4 2.27 exit 0 with 2 failed and 3 exercised; naive exit 0 with 4 failed; pyephem without PyEphem exit 2 with the setup message; tle.js from a Node project exit 0 with 2 failed; reference with `GPCONF_DATA` pointing at this repository's fetched files still 4 exercised and 13 needing provider data. Live test, 2026-09-26, as the owner instructed, on a scratch repository of the owner's that is none of the three in use: `hneogy/gpconf-action-test`, private, created empty in the browser pane on the owner's word after they had seen the form. It holds a public export of this working tree without the corpus's own CI workflow, and the workflow in `docs/handoff/action-scratch-test/`, whose jobs call the Action through the scratch repository's tag `gpconf-action-test-1`, as a maintainer would, so the tag pin is tested too. The tag was pushed before `main` and the workflow runs on `main` only, so there was one run (36249122884). A seventh job, `reference-ubuntu`, was added at the owner's word before the first push, so that one preset runs on all three platforms and macOS can be compared with Ubuntu case for case. All seven jobs passed; each Action step's exit code, read from its raw log: python-sgp4 (2.27, installed by the job) 0, with 2 failed and 3 exercised; naive 0, with 4 failed; pyephem without PyEphem 2, the summary opening "Setup error: nothing was run." and the job green only because it expects that failure; tle.js 5.0.3 in a Node 22 project 0, with 2 failed; reference on macos-26-arm64, ubuntu-24.04 and windows-2025-vs2026 0 each, with 4 passing and 13 needing provider data. The three reference summaries are character-identical, compared by a script over the run page rather than by eye: the seventeen case rows, the count line and the gate line. Windows, not run before: the composite step ran under Git Bash (`C:\Program Files\Git\bin\bash.EXE`) with the image's `python`, and the Action's folder as a Windows path (`D:\a\_actions\...`) worked in the shell text; the step took 2.9 s, against 0.7 s on macOS and 0.6 s on Ubuntu. The fault the live test found: the runner's plain output ended with its usual advice, "Provider data is not shipped with the corpus; fetch it with" a command naming `tools/fetch.py` in the Action's folder and `--data` with the Action's empty data folder, and every missing item in the JSON report, which is the Action's `report` output, carried the same command. In the Action that advice is wrong: the Action never fetches, and the folder is thrown away with the job; on Windows the command also named `python3` and quoted a Windows path the Unix way. It never reached the job summary. The fix: `gpconf run --no-fetch-hint` (new, in `--help`), `Runner(fetch_hints=False)` underneath, leaves the fetch command out of the closing line, out of each missing item, which now reads "not on disk: provider data is not shipped with the corpus", and out of the drift message, and changes nothing else; `tools/action_report.py` passes it. Rejected: an environment variable, which the command line in the log would not show; and leaving the log as it was because the summary was right, since the JSON report is an output a maintainer's later steps may read. Also seen, not acted on: the tle.js step took 10 s against under 1 s for the Python presets [inferred: Node starting once per call; not examined]; and every Ubuntu job carried GitHub's notice that `ubuntu-latest` moves to Ubuntu 26 from 2026-10-19, the open item already listed. The scratch repository and its run are kept (owner: delete nothing). `PUBLIC_ALLOWLIST.txt` gains `action.yml`; `tests/test_export.py` checks that it and its script are exported. README: a CI paragraph after the presets. Tests: `tests/test_action.py` (new, 12): the composite definition, inputs only through the environment, no fetch and no install, the outputs and no badge, and the script's behaviour for a passing preset, failed cases, an unknown preset and a missing library, a Node preset without its library, and offline whatever `GPCONF_DATA` says; and, for the fix, no fetch command in the Action's log, summary or JSON report with every status unchanged, the command still named by a run without the flag with the same case table, and the drift message a sentence either way. 237 tests pass in this repository: seven skipped under the system python3 (three need `GPCONF_TEST_NODE_PROJECT`, four need python-sgp4 or PyEphem), one under the repository's `.venv` with the scratch Node project set (PyEphem, not installed there); a fresh public export (201 files) runs 235 under the system python3 with 21 skipped, every Action test among those run.

The first build read the plan's words, "cut to 68 characters", as a cut at the end, which takes only the checksum digit and leaves every value readable; the owner had the cut moved mid-line, since a short line that still parses to correct values is not the garbage case, and input 1 already covers the acceptance of a malformed line. (3) The 0 in column 26 of line 1, the second fractional digit of the epoch, replaced by the letter O; a letter counts 0 in the checksum, as the 0 did, so the checksum stays valid and cannot catch it. (4) Line 2 removed, line 1 followed by the next set's name line. (5) A CSV that ends inside its last row's MEAN_MOTION_DOT value (-0.00000023 cut to -0.000000; MEAN_MOTION_DDOT and the line ending missing), and a JSON array with its closing bracket and line ending removed. Every TLE input sits between the two neighbours; the CSV holds them before the cut row, the JSON holds all three complete. Everything is rendered by the corpus from values in the public `expected.json` files, and the tool reads no provider file, so a public clone rebuilds the same bytes [tested: a test rebuilds them, and passes in a public export]. The TLE lines come from the renderer that reproduces CelesTrak's lines (304 of 304), checked against each record's frozen TLE fields, so for these three records the unedited lines equal CelesTrak's own: their values were already public in `expected.json`, and the files are assembled by the corpus, not provider responses. The CSV and JSON follow CelesTrak's column order and CRLF endings with the frozen values in plain decimal notation. The grading (kind `corrupt-input`, `Runner.run_corrupt_input`, six new checks): each file gives two items. The input's own check covers the corrupt record: refused with a reason passes, a record built from it with other values fails as misidentified, and a silent drop fails; read as the record it carries, it fails, except on input 1, where it is reported as "validates no checksum" (decision 2). `corrupt-input-neighbours-load` covers the valid records: they must load with their values. A parser that raises on a file has refused it as a whole, with the exception as its reason: for the two cut files that passes, the complete records given up reported as info (decision 3); for a TLE file it fails the neighbours item, since the valid sets are lost. The JSON, which has no corrupt record, passes on a whole-file refusal or on a refusal reported with a reason, and fails on silent partial loading. The counts ride on the input's item in the existing keys (expected, returned, loaded, misidentified, refused, refused_matched, dropped and the rest), and no new report shape was added. The shifted column stays held (decision 4). The control needed changes: as committed, the reference adapter failed its own case on four items. It raised on the whole file for line 2 cut short and for the letter, so the neighbours were given up. It passed over the orphan line 1 with nothing said. And its reader built a record from the cut CSV row, reading MEAN_MOTION_DOT as 0 and MEAN_MOTION_DDOT as None [tested, with HEAD's reader and adapter against the new runner]. Changed in `gpconf/reference.py`: a non-numeric TLE field is now a ValueError naming the field; a letter used to raise `decimal.InvalidOperation`, which the runner reported as an internal error of the corpus, a gap in D-117. `read_csv_text` now rejects a row whose field count differs from the header's. Rebuilding every case's `expected.json` with these readers changed no value and no hash [tested: the diff held only `generated_at` and check and coverage texts that the frozen files predate; those files were restored]. Changed in `gpconf/adapters/reference.py`: `tle_sets` reads TLE sets one at a time. It refuses a set the strict reader rejects, with the reader's reason, and refuses an orphan line 1 or line 2, so the sets after it load; a valid file gives exactly `read_tle_text`'s records [tested]. The adapter does not declare the refusal channel, since tests use its output as plain records; `tle_sets` sits after the class so that the lines `docs/ADAPTERS.md` quotes did not move. The three built-in adapters. The reference passes: input 1 is reported, inputs 2 to 4 are refused with the neighbours loaded, and both cut files are refused whole by the reader, the complete records given up counted. The naive adapter fails three items: it builds a record from line 2 one character short (mean motion 1.623733631, eccentricity 0.148004 and mean anomaly 45.3718, each read one column off), it raises on the whole file at the letter (float()) so the neighbours are lost, and it passes over the orphan line 1 without reporting a refusal; input 1 is reported, and both cut files are refused whole, which passes. python-sgp4 2.27 through its built-in adapter: a finding was recorded, kept in `docs/handoff/corrupt-input/` under the D-134 convention. For that adapter the orphan's outcome is the adapter's own line pairing, not the library's, since python-sgp4 reads one set at a time. Other changes. `tools/cases.py` gains the six checks and the case, placed after `tle-writer-alpha5` so that no case number moves (the writer's "must stay last" comment now says what it means). `tools/make_expected.py` gains `build_corrupt_input`, and `meta_for` keeps a provenance record's own provenance. `tools/make_manifest.py` gains the interpretation text, with no library findings. `manifest.json`, `MANIFEST.md` and `fixtures/corrupt-input/` were regenerated; the other `case.md` files came out byte-identical. CI's two offline runs gain the case. Tests: `tests/test_corrupt_input.py`, 20 tests: the files match their provenance and are rebuilt byte for byte; each TLE input is one stated edit of the clean rendering; the control and the naive adapter are checked per file; each rule is checked with a parser written for it; the reader changes are checked. In `test_runner`, the offline list and the naive adapter's must-fail list gain the case. `test_action` and `test_install_layout` now expect the count lines the Action and the CLI print from the manifest: 5 of 18 cases exercised offline, 18 cases. Suites: 277 tests OK (7 skipped) under Python 3.14; 277 OK (4 skipped) in the virtual environment with python-sgp4; 275 OK (21 skipped) in a public export [tested, exit codes checked]. Not done here: the count change across the README, the site, `CITATION.cff` and the release notes; FAILURES.md, which would gain the case's row; the version constants; the Batch G re-runs. Alternatives: line 2 cut at its end, the plan's wording read literally and the first build (replaced on the owner's instruction, as above); the reference adapter refusing whole TLE files (rejected: the plan requires the neighbours to load); declaring the refusal channel in the reference adapter (not needed: it refuses rather than drops).

**D-172 (2026-09-27) — A local path removed from three test-shim docstrings, and a test that fails on any absolute home path in an exported file (owner instruction); the fix is forward only, since the path stays in what v0.3.0 published.** Line 2 of the docstrings of `tests/adapters/reference.py`, `naive.py` and `sgp4_adapter.py` should read `--adapter tests.adapters.reference:Parser` (and `naive:Parser`, `sgp4_adapter:Parser`). Instead it read `--adapter tests.adapters.`, then the absolute path of the owner's working copy (the macOS home folder of the owner's user name and the Dropbox folders under it down to the repository), then `referencearser`. The cause: the files were written through a zsh shell in commit 5d67cd8 (v0.3.0 stage 2, D-151), where `$name:Parser` applies the `:P` (realpath) modifier to `$name` and leaves `arser`. `CLAUDE.md` already says to write `${a}:Parser` and never `$a:Parser`; the rule existed and did not stop this, so the guard is now a test. In `tests/test_export.py`, `test_no_absolute_home_path_in_any_exported_file` reads every file of a fresh export, whatever its type, for an absolute home path of any user, in the three shapes: macOS and Linux (`/U…/<name>`, `/h…/<name>`, root's home), and Windows with a drive letter and backslashes, escaped backslashes or forward slashes. A path joined to a word character, as in a URL or a relative path, does not count. `test_the_home_path_guard_knows_every_shape` checks the pattern against a sample of each shape, including the one this leak had (after a dot), and against four strings it must not take for home paths. The one allowed path is the fixture of `tests/test_install_layout.py`, the macOS home of a user named u, allowed by file and path together. The pattern is spelt with character classes and the samples are assembled at run time, so that the test file does not match itself. Before the docstrings were fixed the test failed on exactly the three shims and nothing else [tested]. The fix is not retroactive. The path is in the v0.3.0 tag (tag object f3a7387 on 627f66f), and so in the source archives GitHub serves for the v0.3.0 release and in the v0.3.0 Zenodo archive, record 22986178, whose one file, `gp-omm-conformance-v0.3.0.zip`, is GitHub's archive of the tag [inferred from its source; the tag's tree carries the three files, tested with `git grep` on the tag]. It is also in public main's history. None of these is rewritten: tags and published history are not rewritten here, and the files of a published Zenodo version cannot be replaced. The PyPI files do not carry it: the wheel and the sdist of gpconf 0.3.0 contain no `tests/` files and no such path [tested on the local copies, whose SHA-256 equal PyPI's, 74611c02… and 21983403…]; the owner's instruction had listed them among the places, and the check found them clean. v0.2.1 and every earlier tag predate 5d67cd8 and are clean [tested: `git grep` on v0.2.1]. What leaked is a user name and a folder layout, nothing sensitive: no credential, no token, no data. So the answer is to fix forward, in the next export and in the next release's archives, rather than yank or re-release v0.3.0. A yank would withdraw a release whose files on PyPI are clean, and would remove nothing from the tag or from Zenodo. Alternatives: yanking or re-releasing v0.3.0 (rejected, as above); rewriting the tag or main's history (rejected: published history is not rewritten); a check for this one path, or for the owner's user name alone (rejected: the guard has to catch the class, any user's home path in any of the three shapes); relying on the `CLAUDE.md` rule alone (rejected: it existed).

**D-175 (2026-09-27) — The corrupt-input case compares every record a parser returns from an input with the same parser's reading of the same records unedited, three files that now ship beside the inputs, instead of with the frozen expected values (owner instruction, after the first library run of round two, D-174); PyEphem's row re-stated under it.** What the item was measuring: `corrupt-input-neighbours-load` was meant to ask whether a corrupt input leaves the records around it alone, the question of resynchronisation. It compared each of those records with the frozen expected values as the values check compares them, binary floats within a relative 1e-12 and every core field present, so it asked two questions at once: whether the corrupt input changed the records, and whether the parser reads these records exactly at all. For a parser that fails the values check on 25544 or 20453 anywhere, the second question answered for the first: the item failed in all four TLE files whatever the parser did with the corrupt input, and the report counted records the corrupt input had not touched as misidentified, built from garbage. The same comparison sorted the corrupt record itself into "read as unedited" and "built from garbage", so a parser that validates no checksum and reads imprecisely would have had input 1 failed as garbage where owner decision 2 says to report it (shown with a probe, below). Why it looked right: the three built-in adapters read these records exactly or within the tolerance, so on every run before the first library the two questions gave the same answer. PyEphem 4.2.1 keeps seven fields in single precision and no second derivative (round one's findings, which every values item already reports); it reads both neighbours in every file exactly as it reads them with no corrupt input between them [tested], and the item failed four times. The same class as the reverse collapse D-144 found, where per-file checks passed on an empty output once an adapter could refuse the only record in a file: a check whose verdict rested on something other than its question, and which looked right until something ran against it. There a pass was earned by absence; here a fail was earned by a different question. The change: `tools/derive_corrupt_inputs.py` writes three unedited files beside the inputs, `derived/corrupt-input/unedited-sets.tle` for inputs 1 to 4, `unedited-rows.csv` with input 5's last row whole and `unedited-array.json` closed, provenance `derived`, each input being its unedited file with its one edit made (a test checks it byte for byte); the six inputs are unchanged, byte for byte. `expected.json` lists the three as sources, nine in all, names each input's unedited file, and keeps the records' expected values for reference, saying that this case no longer grades against them. The runner reads each unedited file once and compares every record returned from an input with that reading, exactly, so any difference is the edit's doing. A record the parser does not return from the unedited file either is not graded; an input whose unedited file the parser refuses as a whole is not exercised; and a record beyond the expected ones counts as built from garbage only when the unedited reading lacks it too; so nothing a parser does to these records anyway is blamed on the edit. How exactly a parser reads them stays the values check's question, asked in the records' own cases, `epoch-year-19xx` and `bstar-and-derivative-forms`. The case is unreleased, so no released check semantics change; v0.4.0 ships it with the comparison. What moved [tested, item by item against the earlier runs]: every status of the three built-in adapters stays, except that python-sgp4's four neighbours items move from pass within tolerance to exact pass, since the comparison is now with its own reading; texts that named expected values now name the unedited reading; `docs/FAILURES.md` changes in three such texts and its timestamp, and its failing counts (naive 15 of 18, python-sgp4 8 of 18) do not move. PyEphem 4.2.1's row re-stated: 7 of 18, as under D-174; the four neighbours items move from fail to pass, no other item changes status, and the gate is identical; the detail is in the handoff note. An adapter with PyEphem's precision over the reference readers, so that it handles every corrupt input exactly as the reference does, failed five items under the old comparison, input 1 among them, and passes under the new one with the reference's items [tested: a probe kept in `docs/handoff/corrupt-input/`]. Also changed: the case's check texts, evidence basis and coverage, its interpretation in the manifest, the README's case row and the changelog's entry say what is compared; `manifest.json`, `MANIFEST.md` and the case's `case.md` regenerated; `tests/test_corrupt_input.py` gains six tests: the unedited files against the inputs, the precision adapter passing where the values check fails it, a neighbour the corrupt input changes failing, a parser that cannot read the unedited file not exercised, a record it does not return unedited not graded, and a record it returns unedited too not blamed on the edit. Suites: 287 tests OK with PyEphem installed (6 skipped), with python-sgp4 installed (6 skipped) and with neither (9 skipped); CI's two offline commands exit 0 and 1 as before; an export would copy 228 files, six more than before [tested, exit codes checked]. Alternatives: comparing at each field's printed resolution (rejected: PyEphem's missing second derivative still fails it, and a parser that keeps one field with fewer digits than the TLE prints would fail on precision again); keeping the expected values and exempting the fields a parser fails in the values check (rejected: it ties this case to other cases' results and to provider data a pip-installed runner may not have); undoing each edit at run time instead of shipping the unedited files (rejected: the runner would need each edit's inverse, where a file on disk can be read and pinned by its hash); falling back to the expected values where a parser does not return a record unedited (rejected: it brings the conflation back for exactly the parsers it would serve).
