**D-194 (2026-09-28) — v0.5.0 planned, not built (owner decisions): one release, holding reproducible package builds, an "unsupported" answer for vector hooks run by command, and the gate's counts, in that order; and a finding settled: the gate's outcomes had two definitions, shipped together in v0.3.0 and v0.4.0, and v0.5.0 makes the one that splits the records authoritative.** The finding: the README's gate section ("records are counted as loaded ..., misidentified ... or dropped (no record came back)") and `gpconf/gates.py`'s docstring (D-142: "Per record and format there are four outcomes ... dropped (no record and no refusal)") define one outcome per expected record, and every gate line published on the corpus's site follows them; `docs/ADAPTERS.md` (D-161: "A record returned with the wrong catalog number is counted twice, as a misidentified record and as a dropped expected one: an adapter that returns 0 for every Alpha-5 field of a 256-record file shows 256 misidentified and 256 dropped") and the runner's comment over the counts define `dropped` per expected id, so a record returned under a wrong id counts twice, and the runner's arithmetic and headline follow that [tested: the texts at both tags]. On the v0.4.0 hand runs that doubles 256 records for four libraries and 1 for a fifth [tested: each run's `gates`]. The split is authoritative, not to be reopened: it answers the gate's own question, one outcome per object, where the double count sums to more objects than there are; it is what three of the four published descriptions and every published gate line already say, so nothing published moves; the adapter guide's sentence described the code after it was written, while gates.py's docstring is the definition the gate was designed to; and nothing is lost, the per-id count staying in the report under its own name. v0.5.0 therefore gives `dropped` the split meaning (the expected records with no record returned at all and no refusal), keeps today's count as `ids_not_returned`, prints the headline from the split, and withdraws the adapter guide's sentence quoted above; changing `dropped`'s value for parsers that misidentify stays within a minor release, since the gate is a headline and never a check and no `expected.json` schema changes. The other two items: `tools/stage_package.py` takes `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` (the tag's commit time), stamps the staged files with it and fixed modes, and passes it to the build, normalising the sdist if two builds still differ, verified by two builds giving identical SHA-256s [untested until built]; a vectors command may answer `{"unsupported": "<reason>"}`, which skips that hook's item as a missing Python hook does, an additive protocol change (a minor version under the README's rule), chosen over exit 3 because a non-zero exit already means a rejection there. The vector change moves only items of runs that pass a vectors command, those of three hand-run libraries, and no case count [tested: the round-two reports]. One release, because the vector change needs a minor version anyway, the gate fix fits it, the build change takes effect only when a release is built, and none of the three moves a published case count or site figure. The plan is in the private handoff (`docs/handoff/v0.5.0-plan.md`). Alternatives: the double count authoritative (not taken: it would move the README, gates.py, the site's definitions and a published line, and it cannot be read as an answer to the gate's question); keeping `dropped` as the adapter guide documents it and adding a split count beside it (not taken: two meanings of one word, one in the headline and one in the JSON); three releases (not taken: three checklists for no change a reader would see between them).

**D-198 (2026-10-01) — PyEphem #297 closed as completed by its maintainer at 2026-10-01T12:14:28Z, with no change to `readtle()`, open to comment and to reopening; his suggestion, to call Vallado's C++ directly rather than through python-sgp4, which carries small backwards-compatibility tweaks of its own, becomes the specification of the Vallado harness in the v0.5.0 plan (owner); the README line of D-197 stands either way (owner).** The closing comment (https://github.com/brandon-rhodes/pyephem/issues/297#issuecomment-5931180707; the closure at the same second, `state_reason` completed, the issue not locked [tested: GitHub's API]) says, in order: thanks for the context; that we should see if we can call Vallado's C++ directly, perhaps through a simple C compatibility tool that reads and writes the struct, because python-sgp4 makes a few small tweaks of its own that were necessary for backwards compatibility for its user base, so that calling Vallado ourselves would be an independent data point on how the reference library behaves; that since neither side has seen the letter in the wild, and PyEphem is a legacy library he is trying not to add code to, he closes the issue for now; and that further thoughts are welcome as comments, with reopening later if a future situation warrants adding input validation where, historically, there has been none. What this changes in the record: the D-197 Vallado finding was made on python-sgp4's copy of `SGP4.cpp`, which the maintainer now says is not Vallado's code untouched. python-sgp4's own history shows one change to the line-1 `sscanf` of `twoline2rv`, Vallado's `%5ld` to `%5s` for Alpha-5, and nothing else in that function's parsing [tested: `git log -p` on the file], so the tweaks he means are elsewhere in the file or in the initial copy, unknown until the archive is fetched; the handoff's open question on byte-identity is answered in part (not identical) and narrowed to which lines. The v0.5.0 plan takes the suggestion as the harness's specification: fetch the archive linked from celestrak.org/publications/AIAA/2006-6753/ (one CelesTrak request, on the owner's word), compile its `twoline2rv` behind a harness of the corpus's own that fills and reads the `elsetrec` directly, as `batch-g/vallado/harness.cpp` already does against python-sgp4's copy, and run the cases through a recipe in `harnesses/`, as libsgp4's; the data point is independent of python-sgp4 only when the archive's code is what runs. **D-205 (2026-10-02) — v0.5.0 item 2, the runner side (owner instruction): a vectors command may answer `{"unsupported": "<reason>"}` and a Python hook may raise `gpconf.runner.Unsupported`, and the hook's item then skips with the reason, as it does for an adapter without the hook; an operation is unsupported for all of its vectors or none, and a mix fails the item; any non-zero exit of a vectors command stays a rejection, exit 3 included; an unsupported answer without a reason is malformed. Built and tested, not committed; the three shipped vector harnesses do not yet give the answer, and their adoption and re-runs are the next step, on the owner's word.** Why JSON and not exit 3: in the vectors protocol any non-zero exit already means a rejection, so giving 3 a meaning would turn existing adapters' rejections into skips, while the JSON answer was malformed before (it failed under D-118) and so changes no valid answer's meaning; a test exits 3 with the unsupported answer and is still rejected. Additive under the README's rule: every existing answer keeps its meaning, a harness that does not adopt the answer gets today's results, and the three built-in Python adapters raise nothing new [tested: 305 tests OK, 7 skipped, the tests that pin the built-in adapters' results among them]. The change, in `gpconf/runner.py`: `CommandParser._vec` reads the exit code first, then `unsupported` (a non-empty string, else the answer is malformed), then `error`, then `result`; `run_vectors` wraps each hook in `_HookCalls`, which counts the vectors the hook declares unsupported, the valid-vector loops pass over such a vector, and `_vector_item` writes the item: skip with "parser reports <hook> unsupported: <reason>" when every vector was declared unsupported, fail with the count when only some were, else pass or fail on the vectors as before; the skip for a missing hook is unchanged. Why all or none: a library has the operation or not, and an adapter answering unsupported for the vectors it cannot handle and results for the rest would hide failures behind a skip. `docs/ADAPTERS.md`: the protocol paragraph rewritten and a note under the hooks table; its tle.js sentence still says `alpha5_encode` answers an error and the item fails, true of the shipped harness until the next step rewords it with the harness. Tests, ten in `tests/test_vector_unsupported.py`: the Python raise skips the item with the reason and the case passes; a partial declaration fails with the count; an empty reason skips with "no reason given"; any other raise still fails its vector (D-118); an adapter without the hook skips as before; the command answer raises `Unsupported` with the reason; exits 1, 2 and 3 are rejections whatever the answer says; an empty or non-string reason is malformed; error, result and empty answers keep their meaning; end to end through `--vectors-cmd`, a command lacking two operations skips their two items and passes the other three. What moves when the harnesses adopt it, from the plan's table of the round-two reports: tle.js's `alpha5-encode`, `ccsds-epoch-strings` and `catalog-number-is-integer` items and libsgp4's and astroz's `alpha5-encode` from fail to skip, no case count and no site figure. Noticed, not changed: a ResourceWarning for an unclosed `manifest.json` handle at `runner.py:439` under verbose test runs, older than this change.

**D-217 (2026-10-03) — The second audit, decided (owner): a narrow audit by a named human, not yet; the grader first, the answer key second, a sample of the hand-run recipes third, with the live-tier limit stated in the audit's own scope; sought as two small asks rather than one large one. It answers the validation half of JOSS's required assertion and not the design-decisions half.** Where things stand: `AUDIT.md` covered v0.1.0 and was performed by a separate AI session, not a human, as the README says; nothing since has been separately audited. Since that release the code under `gpconf/`, `tools/` and `tests/` has changed by about 8,900 lines and the fixtures by about 28,000, with two cases added [tested: `git diff --shortstat v0.1.0` on the public repository, 2026-10-03]. What the audit covers, in this order. (1) The grader: the runner's judgement of a parser, that is the fail-closed rule, the tolerances, the refusal channel, the gate's counts and the unsupported answer, read and attacked with deliberately wrong parsers. It comes first because most of the code written since v0.1.0 is there, the first audit recomputed values and looked least at it, and the fixes of v0.2.1 were all cases of the corpus reporting a success it had not earned. (2) The answer key: the expected values of the cases added or regenerated since v0.1.0, recomputed with a reader that is not the corpus's. (3) A sample of the recipes: two or three of the hand-run libraries rebuilt from their recipes and run, since those results name other projects. Out of scope: the site, the prose, the decision log. The live-tier limit, stated in the audit's scope and not left for the auditor to discover: the live-tier expected values were frozen from provider responses of 2026-09-21 that the corpus does not redistribute, so an outside auditor can re-fetch and hash-check the stable-tier sources but cannot recompute the live-tier values unless shown those bytes; the audit is scoped to the stable and derived data unless that is first settled with the provider. Shape: a named human with standing in the field, the report published under their name; two small asks to two people (recompute a set of stable records with a reader of your own; try to make a wrong parser pass) rather than a week asked of one. Not yet: the surface moved five releases in two weeks, an audit should be of the release it will be cited for, and a reviewer is more likely to come from use than from a cold request. What it answers and what it does not: JOSS requires a submitting author to assert that human authors "reviewed, edited, validated all AI-assisted outputs and made the core design decisions"; an independent human audit is the strongest answer to the validation half, and is the engagement beyond the author that JOSS's single-author check looks for; it does nothing for the design-decisions half, which is a fact about the past that only a reading of the record settles. A further AI audit is worth running before a release as hygiene, and is not this. Alternatives: an audit of every surface (not taken: two to three weeks of a reviewer's time by estimate, most of it of low value); a second AI audit presented as the answer (not taken: it adds nothing outside the project); an audit now, of v0.5.0 (not taken: stale by the time it matters). Nothing is asked of anyone by this entry: the owner makes the asks.

**D-218 (2026-10-03) — Reversal of one choice in D-216: the Vallado harness no longer reports the reader's error flag as a refusal. The flag is carried in the record as `_error`, with a note on standard error; the `sgp4` preset, which ignores the same flag from python-sgp4, was right, and the open question is closed (owner ruling on the agent's analysis).** What the flag is [tested: source read at the pin]: `satrec.error` is the propagation model's return code on the elements. `SGP4.cpp` documents it in the headers of `sgp4init()` and `sgp4()` ("return code - non-zero on error", codes 1 to 6) and not in `twoline2rv()`'s, whose one documented output is the structure; `twoline2rv()` resets it at its top, and it is set when `sgp4init()` runs `sgp4()` at time 0. python-sgp4 documents its attribute as the "Error code (1-6) documented in sgp4()". Why it is not the reader's refusal [tested: a probe on the reader, with the caller's structure in three states]: for the corrupt-input case's line 1 with no line 2 after it, the flag is 2 when the structure starts zeroed, as the harness's does, and 0 when it does not, while the reader does the same thing each time and reports nothing. So the refusal D-216's harness reported was made by the harness's own zeroed structure, and the item it passed credited the reader with a check it does not make. A refusal in this corpus is the reader declining its input: an exception, or the reader's own return, as Gpredict's is (D-178); a propagator's status that depends on what the caller's memory held is a value. **D-223 (2026-10-03) — The finding of D-179 reported to gods-eye-view as issue #906, on the owner's word; the owner's hold of 2026-09-27 on it lifted.** The hold was until #751 or pull request #767 closed, a third thread on that repository the same day being too much. The finding, which this log can now state: the application's TLE reader takes a group in fixed steps of three lines, so one set that is missing a line puts every later set out of step and each is skipped; the rest of the group is dropped, and nothing reports it. Eight sets with the second one's line 2 removed give one entry where the whole text gives eight [tested: the report's own reproduction, run on a clean checkout of v0.2.1 before filing]; the corpus's missing-line file followed by five more sets leaves one catalog entry where the unedited text leaves eight, the layer logs the group as loaded with one satellite, and the application's `next_satellite_pass` tool says that a satellite which is in the text is not in the group [tested: the recipe's harness and a probe at v0.2.1, D-221; first at ce671ce, D-179]. The loop is `src/sources/tle.js:12` since v0.2.0; its own test covers a broken block of three lines, which keeps the step. The text: under the outreach convention, through the repository's bug form, which is the only way in and has seven required fields; the title keeps the form's "bug: " prefix (owner). Two changes by the owner to the draft: the field that asks for the setup check's output says it will be run and pasted if wanted, where the draft only declined; and one sentence offers a patch. The owner's reason for the second: the convention's stop at the number is for a first report to a stranger, and this repository already holds the owner's pull request and a confirmed issue. The report names the corpus's corrupt-input case and nothing of its counts; its element lines are the application's own test fixture with the catalog number varied. Not a duplicate [tested: the application's known-issues document and searches of its tracker, before filing]. Filed 2026-10-03T22:37:39Z from the owner's account: https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view/issues/906, labelled `bug` by the form; the stored title and all seven fields equal the final form [tested: the API]. D-179 and D-221 take the link in place, the one edit the Batch G convention allows. **D-228 (2026-10-03) — v0.5.1, first of its items: the fetch stops at the first response its list does not expect, a refusal above all; such a response is kept beside the data and is never read as data; and after a refusal no request is made for two hours (owner instruction, the two additions approved with it).** Found on 2026-10-03, when the corpus's description of its own fetch was checked against the code. What was wrong, in two parts. First, the fetch list's `allow_error` flag sat on 21 of its 64 entries, 18 of them in a user's run of 61, and let any HTTP error pass on them: the 404 it was written for, and equally a 403, a 5xx or a refused redirect. Six of the 21 are recorded as answering 404; the other fifteen answered 200 when captured. CelesTrak's usage policy asks machine-to-machine software to stop querying on any response that is not an HTTP 200 and to have a person look, and its GP formats page says a 403 or 404 will not change by repeating the request (as recorded in `docs/RESEARCH.md` §3 and §11.1; neither page was re-read for this entry). Second, a response the fetch did not expect was written to the data path itself, "so it is never re-requested", and the runner then read it as provider data: with a stand-in refusal page in place of `analyst.csv` the reference adapter failed the case, "reference reader found 0 of 565 expected records" [tested 2026-10-03 with a stand-in page, no request made], a failure charged to whatever parser was under test. What changed. (1) `allow_error` is gone; an entry recorded as answering 404 carries `"expect_status": 404`, and a test holds the list to the manifest. The run goes on past a response only when it is an HTTP 200 that is neither an HTML page nor empty, or the expected 404 with the provider's no-data text (`No GP data found`, `No SupGP data found`). Anything else ends the run at once with exit status 2: a 403 or 429 on any entry, a 404 where data is expected, a 404 with another body, a redirect, a 5xx, a 2xx that is not 200. Nothing is retried and no further request is made. A network failure still exits 3 and keeps nothing. (2) The response is kept as `<file>.unexpected`, with its metadata as `<file>.unexpected.meta.json`, beside the data and never in its place; if the file was already on disk, a refused refresh leaves the earlier data standing. The fetch treats the URL as answered: a later run does not ask again, short of `--force` two hours or more after that answer, and an expected answer then removes the kept one. (3) After a refusal, HTTP 403 or 429, no request at all is made for two hours, with or without `--force`, and the dry run says the same; without this each re-run would ask the next URL of the list and collect one more refusal. A kept response is the only record this needs: no marker file. (4) The runner reports a file whose last answer was kept this way as `not-fetched`, with the status and time the fetch recorded and no fetch command, since a plain fetch does not ask again; the case's JSON carries it under `unexpected`, and a line under the count line says how many files are missing for that reason. It also refuses to read a response that a fetch before this change saved in the data's place: a provider file whose metadata records a status other than 200 and other than the one the manifest records for it is `not-fetched`, not parsed. The recorded 404 bodies are untouched by all of this: they are the empty answers the corpus hands to a parser (D-143). The stop message says what to do: on a refusal, read the kept response, which says why; otherwise report it to the corpus, since the list may be out of date. Consequences accepted: thirteen entries of a user's run that answered 200 at the capture lose their tolerance, so an endpoint whose answer changes for good stops each user's run once at that URL until a release updates the list; that is the policy's stop-and-report working as meant. The fetch's metadata now names `tools/fetch.py v3`. Alternatives: keeping the flag and narrowing it to 404 (rejected: a 404 with another body, or on an entry that expects data, is still not the answer the list knows); leaving unexpected responses on the data path with a marker in their metadata (rejected: a file whose metadata is lost would be read as data again); a marker file for the two quiet hours (not needed: the kept response records the status and the time). Not changed: which URLs are requested, the pause, the two-hour rule for `--force`, re-captures, stable-tier reuse, the drift check, any case, check or expected value. Tests (`tests/test_fetch_stop.py`, 21, the real request function against a stand-in opener with socket creation blocked): the known 404 passes; a 403 stops the run on a strict entry and on one that expects a 404; a 404 with another body, a 404 where data is expected, a 500, a redirect, a 204, an HTML page and an empty body under 200 each stop it; no answer exits 3; the kept response is not asked again, is with `--force` after two hours, and a good answer clears it; a refused refresh keeps the earlier data; two quiet hours hold for every form of the command and end on time; a 429 is a refusal and a 500 is not; the list agrees with the manifest; the runner reports a kept response and an old in-place one as `not-fetched`, never as a failure, and still reads the recorded 404. Suite 331 OK. Not covered by a test: a real refusal from CelesTrak, which no test may provoke.

**D-229 (2026-10-03) — v0.5.1, second item: the ten launch-window requests leave the fetch; a provider file that no fetch requests is reported as `not-available`; and wherever the corpus states a count it now says the count was measured with launch-window files that a new user's fetch cannot obtain (owner instruction; no library is re-run).** What was wrong. The fetch list asked for the Starlink G15-27 post-deployment file in five formats and for the launch nominal 799501621 in five, and stopped the run on an error from nine of the ten. The corpus's own case documents call both perishable ("nominals exist only for roughly 5-8 days after a launch", "this post-deployment file is replaced after cataloguing"), and the site's tracker counted 27 nine-digit ids in the Starlink supplemental file up to 2026-09-24 and none on 2026-09-25 [tested: the tracker's history]. So a fetch built on those requests stops for every user once the window has closed. Whether the ten still answer was not tested, on the owner's ruling: the fetch is to stop depending on the answer. Nor had anything shown it: no first-time fetch had been made since the captures of 2026-09-21, the release checks running offline [the three release checklists; the fetch tests stand a stub in for the request]. What changed. (1) The ten entries carry `"launch_window": "Starlink G15-27, launched 2026-09-20"` and stay in the list as the record of the corpus's own captures. No run plans one, under any flag, and each run says so in a line. A user's run is 51 requests and 12,511,746 bytes, with four expected 404s; a later corpus version requests 29, the 22 stable files being copied. A capture that is on disk, as in the maintainer's clone, is still compared with the manifest. (2) The runner learns those ten paths from the fetch list, which ships with the corpus, and reports a missing one as `source-present: not-available`, naming the launch and giving no fetch command. `not-fetched` would send the user to a fetch that does not bring the file, and `not-exercised` is kept for data that was read and lacked the feature (D-148). A case takes the status when none of its provider files can come from a fetch; it ranks below `not-fetched`, so a case with anything left to fetch says that. The table gains an `n/a` column, the count line "N not available", the JSON counts a `not-available` key, and the Action's summary the same count. Below the count line the runner names the case that cannot run and the cases judged on their other files, and says that published counts were measured with those files. A file that an earlier fetch saved in a capture's place, the provider's no-data answer once the window had closed, is `not-available` too and is not read. (3) Which cases, in the public copy: `supgp-celestrak-classification-c` names all five of its provider files among the ten and cannot run from a fetch at all; `nine-digit-supgp-launch-nominals` names five of six and runs on the full Starlink supplemental file alone, where its nine-digit check says `not-exercised` outside a launch window and the others (values, integer ids, classification C, the extra columns) still run; `csv-json-omitted-mandatory-fields` and `omm-xml-schema` name two each and run on the rest. `mean-motion-derivative-convention` and `tle-vs-omm-precision-loss` list the post-deployment pair among their sources but open it only on the maintainer's copy, the supplemental pair being withheld from the public one (D-049). What is lost to a user: a supplemental record in five formats, with element set 0, the 72000-series ids and the TLE epoch of a SupGP record, and a nine-digit id in JSON, XML and KVN. (4) The published counts. Every count the corpus has published was measured on the maintainer's copy, captures included. For the built-in presets a run from a user's fetch shows 16 cases passing for the reference adapter where 17 are published, 14 failing for the naive adapter where 15 are, and 6 for python-sgp4 where 8 are [tested 2026-10-03, in the maintainer's tree and in an export alike, against a stand-in for a user's data folder: every provider file but the ten captures and the three re-captures; the full Starlink file with and without its nine-digit rows gives the same three counts]. No hand-run library was run again (owner). For six of the eight hand-run rows the failing cases include `supgp-celestrak-classification-c` [the kept reports], so a fresh fetch reproduces at least one case fewer for each; tle.js's row does not include it, and SatDump's row is still the first-round one. In place of re-runs, one sentence stands wherever a count appears: the README, `docs/FAILURES.md`, the recipes' index and each recipe's README, and the runner's own output; the site's pages follow under their own decision. A finding made on the way, about the counts and not about this change: a reader that takes no row of CelesTrak's supplemental CSV fails the two pair cases on the maintainer's copy and passes them in the public copy on the same data, because the item that fails is the supplemental pair's own file, which the public copy does not open [tested with a stand-in reader: five failing cases against three]. libsgp4's published count holds two cases of that kind, and SatDump master's second-round count two [the kept reports], so those four were never reproducible from the public corpus, with or without the captures. Not changed by this entry: any case, check or expected value, and any published count; the generated `MANIFEST.md` and `case.md` files, whose sources in `tools/cases.py` now state the above, are regenerated with the release. Alternatives: keeping `not-fetched` and changing only its sentences (rejected: the count line would go on saying a case needs fetched data that no fetch brings, the kind of unearned status D-148 removed); a flag that asks for the ten again (rejected: they belong to one launch); giving the supplemental cases a source that is always served (not in a patch: it changes a case's sources, needs new captures and a re-run of every library; a candidate for a later version). Tests: `tests/test_not_available.py`, 13: the list, the plans and the runs never hold a capture; the status, its rank, the count line and the absence of a fetch command; a copy without the fetch list falls back to `not-fetched`; an old in-place answer is not read. Existing tests moved with the counts: 51 planned requests, 22 reused and 29 requested on a later version, 12 cases needing data and one not available before a fetch, 16 passing after one, and 17 with the maintainer's captures. Suite 345 OK in the maintainer's tree and 343 OK in an export.

**D-230 (2026-10-03) — v0.5.1, third item: the README's "Fetching responsibly", the fetch's help text and the quick-start comments no longer present the two-second pause as CelesTrak's policy, and the CSV default is said of the queries it belongs to (owner instruction).** What was wrong. The section opened "`tools/fetch.py` follows CelesTrak's published usage policy" and listed "2 s between requests" under it. The fetch's docstring, which `gpconf fetch --help` prints, put "requests are sequential with a fixed pause between them" under "Rules (CelesTrak usage policy …)". The quick-start comments said "~60 requests, ~12.6 MB, 2 s apart". CelesTrak's pages, as the corpus records them (`docs/RESEARCH.md` §3 and §11.1; not re-read for this entry), give a cadence for data, once per update and two hours for GP, a rule for responses, stop on anything that is not a 200, and limits, 50 errors in two hours and 100 MB a day. They publish no interval between requests. The pause is the corpus's own choice, and the corpus had been crediting it to CelesTrak since the fetch was written. What changed. The section is three things CelesTrak asks, each followed by what the fetch does about it, and then what is the corpus's own: requests one at a time with a two-second pause, no redirect followed, nothing retried, no URL twice in a run. The help text is split the same way. The quick-start comments give a user's run as the fetch list has it, 51 requests and 12.5 MB, once per corpus version, where they gave the manifest's totals, which count three maintainer-only re-captures. Two more corrections in the same paragraphs. The advice to leave out the legacy SATCAT with `--skip-case satcat-70000-cutoff` is removed: it also leaves out two first-record files filed under that case, which four other cases read [tested 2026-10-03 on the list as released in 0.5.0: the dry run then plans 54 of 61 requests; the manifest's sources]. And "CelesTrak's default format has been CSV since 2026-05-09" becomes "For GP and SupGP queries CelesTrak's default `FORMAT` has been CSV": the default is those queries', as its GP formats page and its SupGP query page say (RESEARCH §2.1), while its SATCAT queries documented JSON as theirs when read on 2026-09-20 (§2.6). The corpus relies on no default: every request names its format. Not changed: what the fetch does, which D-228 and D-229 changed; the pause itself; the changelog's earlier entries, which are history. The site's README and tracker page state the pause as the site's own rule and need nothing for this. Tests (`tests/test_fetch_text.py`, 7): the pause appears only after the sentence that calls it the corpus's own; each of the three asks is in the section; the figures the README states equal the fetch list's and the manifest's, so they cannot drift again; the expected 404s are TLE requests for objects above 99999; the old SATCAT advice is gone; the CSV default names its queries; the help text is split.

**D-231 (2026-10-03) — v0.5.1, fourth item: the legacy SATCAT file is fetched only on request, with `--include-satcat`, and a user's run becomes 50 requests and 3.1 MB (owner decision, on a point the plan raised unasked).** Why. `pub/satcat.txt` is 9,379,866 of the 12,511,746 bytes a user's run downloaded, three quarters, and one case reads it: `satcat-70000-cutoff`, a data check the runner makes on the file itself. It counts the catalog numbers, finds none at or above 70000, and reports `not-exercised` for every parser, "the parser under test was not involved" (D-129). CelesTrak's usage policy asks software to download only the data it needs (as recorded in `docs/RESEARCH.md` §11.1), and no parser needs this file. What changed. The entry carries `"opt_in": "satcat"`. A fetch leaves it out and says so in a line; `--include-satcat` brings it; `--force` does not refresh a copy that an earlier fetch left on disk unless the flag is given, so a clone that fetched under 0.5.0 does not download it again unasked, and such a copy is still compared with the manifest. A user's run is 50 requests and 3,131,880 bytes, with four expected 404s; a later corpus version requests 28. The runner: without the file the case reports `not-fetched`, as a provider file that is not on disk always has (D-148); the item names the flag; and the line under the count says that the case waits on a file the fetch brings only on request, that no parser takes part in the check, and how to fetch it. The general fetch command is no longer printed on its account, a plain fetch not bringing it. So the control run from a fresh fetch reads 16 cases passing, one needing fetched data and one not available [tested against a stand-in for a user's data folder]. With the file on disk the case reports `not-exercised`, as before. The README's fetch section gains CelesTrak's fourth ask, download only what you need, with this as what the fetch does about it. Alternatives: reporting `not-exercised` when the file is absent, so that the count line would not say that a case needs fetched data (not taken: `not-exercised` is the status of a check that was made and involved no parser, a missing provider file has been `not-fetched` since D-148, and the sentence under the count line says that nothing about the parser depends on it; it is one status and two tests if the owner prefers the other reading); putting the case's six small SATCAT records on request as well, since no parser check reads them either (not done: they are under 2 kB together); dropping the case (no: that the legacy file stops at 69999 is a fact the corpus states, and the check is what holds it). Not changed: the case, its check, its expected values. Tests (`tests/test_fetch_optin.py`, 11): one entry is on request and it is most of the bytes; a plain fetch and its dry run leave it out and say how to ask; the flag brings it; `--force` leaves a copy on disk alone unless it is asked for, and the two-hour rule holds for it; skipping the case is not the way to leave it out; the runner's item names the flag; the report says what the case waits on; before any fetch the case is one of those with nothing on disk; with the file the check is made and reports `not-exercised`. The counts in four other test files moved with it.

**D-232 (2026-10-03) — The SATCAT case reports `not-exercised` when its file is absent by default, with a line saying that `--include-satcat` runs the check; the `not-fetched` that D-231 chose is reversed (owner decision).** The owner: saying that the case needs fetched data tells every user to fetch the file that was just made optional. D-231 had the case report `not-fetched` without the legacy file, so the count line of every default run said that one case needed fetched data, and the line below it gave the command. What changes. When the legacy file is not on disk, and no kept response says that a fetch asked for it and was refused, the case's one check, `satcat-legacy-below-70000`, is recorded `not-exercised` with the detail that the data check was not made, that the fetch brings the file only on request and that the parser under test is not involved, followed by the flag, and by the command where a run names commands. The case's status is then what it is with the file, before a fetch and after one. The count line no longer counts it among the cases that need fetched data. One line under the count says that the case is a data check on a file the fetch brings only on request, that it was not made, that nothing about the parser under test depends on it, and that `--include-satcat` runs it. The JSON result carries the file and the flag under `on_request`. A file that was asked for and refused is still `not-fetched`, with what the fetch recorded (D-228). Why this is not the status D-148 took away. D-148 kept `not-exercised` from a case whose parser checks never ran for want of data, since the word would claim that the data lacked a feature when no data had been read. This case has no parser check: with the file its status is `not-exercised` because no parser is involved (D-129), which is as true without the file, and the item says in so many words that the check was not made. So the control run reads 16 cases passing, one not available and one not exercised from a fresh fetch, and 5 passing, 11 needing fetched data, one not available and one not exercised before any fetch [tested against stand-ins for both folders]. The case's six small SATCAT records are still `not-fetched` until a fetch and are counted in its `n/f` column. Not changed: the fetch (D-231), the check, the case's expected values. Tests: the runner's and the command line's in `tests/test_fetch_optin.py` rewritten and one added, 12 in the file: the status and the item with and without commands, the line and the absence of any fetch advice, the reading before a fetch, and a refusal kept for the file; the count lines in `tests/test_install_layout.py` and `tests/test_action.py`; the public clone's branch of the SATCAT test in `tests/test_runner.py`.

**D-238 (2026-10-04) — The letter to Dr. T.S. Kelso of CelesTrak was sent by the owner, from the owner's own address, on 2026-10-04 at about 07:53 EDT (11:53Z): the first direct word to CelesTrak's operator on how the corpus uses celestrak.org, sent before the corpus is announced to people who would run its fetch.** The sending is the owner's statement [the session did not see the message; the time is the owner's "now" read against the session's clock]. The text is the one committed privately as final on 2026-10-03, the fourth draft with the owner's two edits, 850 words, unchanged at sending (the owner's statement of 2026-10-04). What it says: who the maintainer is, and that the corpus was built with AI assistance and its first release audited by a separate AI session with no access to the build context; that no response from CelesTrak is redistributed, the corpus publishing expected values derived from the responses, each response's URL, time and SHA-256, and 604 TLE lines rendered from CSV records, with supplemental element values withheld from the public copy; how a user's fetch behaves, in the figures measured at v0.5.1's release (D-235): one run of about two minutes, 50 requests one at a time, 3.2 MB, neither the Active nor the Starlink group, the legacy SATCAT file only when asked for, a file on disk never requested again; that the fetch stops at the first non-200, keeps the answer for the user to read, retries nothing and asks nothing for two hours after a 403 or 429 (D-228), with one exception, four TLE requests for objects numbered above 99999 that are known to answer 404, of which the letter is the report to a human that his usage policy asks for; what the site's tracker requests each day, and that any other error ends its run (site S-080); the offer to stop requesting those 404s if he would rather, and to adopt a different cadence, a cap or a mirror; the three things the corpus says about his service, two read from his GP formats page and one the corpus's own observation, that his TLE rendering truncates the eccentricity where Space-Track rounds it (line 2 reproduced for 304 of 304 sets with truncation, 257 with rounding), each offered for correction; and that #172 is filed and taken up (D-236), anything further going to that tracker first. **D-239 (2026-10-04) — A count agrees in number with the words beside it, in everything the runner, the fetch and the Action print: one case passes, fails, skips or needs fetched data where two pass, fail, skip or need it, and no line hedges a plural with a bracketed s (owner).** The slip was seen in the Action's summary at the v0.5.1 release (D-235): "1 need launch-window data that no fetch brings". The owner asked for it fixed, and for every other count joined to a fixed phrase to be checked and fixed the same way. The audit: every formatted string in `gpconf/` and `tools/action_report.py` in which a value is followed by words, 218 of them, each read in its source. Three kinds needed work. A noun hedged as "record(s)", about sixty strings: the count line's "case(s)" and the lines under it, the fetch's "request(s)", "file(s)", "capture(s)" and "minute(s)", check-tle's summary, and some forty item details. A plural noun that can meet a count of one: "expected records", "ids", "pivot vectors", "valid epoch strings", "characters", "bytes", "objects", "entries", "vectors", "fields". And a verb or a pronoun that has to follow the count: "need", "have none of their", "report", "name", "are judged on their", "are missing … for them", "were reused", "match", "differ", "remain", "were given up", "as the parser reads them". The fix, one way everywhere: `gpconf/words.py`, two functions, `qty(n, noun)` for a count with its noun and `pick(n, singular, plural)` for a word that follows it; one is singular and every other number, zero included, plural. `tools/action_report.py` carries its own three-line `pick`, since the Action's script stands alone. The status words of the count line are verbs and agree like the rest: "1 passes (exact)", "1 fails", "1 skips", "1 needs fetched data"; "not available" and "not exercised" do not change with number. Alternative: taking pass, fail and skip as labels and conjugating "need" alone (rejected: "1 fail" beside "1 needs" in one line is the same slip half mended); it is one function, `count_line`, if the owner would rather have labels. Lines built in one place were moved into functions so that a test can call them: `count_line`; the fetch's `done_line`, `dry_run_line`, `captures_line`, `refusal_line` and `drift_line`; the Action's `counts_sentence`. What does not change: no status, no count and no check, only text. A line whose counts are all other than one reads as before but for the bracketed s, so the count lines published so far stand. The JSON report's item details change in wording where they carried a bracketed plural; a later item-for-item comparison with a kept report shows that as differences of text and nothing else. `docs/FAILURES.md` is generated from those details and by `tools/make_failures.py`, which had the same form in two places ("failing item(s)", "bullet(s)"): both fixed, the three built-in adapters run again on the maintainer's copy (the reference 17 exact with the SATCAT check not exercised, 15 and 8 failing, as at 0.5.1) and the catalogue regenerated: 244 lines as before, differing in the rewording, the generated line, and four details whose cut-off point moved with the shorter text. `docs/ADAPTERS.md`'s sample line reads "0 of 1 record". Left as they are, being a maintainer's console output and not what a user's run or the Action prints: `tools/export_public.py`'s "file(s)" and `tools/stage_package.py`'s "problem(s)". Tests: `tests/test_number_agreement.py`, 22 tests, pins the singular and the plural of the count line, of each line under the table, of the fetch's five lines, of the Action's sentence, and of the item details of a shipped case whose two files hold one record and 256; and it reads the source, so that no string in the code that prints, and no line of the generated catalogue, carries a bracketed plural. Forty existing assertions moved to the new wording, and three that asserted a phrase's absence now cover both numbers. Suite 386 OK (7 skipped); the changed files pass a check against Python 3.9's grammar. No release: it ships with the next one, and nothing is exported by this entry (owner).

**D-240 (2026-10-04) — Nothing parses the count line, and so that nothing has to: the JSON report carries the case totals as numbers in a `summary` object, the README, the adapter guide and the changelog say that a script reads the report or the exit status and never the printed lines, and the catalogue's table says "(1 failing)" (owner).** The owner kept D-239's choice ("Keep the status words agreeing") and asked, before it ships, what parses the count line rather than reads it. The check, by reading each source [tested]: the scratch repository's workflow (D-158) tests the Action's numeric outputs `failed` and `exercised` and the step's outcome, and searches the JSON report for two phrases; `tools/action_report.py` counts `results[].status` in the JSON report and uses the runner's exit status, passing the printed text through unread; the corpus's CI uses exit statuses; the tests hold whole-line assertions, already in D-239's wording, and none takes a number out of a line by matching "pass", "fail" or "skip"; the tools read JSON reports; the site's jobs do not run the runner. What the check found missing: the report held each case's status and its item counts as numbers but no case totals, and the README named neither `--json`, nor the exit statuses 0 and 1, nor the Action's outputs; the adapter guide described the report's fields and the three exit statuses without saying to use them in place of the printed text. Three changes, on the owner's word. (1) `summary` at the report's top level, from one function, `gpconf.runner.status_totals`: `cases`, and a count for each of the seven statuses a case can end in, zeros included, in the count line's order; the count line is written from the same numbers. (3) `tools/make_failures.py` writes a case's failing items as "(1 failing)" where it wrote "(1 fail)": a word that does not vary with the count, and the one the site's findings table already uses. The three built-in adapters were run again on the maintainer's copy (the reference 17 exact with the SATCAT check not exercised, 15 and 8 failing, as before) and `docs/FAILURES.md` regenerated, differing in the table's cells and the generated line alone. The site's `failures.json` is filled from that table by hand at each release: at the next one the cells are read as "(N failing)". Alternatives: leaving the totals to be counted by the consumer (rejected: the Action shows it can be done, but a reader of the README would still reach for the printed line); "(1 fails)" in the table, by D-239's rule (rejected: a cell is not a sentence). Whether the next release is a patch or a minor one is the owner's at the tag: the field is an addition to the report, and the adapter protocol is unchanged. Tests: `tests/test_report_summary.py`, 12 tests: the totals from stand-ins; the summary of a real run held to the cases of its own report, to the printed count line and to the Action's outputs; the field's place among the earlier ones; the sentence in the three documents; the table's cells. It did not see a message, as D-238 says in its own brackets; it read the unfilled "[time]" as a detail to supply instead of a reason to ask; and the "about 07:53 EDT (11:53Z)" in D-238 is the session's clock at the moment it read the word "now", a time no one stated. What was checked for this correction: the session cannot see the owner's mail and so cannot test either statement; no reply from CelesTrak has been logged; nothing else in the records shows a sending. The correction rests on the owner's statement, quoted above, and on nothing inferred. **What is withdrawn.** That the letter was sent, when, and from where. That "from this date CelesTrak's silence is no longer unasked": it is still unasked. That the post announcing the corpus waits for a reply or for a week of silence: no week began, and the post waits for the letter to be sent first, the owner's order of 2026-10-03 unchanged. That the text was "unchanged at sending". **What stands.** The text D-238 summarises exists, as a draft the owner approved on 2026-10-03; its contents are as D-238 lists them. The only contact with CelesTrak's project remains issue #172 (D-204, D-236). **What the draft now needs before it goes**, and why this entry sits where it does: the owner held the v0.6.0 commit for three changes the letter depends on. A user's fetch stops requesting the four known 404s, so the letter's one exception to "stop on any non-200" disappears (D-247), and with it the sentence "no response from CelesTrak is redistributed" needs the one response the corpus then ships. The site's tracker stops its daily Starlink supplemental pull and two weekly requests that answer 404 (site S-083), so the tracker's paragraph changes. And "604 TLE lines" is the wrong unit: they are 604 TLE sets, 1,208 lines of elements (D-248). The letter is redrafted from the released v0.6.0 and sent by the owner. **The rule taken from this.** Something the session cannot observe is recorded as the owner's statement, in the owner's words, with no detail the owner did not give; a message that holds a placeholder is asked about before anything is recorded; and when the owner reports the sending, the entry carries the owner's date and time or none. **Public state.** D-238 was exported in 65ec059 (D-243), so the public log has said since 2026-10-04 that the letter was sent; this entry corrects it at the next export. No other public file says so [tested: a search of the README, the changelog, the documents and the site for the letter and for Dr. Kelso's name finds the data-source credit and nothing else]. The private records that said "sent" are corrected with this entry.

**D-247 (2026-10-04) — One provider response is shipped, as a named exception to D-023: CelesTrak's 16-byte answer `No GP data found`, in `recorded/` with the provenance of every capture of it. A user's fetch no longer requests the four URLs known to answer it, so no request of a user's run is expected to answer anything but 200 (owner's ruling, on a rule question put first).** **The rule question.** D-001 is not touched: it concerns Space-Track bytes and where Alpha-5 element sets come from. D-023 is, by its words: "no raw CelesTrak bytes are shipped", and the body is sixteen raw CelesTrak bytes; the sentence makes no exception for an error message. By its reason it is not: D-019 recorded CelesTrak's silence on redistributing its data as silence and not permission, and the body carries no data, no element, no catalog number, nothing that stands in for a fetch. The same sixteen characters have been in the corpus's public files since v0.1.0, in the runner, which recognises the answer by them, the README, the research notes, the case documents and the expected values [tested: the tag v0.1.0]. The owner's ruling: ship it "under an amended D-023, stated openly as a named exception", and not by reading "provider data" narrowly and saying nothing. D-023 therefore now reads: no raw CelesTrak bytes are shipped but these sixteen. Alternatives: keep requesting the four, the state at 0.5.1, an exception to "stop on any response that is not a 200" that had to be reported to the provider; stop requesting and ship nothing, which takes the empty-answer check (D-143) and six set comparisons out of every user's run; have the runner build the body from the constant it already holds, which ships the same bytes without saying so. **What is shipped.** `recorded/celestrak-no-gp-data-found.txt`, and beside it a provenance file: the five captures of 2026-09-21, which are the four files and the re-capture of one (D-022), with the note that one body was written back by hand from the tool's log (D-013); and the four answers the maintainer's first-time fetch received on 2026-10-04 (D-235); each with its URL, time, HTTP 404, 16 bytes and the same SHA-256 [tested: the manifest, and the metadata that fetch wrote]. `tools/make_recorded.py` writes both and refuses anything but those bytes. **What the fetch does.** The four entries carry `recorded` in the fetch list. No plan requests them, under any flag. A run writes the body to the four paths with metadata that says `provenance: recorded` and `requested: false`, gives the status and the time of the corpus's own capture of that URL, and holds no response header, since no response was received. A file already on disk is left alone, so the maintainer's captures stay captures; a stable-tier one is not copied from an earlier version's cache; and a record whose bytes are not the ones its provenance and the manifest give is refused. `expect_status: 404` is reached now only by the maintainer's re-capture entry. **The figures.** A user's first fetch is 46 requests where it was 50, and 3,131,816 bytes at the snapshot's sizes where it was 3,131,880, with no request expected to answer with an error; on a machine that holds an earlier version's cache, 26 requested, 20 copied and 4 written, where it was 28 and 22 [tested: the suite, on the real list]. The duration is about two minutes [inferred: 50 requests took 2 min 10 s at 0.5.1 (D-235), and four fewer with the pause between them is about ten seconds less; it is measured at the release's timed fetch]. **What a run does.** Where the files are captures, as on the maintainer's copy, nothing changes. Where a file was written from the record, the parser is still handed the body (D-143); the hash item says "the corpus's record of the provider's empty answer … written by the fetch and not requested"; the two checks that compare the TLE answer with the OMM set say "the corpus's record of the TLE answer is 'No GP data found' (HTTP 404, captured …; not requested by this fetch)"; the JSON report lists the files under `recorded`; and a line under the counts says how many there are. A run with no fetched data does not change: the fetch writes the files and the runner does not conjure them, so the offline counts and the Action's stand. Having the runner read the shipped body whenever the file is absent was the alternative, and it would have moved three cases' offline statuses. **What is given up.** A user's run no longer observes CelesTrak giving that answer; it reads the corpus's record of 2026-09-21 and 2026-10-04. For the two live sets a recorded TLE answer is then compared with an OMM set fetched now, and a record can be wrong about today: if the fetched last-30-days group ever holds an id below 100000, CelesTrak's answer that day is data and not the recorded 404. In that case the two checks report `not-exercised` and give the reason; they do not fail, since a stale record is a result neither of the provider nor of the parser. That is a new outcome for an input that did not exist before: for a fetched or captured file the checks behave as they did, and their descriptions in the manifest say what happens with a record. The release stays a minor one on that ground. The site's tracker keeps its daily request for the last-30-days TLE (owner, site S-083), which is now the one place where the answer is still observed. **Fixed with it (owner).** The set comparison quoted `No GP data found` for the SupGP launch-window file, whose body is `No SupGP data found`; it now quotes the text the file holds, which changes one item's wording in the runs that reach it. **Where the exception is named.** Wherever the corpus said that nothing raw is shipped: the README, where the package's contents, "Why no raw files", the fetch's etiquette section and the licence paragraph say it; `NOTICE`, which says the licence does not cover CelesTrak's text; `MANIFEST.md`; `CITATION.cff`'s abstract; the manifest's `design` block, where `provider_data_shipped` is false, `raw_provider_files_shipped`, which held false, lists the one file, and `provider_responses_shipped` describes it; the three case documents. The export allowlist names the two files and the export refuses anything else under `recorded/`; the package carries them, since the installed fetch reads them. The frozen `expected.json` files are untouched. The letter to Dr. Kelso, which has not been sent (D-246), said that no response from CelesTrak is redistributed and described the four requests as its one exception; its next draft says which response is shipped and that the requests are no longer made. Tests: `tests/test_recorded_answer.py`, 22 tests, and the fetch tests that held the old figures; the suite 443 OK.

**D-248 (2026-10-04) — "TLE set" and "line" are used strictly. The two figures the corpus quotes most, 604 and 304, are both counts of sets, and each had been called "lines" in places (owner).** Seen in the draft of the letter to Dr. Kelso, which says "604 TLE lines". Counted from the four derived files [tested]: 604 TLE sets, which are 1,208 element lines, or 1,812 lines with the name line each set has; 257 with the letter A and 347 with the letter T; 603 distinct ids, 270449 being there twice. The 304 are the TLE sets among the maintainer's captures that have the CSV record of the same object beside them, the sample the rendering rules were derived from: 219 analyst, 79 decaying, 2 SupGP and 4 single objects. The renderer reproduces the name line, line 1 and line 2 of each, 912 lines; with the eccentricity rounded it reproduces line 2 of 257, and with the mantissas truncated line 1 of 251 [tested: `tools/validate_render.py`]. Two coincidences, written down so that they are not found again as errors. The maintainer's captures also hold 604 TLE and 2LE sets, in eleven files, re-captures included, all below 100000: the other half of the round-trip test's 1,208. So "604 TLE sets" has two referents, the served and the derived, and a text says which. And a user's fetch brings 304 TLE and 2LE sets, 219, 79 and six single ones: a different 304 from the sample's, since it has the two 2LE sets and lacks the two SupGP ones. **The vocabulary.** A TLE set is one object's lines: line 1 and line 2, with the name line where the format has one. A line is one line. "Record" stays for an OMM record and for what a parser returns, so the runner's item texts do not change. Each figure is said with its noun, and with its lines where a file first states it. Alternatives: "record" for both, which is the word the runner uses for parser output and would blur the two; "element set", which the site's library page uses and which is kept there. **Changed.** The README (the case table, the two sentences on the renderer's validation, the status paragraph); `tools/cases.py` and `tools/make_manifest.py`, and with them `manifest.json`, `MANIFEST.md` and the case documents, regenerated; `docs/WRITERS.md`; the docstring of `gpconf/tle.py`; `CITATION.cff`'s abstract, "derived Alpha-5 TLE sets"; the sentence `tools/crosscheck.py` writes. **Not changed, and why.** `AUDIT.md`, which is the auditor's text. This log, which is append-only: its earlier entries say "lines" and "records" as they were written. `docs/RESEARCH.md` and `docs/PLAN.md`, dated records. `docs/CROSSCHECK.md`, a generated report of 2026-09-21, which takes the corrected sentence when it is next generated. The seven frozen `expected.json` files that embed a copy of the earlier prose (owner: leave them): the runner reads the manifest and none of that prose, as with the check lists of D-143, and a file that holds frozen values is not regenerated for its wording. The derived files' provenance, which already says "TLE records reproduced exactly (lines 0, 1, 2)". The site's About and migration pages and the profile's line follow with the release; the letter's draft is corrected before it is sent (D-246). Test: `tests/test_sets_and_lines.py`, 7 tests: it counts the four derived files and fails on either figure said of lines, or on the shorthand "304/304", in the files the corpus writes today.

**D-252 (2026-10-04) — For the next release, not released (owner instruction): the fetch's `User-Agent` names gpconf, the version that asks and the repository, and the README's size for a user's fetch is the measured 3.2 MB where it said 3.1.** **The header.** Every request of `gpconf fetch` has carried `gp-omm-conformance-corpus/0.1 (fixture fetch, each URL once; see repository README)` since the corpus was built: a name that is not the kit's (D-241), a version that was never the corpus's, and a pointer to a README with no address. It was found on 2026-10-04 while the kit's description of its own traffic was checked against the released code: the 46 requests of the owner's timed fetch at the 0.6.0 release all carried that string [tested: the `request_headers` of the fifty metadata files of that fetch], and nothing in it would let CelesTrak's operator tell from a log what software was asking or which release. It now reads `gpconf/<version> (+https://github.com/hneogy/gp-omm-conformance; fetch, each URL once)`, the version taken from `gpconf.__version__`, so it moves with the release and cannot be forgotten at one. D-007 stands: the header says nothing about the person running the fetch; `GPCONF_CONTACT` appends a contact for whoever chooses to, and `GPCONF_USER_AGENT` replaces the string, both as before. The README's "Fetching responsibly" gives the header and the two variables, which the README had not named (D-007 names one of them). Alternatives: the product name without the version (rejected: the version is what tells an operator whether a release that changed the fetch has reached a user); the site's address in place of the repository's (rejected: the repository holds the fetch list and the issue tracker a stopped run points at, and the site's tracker already sends the site's address under its own header). What does not change: the metadata of the corpus's own captures, which record the header they were made with; the fetch list; any case, check or expected value. A file fetched from now on records the new header in its `.meta.json`, which no check reads. **The size.** The README said "46 requests, 3.1 MB" twice in the quick start and once under "Fetching responsibly". 3.1 MB is the sum of the sizes of the corpus's own captures of those 46 files, 3,131,816 bytes (D-247; 3,131,880 at 0.5.1 with the four requests since dropped, D-231). The owner's timed first-time fetch at the 0.6.0 release downloaded 3,200,451 bytes (D-250), and the one at the 0.5.1 release left 3,201,685 bytes on disk (D-235). The 68,635 bytes between the captures and the 0.6.0 fetch are live data: sixteen of the 46 files differ in size, and nearly all of the difference is the analyst group, larger now in each of its five formats, and the decaying list [tested: the size of each of the 46 files in the maintainer's captures and in the metadata of that fetch]. The site and the release notes of both versions say 3.2 MB; the README now does too. The 3.1 was not a slip: `tests/test_fetch_text.py` held the README's figure to the manifest's sizes, under D-230's rule that the section's figures cannot drift from the fetch list. A user does not download the captures, though, and the test now holds the README to the measured 3,200,451 bytes, with the captures' sum beside it in the same sentence ("where the corpus's own captures of the same files sum to 3.1 MB; the live files change size") and a check that the two stay within a twentieth of each other, so that a fetch list that changes materially fails the test until the fetch is timed again. The timed fetch comes after the upload, so a release's README carries the measurement of the release before it and says which. The changelog's sections for 0.5.1 and 0.6.0 keep "3.1 MB", as published; the Unreleased section says why the README differs from them. Tests: the changed test, and `tests/test_fetch_user_agent.py`, six tests: the default string against the version constant, no contact unless given, the replacement, the header a stubbed request really sends and the metadata records, the README's sentence, and one size in the README's three places. No version constant moves and nothing is exported: this rides with the next release, on the owner's word.

**D-253 (2026-10-04) — `docs/RESEARCH.md`, section 3, gains the usage policy's paragraph on NAT as the owner's account of the page, not as a quotation (owner instruction).** The owner's instruction, 2026-10-04: add "the usage policy's NAT paragraph — he has no way to know how many users reach CelesTrak through one IP address — read from the page as of 2026-10-03". The research record's rule is verbatim quotations with URLs and retrieval dates, and the paragraph's words are not available to a session: no session requests celestrak.org (standing rule), the one session reading of that page, on 2026-09-21, was made for redistribution terms and quoted nothing on this point (section 11.1), and no earlier record of the project holds the text [tested: a search of `docs/`, `DECISIONS.md` and the session's transcript for the paragraph]. So the entry gives what the owner said, in the owner's words, says in its heading that it is an account and not a quotation, and says that until the paragraph is quoted with the page's "Updated" date nothing cites it as CelesTrak's wording. This is D-246's rule applied to a page: what a session did not see is recorded as a statement, with nothing added. One sentence of the entry is this record's own reading and is marked [inferred]: that a hosted CI runner's address is such a shared address and that the per-address limits therefore count its users together. Alternatives: fetch the page (rejected: the standing rule, and a fetch today would not show the page as of 2026-10-03); write the paragraph as a quotation from the owner's summary (rejected: it would put words in CelesTrak's mouth); leave RESEARCH.md alone until the text is at hand (rejected: the owner asked for the entry, and the account, labelled as one, is true as far as it goes). Open: the paragraph's own words, to replace the account when the owner supplies them; listed under the handoff's open questions, since a sentence written to CelesTrak's operator may rest on it. Not exported; it rides with the next export, on the owner's word.

**D-270 (2026-10-09) — The Windows CI job's first run failed 42 of 445 tests (public run 37930807769 on 662da73, 33 failures and 9 errors), every one a portability assumption of the suite or the tooling and none a wrong expected value; fixed and the suite made genuinely Windows-clean rather than skipped, under the owner's gate "if the new Windows job fails, stop and fix it before tagging".** Three causes, from the job's log read whole. **One, line endings:** the repository had no `.gitattributes`, so git on Windows converted text files at checkout; a corpus whose expected values and manifest hash the files as they are cannot allow any checkout to rewrite them, and the conversion cascaded into the stable-source-drift checks, the export comparisons and everything downstream. A `.gitattributes` of one rule, `* -text`, now ships, allowlisted for export. **Two, shell quoting and the interpreter's name:** command lines handed to the platform shell were quoted with `shlex.quote`, whose POSIX single quotes `cmd.exe` rejects, and the fetch hint named `python3`, a name Windows installs do not have. `fetch_hint` now says `python` and quotes with `subprocess.list2cmdline` on Windows (`python3` and `shlex.quote` elsewhere), and the six test modules that build command lines for `CommandParser` quote the same way; `tests/test_not_fetched.py`'s expectations state both forms. **Three, path separators:** `tools/export_public.py` matched manifest paths against the allowlist with native separators (normalised to `/` now), and `locate.user_cache_dir` joined a faked platform's path with the host's separator — it now answers each faked platform with that platform's own joiner (`ntpath`/`posixpath`), and the win32 test expects `ntpath`. **Alternatives rejected:** skipping the failing tests on Windows (a green job must mean the suite passes, not that it looks away), and documenting `core.autocrlf=false` in the README (the repository can enforce byte-exactness itself). **Also set right in passing:** the 0.6.2 changelog entry's sentence that the Windows job's first run "comes with the next public push" (it has now run, and the entry tells what it found), and its two D-262 sentences, which contradicted each other after the adapters' comments changed — the entry now says the comments change with this release's build. The suite on macOS after the fix: 454 tests, OK, seven skipped. The public export, push and CI re-run follow under the owner's standing instruction for this release; the tag waits for the Windows job to pass.

**D-271 (2026-10-09) — The second Windows run (37933368138 on 4d175f7) came down from 42 failures to 15, and every one of the 15 is in the tests' own assumptions, none in the package; fixed in a second round, still under the owner's gate, with no test skipped as a whole.** **The seven that share one cause:** every test that drives the composite Action does it through `run_step`, which ran `bash -c` by name — and on a Windows runner a bare `bash` can resolve to `C:\Windows\System32\bash.exe`, the WSL doorway, which without a distribution prints a notice and exits 1 having run nothing. That fits the symptom exactly (exit 1, no summary written, both runs identical), and is recorded [inferred] from the symptom until the next run proves it: `run_step` now resolves the bash that `shell: bash` means — on Windows the one Git carries, found from `git`'s own location — and, when a step writes no summary, hands the step's output to the assertion message instead of silence, which is what cost this diagnosis a CI round-trip. **The six expectation fixes:** two `relpath` comparisons against `/`-separated literals normalised (`tests/test_export.py`, `tests/test_harnesses.py`'s `files_under`); the `data_root` test's POSIX-absolute inputs now expected through `os.path.abspath`, which anchors a rootless path to the drive on Windows, as the function answers; and the remaining `python3`-and-POSIX-quote expectations in `tests/test_install_layout.py`, `tests/test_fetch_optin.py` and `tests/test_action.py` state the platform's interpreter and quoting, the shadowed assertions behind the first failures included. **The one platform truth:** `tests/test_stage_package.py`'s staged-tree assertion held the tree's POSIX modes, which NTFS cannot carry; the epoch stamp is now asserted on every platform and the mode halves on POSIX alone, which looks away from nothing, because the archive writers never read modes from the tree — `repack_wheel` and `repack_sdist` set 0644 and 0755 themselves (`tools/stage_package.py` lines 200–228, read for this entry) and `test_repacked_archives_depend_on_their_contents_alone` passed on Windows in both runs. The suite on macOS: 454 tests, OK, seven skipped.

**D-293 (2026-10-09) — A parser may not end the run: a `SystemExit` or any other non-`Exception` raise inside the parser under test fails the case, the report is written, and the exit status is 1 (the red team's E9, the owner's highest priority).** On 0.6.2 a `sys.exit()` inside `parse()` unwound through the runner: no table, no JSON report, and the process ended with the status the parser chose, 0 for a bare `sys.exit()` — against the README's "0 when no case failed". Every call into the parser now goes through a guard that turns such a raise into an ordinary exception and counts it; each case in which it happened gains a failing `parser-exit` item, whatever the calling code made of the exception (a hook's "should be rejected" loop would otherwise have counted the exit as a correct rejection). `KeyboardInterrupt` is the user's and passes. An adapter that exits while it is imported or built is a setup error, status 2, nothing run. Not containable in-process, and said so in the code: `os._exit`; a parser that must be isolated runs behind `--cmd`, where the runner owns the status.

A case with no failure in which any check it lists has every item not-exercised by the parser reads `not-exercised`; the JSON names the checks under `voided_by_parser`. No status is added, so the summary's keys and the exit codes are as they were. Measured before it was built: it moves the three red-team adapters and none of the sixteen published runs. Data-caused not-exercised items (no nine-digit id in a fresh fetch) leave the ranking alone.

**D-299 (2026-10-09) — OMM values are graded with no fetched data, in the corrupt-input case (the red team's E15; the owner's ruling).** No case that runs offline compared a CSV, JSON or XML value with an expected one: the shipped OMM files were read only to be compared with the parser's own reading of them (D-175). One derived XML file is added under the provenance of the KVN variants — the ISS first record re-serialised by the same tool, `derived/kvn-variants/v07-xml-ndm-reserialised.xml`, the six released KVN files left byte for byte as they were — and graded here for its values. The records carry negative drag terms, which is what the red team's sign-losing reader needs to be caught.

**D-300 (2026-10-09) — The synthetic sets widened (fix 7; the owner's instruction after the red team's E11): both ends of all 24 letters, and every two-digit epoch year.** The letters file holds the lowest and highest id of each letter, X0000 and X9999, less the two ids a real record of the corpus holds (100000 and 270000, which are never given synthetic elements): 46 sets. A second file holds one set per two-digit epoch year, 00 to 99, under the ids 330100 to 330199 so that each set names the year it tests: the real sets carry the years 26 and 98 only, and a reader's pivot anywhere between was graded on nothing. Same provenance and statement as D-286; D-016 stands. The derived case holds 750 records in six files, 604 of them derived from real records, which remains the figure every text gives for real derivations; the writer case, which inherits them, 756.

**D-303 (2026-10-09) — The fresh-session red team, its fourteen escapes mapped, and what is left open.** The owner had a fresh session, on another model and blind to the repository, audit gpconf 0.6.2 from PyPI with the brief SM-26 was given; its folder is kept whole in the private handoff and its adapters ship in `tests/adversarial/redteam/`, credited "fresh-session red team, 2026-10-09". Of its fourteen escapes, seven used routes D-280 to D-286 had already closed (E1 with its command-line form, E2, E3, E4, E5b, E7, E11); five were new and are closed by D-293 (E9), D-294 (E8), D-296 (E5a), D-299 (E15) and, for E6, not yet — below; two the report itself says contradict nothing, and they stay as designed: E10, a writer's secondary fields are information because orbit-fitting tools regenerate them, and E17, a float within the documented 1e-12 passes as `pass-tolerance` with its bias statistics. Its other findings are D-295, D-297, D-298, D-301 and D-302; one is left as designed and said here: a set with a `record_filter` does not flag extra ids, since its oracle lists a stated subset. **E6 is open, by the owner's instruction to measure first.** The escape: an epoch returned as text is parsed by the runner's own reader, so a parser with no day-of-year support passes by handing the text back. The rule first chosen — `parse_epoch` must return a datetime, `parse()` a datetime or calendar-form text — was run against all seventeen adapters before being built: the hook half moves nothing, every adapter's hook already returns a datetime; the text half would move thirty case verdicts in eight published runs, because the corpus's own harnesses and presets return TLE epochs as year and day-of-year text for the runner to normalise — a convention of the harnesses, not a defect of any library. A narrower rule, which fails only a non-calendar epoch that is the input's own text passed back, moves no published verdict and one of the corpus's own: the reference adapter passes a KVN day-of-year epoch through, and would have to parse it. Nothing of E6 is built; the choice is the owner's.
