**D-306 (2026-10-10) — E6 is built on the owner's ruling: `parse_epoch` returns a `datetime`, and a record whose epoch is the input's own text handed back unparsed fails; the full calendar-only rule was measured and rejected. This closes the question D-303 left open.** The escape, the red team's E6: a parser with no day-of-year support returned the epoch text as it found it, and the runner's own reader parsed it, so the parser passed on the runner's work. Built, in two halves. The hook: `parse_epoch` must return a `datetime`; a string fails `ccsds-epoch-strings`, whatever it says. A command answers in text, as its protocol has it, and the runner converts that; the vector's own text sent back as it came, where it is not already the calendar form, is a rejection. The records: an epoch that is a string, is not in the calendar form `YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.f]`, and stands in the input as returned, fails that record's `values` with the text quoted. The reference adapter now parses a KVN file's day-of-year epoch itself; up to 0.6.2 it passed that one file's text on, which was the same fault in the control. **What the rule leaves alone, by design:** the corpus's own harnesses and presets return a TLE epoch as year and day-of-year text that they build from the library's numbers, and the runner normalises it. That text is in no input, so nothing was handed back unparsed, and it is read as before. **Why the full strict rule (a `datetime` or calendar text, nothing else) was rejected:** measured before building, on the seventeen runs (`docs/handoff/v0.7.0-evidence/e6-measurement.json` in the private handoff), it moves 30 case verdicts in ten runs, 29 of them in nine library runs and one the reference adapter's KVN case, and every one is caused by the form a harness of ours chose to write, none by a library's reading of an epoch: tle.js, satellite.js, astroz, Gpredict, gods-eye-view and SatDump's harnesses write day-of-year text, and the tle.js API mode a calendar form with `Z`. A rule that fails published rows for our own harnesses' formatting would report nothing about the libraries. The hook half alone moves nothing, and the narrower text rule moved no published verdict and only the reference's one KVN file, which is why the reference was changed with it. (The handoff's first summary of the measurement said eight runs; the file says ten, and the file is the count.) Alternatives: the full strict rule (rejected above); rewriting every harness to emit calendar text first, then the strict rule (a change to the published recipes to close a route the narrower rule already closes; not now); leaving it open (the owner ruled). Adversarial adapters, per the Grader changes rule: the red team's `e06.py` `Win` stood on the records as the file wrote them, which is the base it was written against, fails the vectors case and the KVN case, its twin, which refuses such text, fails both; a command that echoes the epoch fails the hook; and a parser returning day-of-year text it built itself still passes, which holds the exemption to what it says. On the final tree: the suite, 500 tests, OK; the sixteen published runs and the owner's Swift library re-run, no case status, item status, detail or summary line different from the run before this change, and no case status different from the published reports; the 20,000-mutant gate at seed 20261009, 5,584 survivors, every one in an allowlisted category, exit 0; the CI command at 5,000, 1,433 survivors, exit 0. Reason: an epoch is the parser's to parse, and the grader should not do a parser's work for it; but a rule is worth having only where what it fails is the library.

The owner's statement: the owner ran the reproduction on 2.27 with the compiled extension before filing and got `I0000`, `J0000`, `O0000`, `P0000`. The finding: with the compiled extension, `sgp4init` writes satellite numbers 180000 to 189999 with the letter I and 230000 to 239999 with the letter O, where Alpha-5 skips both and the pure-Python `Satrec` writes J and P; the two comparisons are in `Satrec_sgp4init` in `extension/wrapper.cpp`, python-sgp4's own code, on 2.27 and on master `8126f77`. It was found by the synthetic letter sets of D-286 and D-300 on their first run, and no catalogued object is in either range. Then: the three built-in reports were run again under 0.7.0 and `docs/FAILURES.md` rendered from them, with the issue's link in its introduction. Case statuses are those of the 0.6.1 reports (reference 17 pass and 1 not exercised, naive 15 failing cases, python-sgp4 8); failing items move from 79 to 81 for the naive adapter and from 24 to 26 for python-sgp4, the two new python-sgp4 items being the writer case's catalog field and round trip on the four affected ids. The README's Upstream section lists the report. The 0.6.1 reports are kept in the private handoff. Not done, the owner's: the fix's pull request waits for the maintainer's yes; the `export_omm` pull request is a separate matter and stays held until 2026-10-19. Alternatives: regenerating before the report (it would have published the finding ahead of the maintainer hearing of it; the owner's order was report first). Reason: a maintainer reads of a defect in their inbox before the corpus prints it.

**D-309 (2026-10-11) — Gpredict's letter-in-epoch report is answered: #427 was closed as completed on 2026-10-10 at 23:56:59 UTC by pull request #430, a contributor's fix (Wahaj18) merged by the maintainer as `f05abf3`; the fix was checked with the recipe's harness and holds.** [tested: GitHub's API and a local build, 2026-10-11, after the owner's statement.] The report was the corpus's, of 2026-09-28 (D-193): a letter O in place of a 0 in line 1's epoch field passed `Good_Elements()`, and the epoch was read up to the letter. The fix adds a check to `Good_Elements()` that the epoch field is a well-formed number, and a test. Gpredict's own `test-001.c`, built the same way at `f05abf3`, exits 0. One thing about the harness: the fix calls GLib's `g_ascii_isdigit`, which the recipe's stand-in for GLib does not define, so the check added one line to a scratch copy of the stand-in, the ASCII digit test that the function is; the recipe as published is pinned to v2.6 and builds as it did, and its stand-in gains that line when the row is re-run on a release that carries the fix. The fix is in no release, Gpredict's latest being 2.6, so no row and no count moves. Recorded in the README (the fixes table's Gpredict row, whose date moves to 2026-10-11 with its other expiring cells checked again that day: sgp4 2.27 on PyPI, satellite.js 7.1.0 on npm, Gpredict v2.6; and the Upstream section) and in `docs/LETTER-IN-FIELD.md`'s Gpredict paragraph. It is listed in the table under the table's own rule: it followed a report made from the corpus's results and answered it, though the corpus did not write it. These ride v0.7.0; nothing is public before it, the site included. No reply was posted; the owner's thanks are the owner's. Gpredict's source, GPL, stays out of this repository; the runs' output is in the private handoff. **D-310 (2026-10-11) — The licence changes with v0.7.0: Apache-2.0 from this release, MIT for every release up to 0.6.2, which stay as published (the owner's rulings after an attribution review).** What the review found first: the corpus was MIT everywhere it says a licence (LICENSE, `pyproject.toml`, `CITATION.cff`, PyPI's metadata for 0.6.2, GitHub's detection, the site); every copyright line names NEOGY LLC and the year 2026, the first commit being of 2026-09-20; the history of both repositories has one author, the owner, and no outside pull request; and what is in the repository without being NEOGY LLC's is four things, each already marked or marked now: the CCSDS/SANA schemas (`schemas/SOURCE.md`), CelesTrak's 16-byte answer (D-247), a patch against python-sgp4 in `docs/upstream/patches/`, and SM-26's adapters. So NEOGY LLC can relicense what it holds. The rulings: (1) Apache-2.0 from v0.7.0. `LICENSE` is apache.org's text unaltered, held to it by its SHA-256 in a test; `pyproject.toml`'s licence expression and `CITATION.cff` say Apache-2.0; nothing already released changes. (2) `NOTICE`, which Apache-2.0 requires a redistributor to carry: the copyright line, the site, the concept DOI, a request for credit when the corpus, its expected values or its verdicts are used, the name note, and the scope note it carried before (D-219). The request is a request; the licence does not make citation a condition. (3) The years are 2026. (4) Every source file of NEOGY LLC's carries two lines, `SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0` and `Copyright 2026 NEOGY LLC`: 129 files (Python, the Node adapters, the harnesses' C, C++ and Zig, the workflow, the Action, `pyproject.toml`), after a shebang where there is one; not data, not prose, and not the three things that are not NEOGY LLC's to mark. The adapter guide's seven line references move by two. (5) `tests/adversarial/sm26.py` is SM-26's work, contributed in issue #1 and kept verbatim; no licence was stated with it, so its header now says it is not covered by the project's licence pending SM-26's permission, which the owner asks for in the reply on that issue; if SM-26 agrees, the header changes in a later commit. It is in the repository and in no package. (6) The README gains "Cite as" under the install block, and the line "gpconf is a name of NEOGY LLC. Forks are welcome under a different name.", a claim from use, with no registration recorded here. (7) One licence for code and data for now; and publishing through PyPI's Trusted Publishing with attestations is planned for the release after this one, not this one (`docs/PLAN.md`). Why Apache-2.0: it makes the notice travel with copies, asks that changed files be marked, and says in terms that the licence grants no right to the name; its costs are a longer text and that code under it cannot be combined into a GPL-2.0-only work, which matters to a project wanting to vendor the code, not to one running the kit. Alternatives: staying MIT (credit rests on one line that is easily dropped); a separate data licence such as CC BY 4.0 for the corpus and this log (credit as a condition, at the price of two licences in one package and of projects hesitating to vendor fixtures; revisit if the text is reused without credit). Tests changed with it: the licence test, the Action's first-line test, the harness-copies test (the one-off runs' originals carry no header), the recorded answer's sentence. The site's licence sentences change in its own repository and go out with the release, not before. Sentences in documents dated before this entry that call the corpus MIT (the original plan in `docs/PLAN.md`, the strf note) describe it as it was and are left.

**D-311 (2026-10-11) — A record fails when the parser returns more copies of its id than the input holds; the second half of D-281 is reversed (the owner's ruling on the second blind audit's F1).** D-281 had every returned copy compared and, by the owner's design call of that day, let an exact duplicate count in `extra` and fail nothing. The second blind audit, a fresh session given the 0.7.0 candidate's wheel and sdist alone, used exactly that: its `win_f1_dup_exact` returns every record twice, 1,208 records for a 604-record corpus, and ended with no failing case. A parser that emits each record twice is wrong, and the corpus said it was right. The rule now, in the owner's words: "a record fails when the parser returns more copies of its id than the input holds", exact copies included. Not "any duplicate": no frozen input holds an id twice, so there the rule is one copy; but a file read live could carry an id twice, so the comparison takes how many records of each id the input holds, from the frozen records or from the reference reader's reading of the same bytes, and fails the surplus. What stands: D-281's first half, every copy compared, a copy that disagrees fails its record; D-194 and D-207, one outcome per expected record, the outcome of a record with a surplus copy in a values item being a failed item with the record still counted as loaded; and `extra` and `duplicate_copies`, which count the surplus. Measured before building: `duplicate_copies` is 0 in every item of the sixteen published runs and the owner's Swift library (the reports of the 2026-10-10 re-run), so no published verdict moves. The fuzzer's allowlist loses `duplicate-exact`: a surviving exact duplicate is an escape again. Measured after: 20,000 mutants at seed 20261009 leave 4,105 survivors where they left 5,584, every one in an allowlisted category, the 1,479 exact duplicates now killed; the CI run of 5,000 leaves 1,060 where it left 1,433; both exit 0. With the full maintainer data the win had already failed five cases, but only through the XML wrapper's record count; a reader doubling TLE records alone passed with data too. **The review.** Before it was committed the change was read by a separate reviewer that had not written it, with D-194, D-281 and this entry, and asked to break it. It found no correct parser that newly fails: the reference adapter on the full data reads as before, and no frozen record list and no file on disk holds an id twice. It found four places where a surplus copy still got through, each confirmed by running an adapter, and each is closed here with its adapter in the tests: (1) the KVN file whose `NORAD_CAT_ID` keyword is absent, whose record is matched through the records that carry no id: the first form of this change exempted it, and had also dropped it from `duplicate_copies`; it is counted and failed like any other. (2) The one snapshot file compared on a subset of its records (27 of 11,141, the nine-digit ids): an id outside the subset is not compared, and a second copy of it was not seen; such an id returned more often than the reference reader holds it in the file now fails. (3) The corrupt-input case: the first form turned a doubled neighbour into the outcome "changed by the corrupt input", which moved the case's counts and blamed the edit; now the outcomes and counts are those of a parser that returned one copy, and the surplus is a failure in its own words on the neighbours item and, for the corrupt record, on its own item. (4) The unedited file the corrupt-input case compares with was value-graded nowhere for TLE, so a parser that doubled that one file passed; a record returned twice from it now fails there. Limits that remain, stated: where a live file holds an id twice with different values, every copy is compared with the one record the oracle keeps for that id, so a correct parser fails there; the reviewer confirmed it by appending such a row to a copy of a provider file, it predates this entry (D-281), and no input, frozen or among the maintainer's captures, has it. Where the input holds an id twice, `expected` still counts ids, so the second record is in no outcome count. The cases that compare formats with each other or check facts make no surplus check of their own; in a full run every source they read is value-graded in another case, so this shows only when such a case is run alone. And the gate's headline for a doubling parser still says the records were read, with the surplus beside it, as D-298 has it: the gate is a headline, not a check. Alternatives: "any duplicate fails" (wrong for a live file that holds an id twice); leaving D-281 as it was and showing the surplus in the headline only (a doubled output is a defect a conformance kit should fail, and nothing published depends on tolerating it). Adversarial adapters, per the Grader changes rule: the red team's win fails three cases and its twin, a second copy that disagrees, fails as before (`tests/adversarial/redteam2/`); one test holds the other half of the rule, two copies passing where the input holds two; and four hold what the review found.

**D-312 (2026-10-11) — A run says what its statuses leave out: item skips and field gaps in the case's status cell, a total under the count line, and how many cases were graded when data was missing (the owner's rulings on the second blind audit's F2 and F3, and on offline runs).** The audit's observation: its F3 run printed "0 skip" in the count line while an XML item had skipped inside a passing case, and its F2 run printed `pass` for a case in which a field was never returned; and with an empty data folder a green run is a run on five cases of eighteen. Nothing was graded wrongly, and the headline read cleaner than the run. Built, with no new status, no changed count and no changed exit code: a case that did not skip as a whole shows in its status cell the items that skipped and the files in which a field with expected values was never returned, as `pass (1 item skipped)`, `pass (5 field gaps)`, or both; a sentence under the count line totals them across the run; when cases were not graded for lack of provider data a line says how many were, `5 of 18 cases graded offline; not a full conformance result.` where no provider file was read at all, and with the number still needing a fetch where some were; the JSON report gains `inside_cases` (`items_skipped`, `field_gaps`, `cases_graded`) and a result with either of the first two carries `annotations`; the Action's table shows the same status cell. `status`, `summary` and the count line are as they were, so a script that reads them reads what it read. The adapter guide's three sentences on `Unsupported` (a format, `write_tle`, a vector hook) said a skip "means exactly that: the parser has no reader for the format"; they now say what the runner checks, the same answer everywhere in a run, a mix failing, and that the absence itself is the adapter's claim, reported and counted and not verified. Alternatives: a new status such as pass-with-gaps (it would move published rows of libraries that honestly read TLE only, for nothing they do wrong); failing a skip (a library without an XML reader is not a wrong library). Also corrected while there, each verified against the tree: the README's writer-case row said 610 inputs where the case holds 756 (606 frozen records and 150 synthetic-derived), a coverage note said 22 synthetic inputs where there are 46 letter sets, and the guide's sample run named 0.6.1 with 12 items where the derived case has 18.

**D-313 (2026-10-11) — Six of the second blind audit's seven wins stand as designed; its report is kept whole and its nineteen adapters are in the tests.** The audit (`REPORT.md`, 2026-10-11, kept in the private handoff with its folder) was run by the owner as a fresh session on the 0.7.0 candidate's wheel and sdist, with the brief of 2026-10-09 and a list of the areas that had changed, and no access to the repository, this log or the earlier report. Its conclusion, which a re-run of every adapter on the tree confirms: no compared value escapes; every win avoids comparison through a documented outcome; and the guards it tried against the earlier fixes (a process exit, an epoch handed back unparsed, no records from a file that has them, a float catalog number, a format unsupported for some files only) hold. F1 is closed by D-311. The other six, and why each stands: **F2**, a field the parser never returns is not compared: the protocol asks an adapter to leave out what its library does not keep rather than invent it (D-284), and the gap now shows in the status (D-312). **F3, F4, F5**, `Unsupported` for a whole format, for every record of the writer, for every vector of a hook: a library may truly lack the reader, the writer or the operation, and the runner cannot tell that from a hidden one; it holds the answer to all-or-none (D-205, D-280), counts the skip in the status (D-312), and no longer claims more in the guide. **F6**, a writer that zeroes the derivative and the counters: fitting tools regenerate those by design, and the case reports them as information (D-095). **F7**, a parser that drops a record from the unedited file as from the edited one: the corrupt-input case compares a parser with itself (D-175), so it has nothing to measure, and it reads `not-exercised`, never `pass` (D-294); the record is value-graded once provider data is fetched, where that adapter fails three cases. One correction to the report: under F3 the XML file skips in the corrupt-input case only, where it has been graded since D-299, not in the KVN case as well. Its seven wins, seven twins and five guards are in `tests/adversarial/redteam2/`, credited "fresh-session red team, 2026-10-10" and kept as written but for the header; the tests hold F1's win to failing, the six to ending with no failing case and to the run saying so, and every twin and guard to failing as reported. The release differs from the build the audit read in the F1 rule, the summary text of D-312, the licence and headers of D-310, and README and guide text.

**D-314 (2026-10-11) — Two standing rules for grader changes and releases (owner): a blind red team before every tag, and a separate reviewer before every grader commit; and for v0.7.0 the gate is met.** The red team: a fresh session started by the owner, a different model from the one that built the release, the built package only (wheel, sdist, a fresh environment, an empty data folder and the brief), before any tag; its report triaged for the owner before anything is built from it, and what it finds kept in `tests/adversarial/`, credited. The brief is a template kept in the private handoff. The rule applies in full from the release after v0.7.0. For v0.7.0 the owner ruled the gate met by the blind pass of 2026-10-10 on the candidate together with the separate review of the change that followed it (D-311): the audit read the candidate, the change it led to was read by a reviewer that had not written it, and that reviewer was not blind. The review: every grader change is read before commit by a reviewer agent that did not write it, given the diff and the entries it rests on or reverses, and its findings go to the owner before the commit. Both rules are in `CLAUDE.md` beside the Grader changes rule they extend, and in the release checklist. Why both: the two audits found what the author's own tests had not, fourteen wrong parsers that passed and then seven; and the first separate review, of a change of some forty lines, found four more. Alternatives: the reviewer alone, with no blind audit (it reads with the repository's context in reach, and sees what the author saw); an outside human audit each release (wanted, and asked for in issues #1 and #2, but not something a release can wait on).

**D-315 (2026-10-11) — Two small changes to what a run says, on the owner's instruction, each read by a separate reviewer before commit: an input that itself holds an id more than once says so wherever a parser could be blamed for it, and a data folder with only the SATCAT files is not called offline.** D-311 states a limit: where an input holds an id more than once with records that differ, the runner keeps one record for the id, and a correct parser's other copy fails against it. The owner: "make sure a failure caused by an input that itself holds an id twice says so plainly in the item text, so a correct parser isn't blamed." Now: when a file is loaded and the reference reader finds an id held more than once with records that differ, the case carries an information item on that file, `input-holds-an-id-more-than-once`, naming the ids and saying that a failure on them in any item that reads the file may be the input's doing; every case kind that reads the file carries it, and the command prints it without `--verbose`, beside the failures it may explain. In the values item a value that differs is marked only when it is in a field in which the input's own records for that id differ, "[the input holds this id 2 times, with records that differ in mean_anomaly]", and one sentence after the list says a value so marked may be the input's doing, not the parser's. The item still fails: the runner cannot tell. A surplus copy, a wrong type, a missing field, a wrong value in a field the input's records agree on, and repeats that are identical carry no mark: those are the parser's own. No status, count or exit code changes, and a run with no repeated id prints what it printed. Second: the line of D-312 said "graded offline" for a folder holding only the SATCAT files, because the data check's items are information; whether a provider file was read is now taken from the sources each case records having loaded. The review took three reads of three versions and found that the first form excused surplus copies and wrong types and left the other checks on the file unannotated, that the second marked per id where it should mark per field and missed the cases that pair formats, and that the edit for the third had deleted two unrelated lines, the label for a drifted stable source, which an existing test catches; restored, with the whole suite run. Limits it found that stand: the same instant written two ways in a repeated row's epoch counts as differing; `docs/FAILURES.md` shows failing items cut at 600 characters, so it would show neither the sentence nor the notice, and no published run has a repeated id. Alternatives: turning such a failure into a pass or a not-exercised (the runner cannot know which of the input's records a copy came from without matching copies to records, a larger change than a release week allows; the text is honest until then); one notice on the values item only (the first form, which left three other checks blaming the parser). Found by the reviewer in passing and not changed here: a correct parser fails `tle-count-equals-omm-count-below-100000` when only some files of a set are on disk; it is recorded for the owner with the hardening review's findings.

**D-316 (2026-10-11) — Gpredict's merged fix for the mean motion's eleventh character, pull request #428, checked with the recipe's harness at its merge commit, as #430 was (owner instruction; D-267 recorded the merge, D-309 the other fix).** [tested: a local build, 2026-10-11; GitHub's API for the state: #428 merged 2026-10-08T09:01:39Z as `dd2edc0` by the maintainer, #426 closed as completed two seconds later.] The report (#426) was that `Convert_Satellite_Data()` copied ten characters of the eleven-character mean motion field, so the eighth decimal was lost on every set, and it named the project's own test data as showing it. The check, with the harness built against `src/sgpsdp/` at each commit and the recipe's stand-in for GLib unchanged: that test set, whose mean motion is printed 16.05824518, reads 16.0582451 at v2.6 (`c9fa018`) and 16.05824518 at `dd2edc0`; two controls whose eighth decimal is 0, one five-digit analyst object and one of the corpus's derived Alpha-5 sets, read the same value at both commits; and Gpredict's `test-001.c`, to which the pull request added an assertion on the parsed mean motion, builds the same way at `dd2edc0` and exits 0. The fix is in no release, Gpredict's latest being 2.6, so the row stays as run and no count moves; the README's Upstream section says what was checked. No reply was posted; the owner's thanks are the owner's. The run's output is in the private handoff, and no Gpredict source is kept (GPL). Alternatives: resting on the merge alone (the corpus reports what it has run, and this takes a minute to run).

**D-317 (2026-10-11) — The repeated-id note of D-315 is withdrawn from v0.7.0 and kept for 0.7.1; the rule of D-311 and its plain failing text stand; the SATCAT-only wording of D-315 stays.** The owner capped the note: "If the reviewer's next round still finds problems, drop the note from v0.7.0 (keep F1's rule and its plain fail text) and list the note for 0.7.1. Don't let it hold the release." The next round, the fourth read, found two. A crash: a file holding both a repeated id whose records differ and two records without a catalog number that differ ended the case with an internal error, a TypeError sorting an id with None, where the commit before it failed each item in its own words; the third version had left id-less records out of the notice but not out of the marks. And a narrow excuse: a value that neither of the input's records holds was still marked as possibly the input's doing. So `gpconf/runner.py` is again what it was at D-311 to D-313, byte for byte: no information item, no mark, no sentence; where an input itself holds an id more than once with records that differ, a correct parser's other copy fails in the plain words of any value that differs, which is the limit D-311 states. What stays from D-315: a data folder holding only the SATCAT files is not called offline, a change the same reviewer read and found sound in every case kind. The whole suite, 520 tests, passes. For 0.7.1: the note done properly means matching each returned copy to one of the input's records, so that the runner knows which values are the input's, instead of marking by id or by field; that is the larger change D-315 set aside, and four reads of three smaller ones say it is the right size. Reason: a message meant to keep a correct parser from blame must not itself be a new way for a run to go wrong, and no input the corpus has, frozen or captured, holds an id twice.

**D-318 (2026-10-11) — A set whose TLE file is absent, or whose TLE the parser does not read, is not compared by count and fails nobody (the owner's ruling on the hardening review's G1).** The two count checks of a TLE-and-OMM set, `tle-count-equals-omm-count-below-100000` and `tle-format-omits-ids-above-99999`, compared the ids of the parsed TLE file with those of the OMM file. Where the TLE file was not on disk they compared nothing with the OMM set and failed: "TLE has 0 records, OMM has 79 ids below 100000". That is a false failure for any parser, the reference adapter included; the review's own second reviewer met it by putting one file of a pair in a data folder, and the released 0.6.2 wheel does the same. A fetch stops on any response that is not 200, by rule, and leaves exactly such a folder. Now: a TLE file that is not on disk makes the comparison `not-exercised`, cause data, saying which file is missing; the file's own item already reads not-fetched or not-available. That holds whatever the OMM set contains, so where the OMM set has no id below 100000 a comparison that used to pass on nothing now says it was not made; no case status moves by it. The same fault from the other side is closed with it: a parser that answers `Unsupported` for TLE has nothing to count, and the comparison skips where it failed, so a parser that reads OMM only no longer fails two cases for a reader it does not claim; all-or-none holds as for any format (D-280), so a parser cannot use this for one file. A TLE file that is on disk and that the parser reads as nothing, or raises on, still fails the comparison, as it must. The owner's wording allowed not-fetched or not-exercised; not-exercised was taken because an item marked not-fetched is counted as a missing provider file in the table and the lines under it, and the set is not a file. What was checked for published results: no published run has a half-fetched set, and the failing text, "TLE has 0 record", occurs in no published report, recipe or page, only in this log and the reviews; the sixteen-run comparison confirms it. Adversarial adapters, per the Grader changes rule (`tests/adversarial/test_hardening.py`): the reference adapter on a folder with one file of the pair, which failed and now does not; a parser that drops every TLE record with both files present, which still fails; a parser with no TLE reader, which skips; and its twin, unsupported for that one file only, which fails on D-280. These four need provider files and so run where the data is, not in public CI. Read before commit by a separate reviewer, which found no problem in it; limits it noted and that stand: only the first TLE member of a set is compared, so a set with a `.2le` beside a missing `.tle` is not compared by its `.2le`; and all-or-none is per format name, so a parser may read `2le` and not `tle`. Alternatives: `not-fetched` for the comparison (counted as a missing file, above); leaving the unsupported side for later (it is the same false failure, found while reading the same six lines).

**D-319 (2026-10-11) — Text a parser returns for an epoch or an element value is read strictly: ASCII digits, a plain decimal grammar, nothing around it; text outside it is a value the runner cannot read, and the file fails as `parse` (the owner's ruling on the hardening review's G2).** The runner turned an element value given as text into a number with `Decimal()`, and an epoch with a pattern whose `\d` was not limited to ASCII. Both are more generous than any reader of orbital data should be: `Decimal()` reads the digits of other scripts, an underscore between digits and whitespace around the number, and `\d` matches the digits of other scripts, which `int()` then reads. Three wrong-on-purpose adapters built from the reference, returning an epoch in Arabic-Indic digits, an inclination in Arabic-Indic digits, and a mean motion as `" 15.204672_81 "`, each ended with five passing cases and no failure. Now an element value that is not a number, text or any other object by its text form, must match `[+-]?(digits[.digits] | .digits)([eE][+-]?digits)?` in ASCII digits, with nothing before or after it. The epoch pattern is ASCII. Text outside the grammar is treated as what `"N/A"` has always been, a value the runner cannot read: the conversion raises and the whole file fails as `parse`, with the value quoted, which is the path the adapter guide already documents. Numbers returned as numbers, `int`, `float` or `Decimal`, are untouched, and so is the protocol that an element value may be a decimal string (D-131). Padding fails: the owner asked first whether any published run returns padded number strings, to allow padding in this release if one did; measured over the sixteen published runs and the owner's Swift library, fourteen return numbers, two return strings (the reference adapter and that library, 172,062 and 172,053 values), every string is a plain ASCII decimal, and no epoch is padded or in other digits; so there is one strict rule and nothing published moves. **The first form and the review.** The first form kept a refused value as an empty one with a note beside it, for the values item to report. A separate reviewer, before commit, found three problems in that, each by running an adapter: the cases that pair a TLE with its OMM have no values item and compare the two readings with each other, and empty equals empty, so a parser with the doubled derivative those cases exist for passed them by padding its text in both formats, where it had failed before; a refused eccentricity or drag term on the OMM side reached arithmetic and ended the case in an internal error; and the corrupt-input case, which normalised records outside any guard, ended in an internal error for an epoch in other digits. All three came from letting a refused value travel on. So it no longer travels: it raises, where the file is read, and the file fails. The corrupt-input case's two unguarded places now fail the file as `parse` too, where any unreadable value, `"N/A"` included, used to end the case in an internal error. Not changed here and listed for the next release: an epoch string with whitespace around it is still read (none is returned by any run); the corpus's own reference reader still reads generously from a FILE, though what it returns is always plain; text with an exponent beyond the decimal range raises as before. Adversarial adapters (`tests/adversarial/test_hardening.py`): other-script digits in an epoch and in an element, an underscore, each kind of padding, and an object whose text form is padded, three failing cases each; their twins, the same value as plain text, which passes, and a wrong value as plain text, which fails; on provider data, the two parsers the reviewer wrote for the pairing cases and one padding the OMM file only, each failing with no internal error; and the grammar itself, accepted and refused forms both. Alternatives: allowing padding (no run needs it, and a padded field handed back is the input's text unparsed, the fault of D-306 in another field); refusing text altogether in favour of numbers (the protocol has allowed decimal strings since D-131, and two runs use them correctly); the first form, a failure on the record alone (it needs every later comparison to know about refused values, and three did not).

**D-320 (2026-10-11) — What the hardening review adds to the tests and to CI, on the owner's rulings: two wrong parsers' item statuses pinned on the full data, the properties that hold in the suite, and the gates split between every push and every night.** The review (mutation testing of the grading code, property-based tests, type and coverage checks; its report is in the private handoff) sorted its findings three ways. The two grading faults are D-318 and D-319. This entry is the test gaps taken now and the CI the owner adopted. **Item statuses.** Mutation testing left the most survivors in the checks that only provider data exercises, and the reason was plain once seen: the suite ran one parser against provider data, the reference adapter, which must pass, so a check could go lenient or stop running and no test would say so. `tests/test_item_statuses.py` runs the naive adapter and python-sgp4 2.27 on every case and holds every item they produce to a recorded status: 254 items with 81 failing, and 389 with 26 failing, the counts the catalogue publishes. It needs the maintainer's provider files, launch-window captures included, so it is a release-time test and skips in a clone, an export and public CI; the golden files hold check ids, file names and statuses, and no provider value. A runner change that moves an item fails it, and the golden file is then regenerated on purpose. **Properties.** `tests/test_properties.py` holds the eighteen properties that hold, for Alpha-5, the year pivot, epochs, catalog-id text, the element-value grammar and the checksum, run with Hypothesis where it is installed and skipped test by test where it is not; the package gains no dependency. The properties the review found not to hold are not there; they are reference-side leniencies listed for the next release. **CI.** Every push: the suite, mypy at its default settings, the properties at 100 examples, and a fuzzer smoke of 500 mutants. Every night, on every tag and by hand (`nightly.yml`): the 5,000-mutant fuzzer, which took five to seven minutes and had been on every push since D-287; the properties at 2,000 examples; branch coverage against a floor set just under what was measured in the public tree, 85% for the package and 80% for the runner, to be raised as tests land and never lowered; and mypy with the bodies of unannotated functions checked, as a ratchet on the count. At the release, by the checklist: the 20,000-mutant run, the sixteen published runs item by item, and the mutation run. mypy at default settings needed one rename in `gpconf/fetch.py` and nothing else; it found no defect in grading. Alternatives: keeping 5,000 mutants on every push (five minutes on every push for a check whose smaller run finds the same classes); a coverage floor on every push (it is the suite again, under a tracer); making the item-status test public by shipping provider data (the corpus does not redistribute it, D-023). For the next release, listed in the private handoff: the reference-side leniencies, the runner's wording for values it cannot read, the repeated-id note of D-317, the surviving mutants once the whole-suite pass has confirmed them, and publishing with provenance.

**D-321 (2026-10-11) — A float is read as its value, whatever it prints as: a correct parser returning `numpy.float64` no longer fails (the owner's ruling on a false failure the review of D-319 found, and which predates it).** The runner turned a float into a decimal by its `repr`. `numpy.float64` is a float, and under numpy 2 its `repr` is `np.float64(1.5)`, which is no number: a correct parser that returns its elements as `numpy.float64` failed every file, "parser raised InvalidOperation", fifteen cases on the full data, in the released versions as in this tree. Found by the reviewer of D-319 while checking that correct parsers were untouched by it. Now the value is taken, `repr(float(v))`, so a float subclass is read as the plain float it holds, and compared within the float tolerance as before. Nothing else in the float path changes: a NaN or an infinite float still ends in the runner's own words (listed for the next release). Adversarial adapters, per the Grader changes rule (`tests/adversarial/test_hardening.py`): a float subclass that prints as numpy 2 prints, so the test runs without numpy, with correct values, which passes item for item as plain floats do; its twin with one wrong value, which fails three cases; and the same two with `numpy.float64` itself where numpy is installed. The owner allowed one review round, the fix to wait for the next release if it found a problem. The round found none in the change: 500,026 plain floats give the same decimal by the old line and the new, NaN and infinity included; `numpy.float64` reads as the plain float of the same bits; a numpy-returning adapter on the full data equals its plain-float twin item for item, where at the commit before it failed fifteen cases; and the released 0.6.2 wheel fails the same way. It sorted one thing as a limit and said so plainly: a class built to return one value from `__float__` and hold another is read by its `__float__`, where before it was read by its `repr`; no library type does either, and `float.__repr__(v)` would read the stored value past both, which is noted for the next release with `numpy.float32`, which is not a float and is still compared as text. Also recorded here, the owner's acceptance of D-318's second half: a parser that declares TLE unsupported skips the count comparison, "since it follows the all-or-none rule"; D-318 states it. Alternatives: converting through `str(v)` (numpy's `str` of a float64 is plain today, and a library is free to change that as it changed `repr`); refusing float subclasses (a correct parser would fail for its number type).

**D-322 (2026-10-11) — The property tests do not skip silently where they are meant to run, and the release date is set (owner's rulings).** D-320 put eighteen properties in the suite, skipped where Hypothesis is not installed. The owner: "Property tests must not skip silently: add hypothesis as a dev/test dependency, and make the CI push job and nightly fail (not skip) if it's missing." Now: `pyproject.toml` has a `test` extra, `hypothesis>=6.100`, for the suite only; the package itself still needs nothing. `tests/test_properties.py` raises at import when `GPCONF_REQUIRE_HYPOTHESIS` is set and Hypothesis is absent, so the run errors; the push workflow sets it on the Python 3.12 job and the nightly workflow sets it, and both then run `tools/ran_not_skipped.py tests.test_properties 19`, which fails unless nineteen tests ran, the eighteen properties and one that counts them, and none was skipped: `unittest` itself exits 0 for a module whose every test skipped. Without the variable, as on a contributor's machine, each property is skipped by its own name, so the run says what it left out. One job cannot run them: Hypothesis needs Python 3.11 or later, and the push workflow keeps a Python 3.9 job, where they are skipped by name and the workflow's comment says why. In the maintainer's environment Hypothesis is installed, and the suite runs them. Second: the owner confirmed the release for Wednesday 2026-10-14, and the four date fields carry it (the changelog's heading, `CITATION.cff`, the README's citation line and the date of its table of upstream fixes). The table's date is the day its expiring cells are checked, so they are checked again on that day before anything is pushed, and the release waits if one has changed. Alternatives: Hypothesis as a dependency of the package (it is needed by nobody who runs the kit); failing everywhere it is absent (a clone without it could not run the suite at all).

**D-323 (2026-10-11) — The release date is Tuesday 2026-10-13, not the 14th of D-322 (owner).** The four date fields carry it: the changelog's heading, `CITATION.cff`, the README's citation line and the date of its table of upstream fixes. As D-322 has it, the table's date is the day its expiring cells are checked, so they are checked again on the 13th before anything is pushed; they were last checked on 2026-10-11 and stood (sgp4 2.27 on PyPI, satellite.js 7.1.0 on npm, Gpredict v2.6). The gates were run again on the commit that carries the date. Not before the 13th: an entry of this log names the owner's Swift library, which the owner ruled may be public only after 2026-10-12.

The fix makes the reader scan line by line and resume past an accepted pair. The check, at release v0.2.1 (`aa16b7c`, the version of the published row, an ancestor of the merge) and at the merge commit, satellite.js 6.0.2 as the application's lockfile resolves at both, Node.js 26.5.0: the report's own eight sets with the second set's line 2 removed give one name at v0.2.1, `SAT 0`, and seven at the merge, every set but the broken one; all eight unbroken give 8 at both. The `corrupt-input` case through the recipe's harness, gpconf 0.7.0: 4 failing items at v0.2.1 and 3 at the merge, `corrupt-input-neighbours-load` now passing (both valid sets around the broken one load). The case still fails, so no case status moves; the fix is in no release, the latest being v0.2.1, so no row and no count moves and the recipe stays pinned. kvnloo, who wrote a reference fix for the same report in a fork, credited the report publicly on #906 (comment of 2026-10-09). **D-325 (2026-10-14) — 0.7.1, the small edges of the grader (owner instruction, from the hardening review's W1 to W3 and the 0.7.1 list): values that are not finite and odd digits fail in their own words, an epoch string has nothing around it, a written line is ASCII, and the reference's day of year, year pivot, catalog-id digits and Alpha-5 input are held to what they are for; on the 0.7.1 branch, not the release commit.** What changed. `as_integer` answers an infinite float or Decimal as "not finite" where `int()` raised and the report read "parser raised OverflowError"; `norm_record` treats a NaN or an infinity as an element value the runner cannot read (it ended the case as "internal error in runner: InvalidOperation"); `norm_epoch` refuses an epoch string with whitespace around it, the rule D-319 gave element text and expressly left out of the epoch, and words a string the epoch reader refuses as the parser's value; a file that fails on such a value reads "the parser returned a value the runner cannot read", in both of the runner's paths and in the gate's note, where it read "parser raised UnreadableValue" or "parser raised ValueError", though the parser raised nothing. `tle.checksum` counts ASCII digits only (`¹` raised inside the runner, and `٣` counted 3), and `writer.check_lines` fails a written line that is not ASCII, with the layout's patterns ASCII too. The reference adapter's `parse_epoch` refuses day 366 of a common year, which `strptime`'s `%j` turned into the next year's 1 January, and `vectors/ccsds-epoch-strings.json` gains `2026-366T12:42:37` as a sixth invalid form; its `parse_catalog_id` takes ASCII digits only; `reference.two_digit_year` takes two ASCII digits or an integer of any integer type from 0 to 99; `tle.to_alpha5`, which the package exports, refuses what is not an integer (`25544.0`, `'25544'`, `True`), where `int()` made each a number it encoded. **The adversarial adapters** are in `tests/adversarial/test_edges_071.py`, each with its twin: an infinite catalog number or counter, a NaN or infinite element as float or Decimal, a superscript or another script's digits in a written line, one element field in another script's digits with the check digit recomputed, an epoch with whitespace around it, an epoch the reader refuses, and a `parse_epoch` that takes day 366; the twins (the same adapters with finite values, with ASCII digits, with the epoch as bare text, and the reference) pass. **The separate review** (CLAUDE.md, "Grader changes") read the first form and found one escape that remained: with the checksum counting ASCII digits only, a writer that put another script's digits in an element field and recomputed its check digit passed the writer case, since the layout's `\d` and the round trip read such digits as the numbers they spell; before the change the same writer passed by keeping the original check digit, so the change had moved the hole, not opened it. The ASCII rule for written lines closes both. It also found the epoch wording, the gate's note, the adapter guide's rows and the citations of D-319 for rules D-319 did not make; each is mended here. A second reading of the mended form found no escape and no false fail; it found an epoch that overflows the years a datetime holds still worded as an exception the parser raised, the adapter guide's row for an answer that is not a list, the ASCII rule missing from the guide and the check's text, a miscount in the changelog, and this entry saying more about another library than the Batch G rule allows; each is mended here. **Measured.** The whole suite, the eighteen properties with the test that counts them, and mypy at CI's settings pass. The three built-in adapters, the thirteen library runs behind the published rows and GPKit were run again under this tree: no case status moves in any of the seventeen reports; the reference and GPKit read "6 invalid strings rejected" where they read 5. A finding about astroz was recorded. The new vector is a specification vector, so the release that carries it is a minor one under the versioning rule. Alternatives: leaving the wording (the verdicts were right; the words blamed the wrong side, which is what the owner's list asked to fix); stripping whitespace around an epoch as the reader did (D-319's reason holds for the epoch: text a parser returns is graded as returned); a property per fix in `tests/test_properties.py` (left for 0.7.1's next step; each rule has its examples in the adversarial file).

**D-329 (2026-10-15) — 0.7.1: the fetch asks for gzip (owner instruction), and what it writes, hashes and records is still the data itself.** Every request carries `Accept-Encoding: gzip`, for a smaller transfer. A gzip answer is decompressed before anything else reads it, so the file written, its SHA-256 and the drift check against `manifest.json` are about the data and mean what they meant; the metadata gains `content_encoding` (`gzip` or `identity`) and `bytes_on_wire`, beside `bytes`, which stays the size of the data. An answer in another coding, which was not asked for, and a gzip body that does not decompress are responses the fetch did not expect: the run stops and keeps the body beside the data, as D-228 does for any other; a gzip answer that decompresses to an HTML page is still one. Tests: `tests/test_fetch_gzip.py`, with the network blocked and a stub opener. The README's paragraph on the fetch's requests says so. No request was made to verify it: whether CelesTrak answers in gzip is seen on the next real fetch, and its metadata will say. Alternatives: writing the gzip bytes and hashing them (every recorded SHA-256 would stop matching); leaving the fetch as it was (it asked for the larger transfer for no gain).

**D-330 (2026-10-15) — 0.7.1: an answer that is not a sequence of records fails in its own words (owner instruction; a grader change, with its adversarial adapters and twins).** `as_records` reads a parser's answer: any sequence of mappings is accepted, a tuple or a generator included; a mapping, a string, bytes or a non-sequence is "the answer is dict, not a list of records", and an entry that is not a mapping is "the answer holds str at entry 1, where every entry must be a record (a dict)". It is applied where the runner first reads an answer (the main path, the corrupt-input case's comparison file and its corrupt inputs, and the empty-answer check), and the file fails as `parse` with "the parser returned a value the runner cannot read". Before, an answer of strings ended the corrupt-input case as "internal error in runner: AttributeError" and read "parser raised AttributeError" elsewhere, though the parser raised nothing; the corrupt-input case's comparison file was set aside with no failure of its own when the answer for it was not a list, which left the case's checks not exercised where it now fails; and the empty-answer check and the corrupt-input case refused a tuple of records that the main path read. The adversarial adapters in `tests/adversarial/test_answers_071.py`: records as strings, a dict in place of the list, one string among the records, and the comparison file; their twins, the same records as a list, a tuple and a generator, pass. Alternatives: requiring a list everywhere (a correct parser returning a tuple would fail for its container, which says nothing about its reading).

**D-331 (2026-10-15) — Corrected: python-sgp4 rejects six of the eight valid epoch strings, not five (owner instruction to check it against python-sgp4 itself).** `vectors/ccsds-epoch-strings.json` said, from its first version (2026-09-20), that a parser hard-coded to `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%f`, python-sgp4's `sgp4.omm.initialize` for one, rejects five of the valid strings. [tested: 2026-10-15, python-sgp4 2.27, each of the eight valid strings put in a real OMM record's EPOCH and read by `sgp4.omm.initialize`, which calls `datetime.strptime(fields['EPOCH'], '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%f')`]: it accepts the two calendar forms with a fraction and no `Z` and rejects the other six, the three day-of-year forms, the calendar form without a fraction, the one ending in `Z` ("unconverted data remains: Z") and the leap second. The sentence now says six of the eight, and which; the file had the same eight valid strings when the sentence was written, so it was wrong from the start, and the leap second is the one it missed. No grading reads the sentence.

**D-336 (2026-10-15) — 0.8.0, 2f: the reference reader reads a file as strictly as the runner reads a parser's answer (D-319's limit) and refuses what the format does not allow; every frozen value is unchanged.** The reference reader made every frozen expected value, and on a user's own (live) bytes the runner compares a parser with it directly: it is the oracle, and under the owner's model a wrong value it lets through is an escape. It read a file's numbers with `Decimal()` and `int()`, which take underscores between digits, the digits of other scripts, Unicode spaces, NaN and Infinity, and it split TLE and KVN files at every line break Python knows. Measured on the reader as it stood (unchanged from e9f6666 to d490afe), with files written from the frozen 1998 ISS record: a KVN `MEAN_MOTION` with a line separator or a form feed inside it read as 16.05, the digits before it; a TLE element set number ` 1_0` read as 10; a TLE set with a form feed inside line 1 was passed over, no record and no error; NaN in CSV, JSON or XML and INF in XML were read as values; `16.050_64833`, the same digits in Arabic-Indic script, and the value with a no-break space after it read as 16.05064833. **What the reader now holds a file to** (`gpconf/reference.py`). A number: D-319's grammar, an optional sign and ASCII digits with an optional point and exponent (`PLAIN_NUMBER`, the runner's `PLAIN_DECIMAL`; integers `PLAIN_INTEGER`), once the format's own padding is taken off and nothing else: a TLE column's blanks; XML whitespace around a number (the vendored ndmxml-2.0.0 OMM schema: MEAN_MOTION is `ndm:revType`, an extension of `xsd:double`, NORAD_CAT_ID `xsd:integer`, whose whitespace rule is "collapse"); the blanks around a KVN value (CCSDS 502.0-B-3 7.4.5 to 7.4.7); nothing in CSV or JSON, where a space is part of the value. NaN and the infinities are refused, JSON's constants named by their key wherever they sit under it. The epoch: a parser's rule (D-319, D-325), nothing around it and a form the epoch reader reads; an XML epoch is a pattern on `xsd:string`, whose whitespace is kept, so padding is invalid there, while a bare point right after the seconds, before Z or an offset, is valid there; an offset from UTC only in XML, whose epochType allows one, since 7.5.10 gives a UTC epoch with an optional Z; an epoch past the years a datetime holds refused in words. TLE: split at CR, LF and CRLF only (`text_lines`), and what older files and saved copies carry around their sets taken off, none of it a value: the padding at a file's end that begins with a DOS end-of-file mark or a NUL and holds nothing but those and line ends, a run of CRs before an LF as one line end (CR CR LF, CRLF text written again in Windows' text mode), a page break (a form feed or a vertical tab) at the start of a line, and a line of nothing but blanks, tabs and page breaks, which reads as blank; a mark or NUL that ends the last line goes with the padding, and a file of nothing but padding reads as empty, which on live bytes fails as an unreadable source (D-113) (`tle_lines`, which the control adapter's `tle_sets` uses too); each line, the name line included, printable ASCII, the blanks between fields blank; the angles and the mean motion unsigned fixed-point numbers, the first derivative a signed one, with no exponent; the eccentricity seven digits; BSTAR and the second derivative a sign or a blank, five digits, a signed exponent, in their eight columns; the element set and revolution numbers and the ephemeris type digits; line 2's catalog field line 1's; the name line's blanks ASCII ones, Space-Track's leading `0 ` taken off; the international designator a year, a launch number and a piece, or blank; a blank classification no value. An element line is one that begins "1 " or "2 " after any whitespace and is longer than a name (24 characters, trailing blanks apart), or one that begins with the line number, any one character and a catalog field (`element_line`, which `tle_sets` uses too); one that pairs with nothing (a blank line inside a set, LFCR ends, a line 2 alone, a line set in from column 1, one with anything but a blank in column 2) is refused, and so is any other stray line that is not printable ASCII (an invisible character before a set's lines, a DOS end-of-file mark on a line of its own); the control adapter refuses each the same way, set by set (D-171). A printable character before both lines of a set still hides the set from both [a limit: no provider writes one]. KVN: split at CR, LF and CRLF; each line printable ASCII, a tab tolerated (7.3.4), and a COMMENT (indented or not) or KEYWORD = value (7.4.3); no assignment before a message's CCSDS_OMM_VERS; units only on the keywords that have units, after a blank, and only units the vendored NDM/XML schemas enumerate for that keyword (`rev/day` or `REV/DAY`, `deg`, `1/ER`, `kg` for MASS, `m**2` for the areas and so on), so a bracketed tail on any other keyword is part of its value. 7.7.1.1 says the units must match Table 4-3 exactly, case included; `docs/RESEARCH.md` records BSTAR's there as "1/[Earth radii]", which no KVN bracket can hold, while the schemas, CCSDS's examples and the corpus's own files write `1/ER` [inferred: the schemas taken as the table's units text; an open question until the table is read again]. JSON: no repeated key, no entry that is no object, text in a text field. XML: well-formed, no repeated element, block or segment (COMMENTs apart, which ommData allows in `<data>`), no markup inside a value, no text between elements, a `units` attribute on an OMM keyword only as KVN's units are allowed (the covariance's elements, which the reader does not read, keep theirs unchecked). CSV: no repeated column, nothing the csv module cannot read, the header included. Any format: no number whose plain form runs past 4,300 digits on either side of the point (`PLAIN_DIGITS`, Python's own limit for the digits of an integer read from text), and none whose exponent is past what `Decimal()` holds; a zero is zero whatever exponent `Decimal()` holds; an integer of more than 4,300 digits is refused in the reader's words; no OMM value comes near any of these bounds. A TLE field outside the rules keeps the reader's words, "TLE <field> field '...' is not a number"; an OMM field names its keyword; a KVN line its keyword. **On live bytes** (`gpconf/runner.py`): the file's epoch is read as an instant before it is compared, which the strict reader makes safe, since it refuses any epoch the epoch reader cannot read; before, a legal day-of-year epoch, a trailing Z, no fraction or a seventh fraction digit failed every parser, the reference adapter included. A leap second, which a datetime cannot hold, takes the instant a second earlier or the next one, as the epoch vectors do; at the last second of 9999 only the earlier, there being no next. Where a file carries no classification, a blank TLE column or an OMM file's empty, null or absent CLASSIFICATION_TYPE, a parser may answer None or `U`, Table 4-3's default, as D-285 allows None or the default for metadata a format does not carry; every frozen record holds U or C, so no frozen comparison changes. The frozen values hold the calendar form already and are unchanged. **Three users of the reader change with it.** `check-tle --against` reads its source records with it, so a records file it rejects is no reference for a round trip: it stops the check with exit 2, naming the file and what is wrong, where since D-119 a bad epoch was read and each record failed its round trip and other faults ended in a traceback; a missing file stops the same way; `docs/WRITERS.md` says so. The writer case and check-tle read written lines with `parse_tle_lines(..., written=True)`: every rule above holds for them but two, the name line and the designator, which the writer contract reports for information and never fails (WRITERS.md, the hooks table): a written designator that is no designator ("UNKNOWN") is no OBJECT_ID, not a failure. And two tests' wrong parsers borrowed the reader for a sloppy reading: the corrupt-input case's C-style reader of a short line 2 now reads the eccentricity's digits up to the blank and ignores the blanks between fields itself, and fails as it did, with the same values in its words; `test_source_reading`'s truncated TLE file, a line 1 with no line 2, is now rejected outright, as a BOM is. **The separate review, eight times** (CLAUDE.md, "Grader changes"), each reader fresh and given the owner's model. The first reading of the first form found: an escape that form made, a KVN line with a Unicode space before its keyword set aside silently; the older form of it, a KVN value broken by CR or LF read as its first digits; the live epoch forms above, a false fail older than this entry; an exponent in the eccentricity or a fixed-point column and two signs on an exponent field read as numbers; an epoch past year 9999 reported as an internal error of the corpus; the writer case as a third user; wording; and, older and low, a repeated element, column or key, markup inside an XML value, units with no blank, line 2's catalog field. The second, of the first mend: a false fail the mend made, an indented COMMENT refused; an escape it made, a JSON constant inside an array read; older escapes, values written over the blanks between TLE fields (BSTAR `-116060-4` over columns 53 to 61 read as +0.000011606, its sign lost), signs in the TLE's unsigned columns, a repeated XML block read first-wins, text between XML elements set aside, a TLE element line that pairs with nothing passed over, a KVN message without its version line skipped, a JSON text field read through Python's `str()`, units taken off any keyword; a UTC offset outside XML; a leap second taking one instant only; the all-files test reading nothing in a public export, where a derived file's empty `http_status` read as an error; counts; and a CSV field past the csv module's limit or JSON nested too deep ending check-tle in a traceback. The third, of the second mend: two false fails it made, a COMMENT directly in XML `<data>` refused and a leap second at the end of 9999 ending the case as an internal error; older escapes, a TLE element line with anything but a blank in column 2 passed over, and the name line read with Unicode `strip()` and held to nothing, the designator's piece unchecked; older false fails, a blank classification read as `' '`, Space-Track's `0 ` kept in a name, an XML epoch with a bare point refused; and wording. The fourth, of the third mend, judged none of its findings likely on real provider files: a test of the column-2 rule that did not guard it; the new name and designator rules failing written lines against the writer contract; an element line with an odd column 2 that is not 69 characters, or with an invisible character before it, still passed over; XML `units` attributes unchecked; which answers pass for a blank classification; a bare point before an offset; wording. The fifth, of the fourth mend: a crash it made, a last line that is not printable ASCII read past the end of the file (IndexError, the runner blaming the corpus, check-tle ending in a traceback, the control raising instead of refusing); a false fail it made, schema-legal `units` on the spacecraft parameters and the covariance refused; older and negligible, a point after an XML epoch's fraction taken off as bare, the element-line rule's words and padded short names, the classification rule's reach, and a written designator that is no designator failing the round trip against the writer contract. Every finding of the five within the model is mended as described above. **The owner's ruling on the fifth reading** (2026-10-15): one more reading, limited to the latest mend's diff, and the commit if it finds nothing the mend made and nothing likely on real provider files; nothing is negligible that is a crash blamed on the corpus or plausible on CelesTrak's or Space-Track's output or common older files, and those are mended; everything else is a limit stated here. And a property test (`tests/test_properties.py`, `ReaderOnAnyBytes`): bytes from nowhere, or a valid file of each format with a few bytes inserted, deleted or replaced, given to the reader and to `check-tle --against` give records or a refusal in words, and check-tle exits 0, 1 or 2, never anything else; 100 examples in CI, 20,000 nightly. At 3,000 it found a crash older than this entry, a carriage return inside a CSV header field raising the csv module's own error from the header, read before the guard around the rows: the runner blaming the corpus and check-tle ending in a traceback; the header is now read inside the guard. And the ruling took in what the fifth reading had left outside the model, an exponent so large that writing the number out filled memory (`1E9999999999`, ten billion digits): such a number is refused in words. **The sixth reading**, of the latest mend's diff, under that ruling: not yet, for two things the ruling does not let stand. (1) A crash older than this entry, in the path the mend said it closed: a number whose exponent is past what `Decimal()` holds (`1E9999999999999999999`, `0E1000000000000000000`) made `Decimal()` raise `decimal.InvalidOperation`, an ArithmeticError and no ValueError, from `plain()` and from inside `json.loads`, so the runner reported the reference reader raising, check-tle ended in a traceback and the control adapter raised; the any-bytes property, with its fixed seed, repeated the same examples every night and never spelt such a number. (2) A false fail older than the fifth reading's mend, plausible on common older (DOS-era) files and never on CelesTrak's or Space-Track's: a TLE file whose every set is valid was refused whole when it ended in a DOS end-of-file mark or carried a page break or a tab-only line between sets or a page break before a name line; it now reads as its sets (above), as it did before this entry. And wording: the bound's sentence (it is on either side of the point; a zero with a large exponent was refused and is zero now; a long number with no exponent was refused in words about an exponent), the units sentence for elements that are no OMM keyword, a runner comment, and the csv module's advice to whoever opened the file, no longer passed on. Outside this change, its own entry next: the runner's TLE/OMM consistency check passes a parser's BSTAR through the TLE field renderer, which raises for a magnitude of 1E9 or more or a non-zero one below 1E-10, outside any guard, so a parser answering "1E99" ends the baseline case as an internal error of the runner [whether a provider ever writes a BSTAR or second derivative below 1E-10 in magnitude is an open question]. And it asked whether the live oracle's leap-second branch held where `strftime("%Y")` pads no year below 1000; the mend's first answer, writing the second instant in the ISO form, did not reach the crash (the seventh reading). **The seventh reading**, of that mend: nothing the mend made but wording, nothing likely on CelesTrak's or Space-Track's bytes, and two older things the ruling does not let stand. (1) A false fail on older files: the DOS end-of-file mark was taken off only as the very last byte, so a file padded with it to the end of an XMODEM block, or with a line end or a NUL after it, was still refused; the padding is now taken off whole, NUL padding with it. (2) A crash: where `strftime("%Y")` pads no year below 1000 (glibc, under the Pythons that leave it so, as CI's 3.9 run may [inferred: which versions is an open question; neither the code nor its test rests on it]), `iso_epoch` writes '999-...', and the leap-second branch read that back with `strptime` and raised ValueError, an internal error of the runner; the second instant is now built from the numbers and written as `iso_epoch` writes, and a test simulates the unpadded year. And: JSON's refusal of a number past what `Decimal()` holds names its key, as NaN's does; an integer of more than 4,300 digits is refused in the reader's words, where `int()` gave advice meant for whoever runs Python; the bound's wording (an exponent's size, not its digits; a zero); and, older and plausible on users' saved copies, a TLE file with CR CR LF line ends was refused as pairing with nothing (the reader before this entry read no set from it, without a word), and now reads. **The eighth reading**, of that mend: one thing it made, outside the model, a hang: the two new patterns were tried again at every byte of a run, so a long run of NULs, marks or CRs not at the file's end took time growing with its square (64 KiB of NULs between two sets, 10 s); the reviewer's own form, string operations and a look-behind, gives the same lines on 499,593 strings it compared and takes 12 ms on 1 MiB, and is the one committed. And wording: the exponent bound (Decimal() holds negative exponents further than positive ones, so the bound is said as what it holds), the line-break limit (columns 1 to 6), the changelog's CR CR LF (it reads for the first time), padding that ends the last line, a top-level JSON entry's words, the platform the year padding depends on; and two tests made to guard more (the unpadded year's second instant, across the year's end, and its twin; BSTAR named). Outside this change, for the runner's own entry: a parser answering a number past what `Decimal()` holds fails as "parser raised InvalidOperation", though the runner raised it, where D-325's words would be right. **Limits, stated and not changed:** a printable character before both lines of a TLE set hides the set (above);
