**D-337 (2026-10-15) — 0.8.0: everything a Python adapter returns is read once into plain built-in values inside the guard, and no check calls a method of an object the adapter made; the threat model stated (the owner's rulings on the separate reviewer's second and third readings of D-334; W0's leftovers, 2g of the plan, done here).** **The model, in the owner's words:** gpconf grades wrong answers. Any wrong value that survives conversion to plain values is an escape and gets fixed. An in-process adapter that attacks the runner itself (patching it, reading expected values, etc.) is out of scope — in-process adapters are trusted not to do that; untrusted parsers use --cmd. `docs/ADAPTERS.md` now says so, in "What the runner reads, and what it trusts", and every reviewer of this change was given it as its brief. **Why.** D-334 read a lazy answer inside the guard and copied each record into a plain dict. The reviewer's second reading found the parser's code still run after the guarded call had returned: (1) a list or tuple subclass's own `__iter__`, which ran in `as_records`, so an exit there ended the run and a raise read "internal error in runner"; (2) the copy `dict(r)`, which called a record's own `keys()` and `[]` outside the guard; (3) the same copy losing what a dict subclass hid from `keys()`, `_refused` among it, so a correct parser failed; (4) D-306 dodged by a str subclass whose `strip()` says nothing or whose `__eq__` lies once; (5) a key that is not text ending three cases as "internal error in runner"; (6) a value's own `__str__` ending the run with `sys.exit()`; (7) text that said more than the code. A first mend, written and not committed, read a dict subclass by what it holds, turned str subclasses into text and caught an exit at the case. The third reading, given the model, found that mend not clean: (1) an escape it made: a dict subclass that holds the right value and hands a wrong one out through every method passed; (2) a false fail it made: a record type that holds its fields under keys of its own and shows the protocol's names failed three cases; (3) older escapes, on the code before and after: text from an object whose `__str__` hands back a str subclass whose `__eq__` always says equal, a datetime subclass whose `strftime()` lies, and the input's own epoch handed back inside a `UserString`, each passing all five cases that need no data; (4) hook answers, int and str subclasses whose comparisons lie, passing the Alpha-5 and year-pivot vectors while computing nothing; (5) a value whose `__str__` raises the runner's own `CorpusIncomplete` ending the run with exit 2 in the parser's words; (6) a twin in the tests that was not exact; (7) wording. All of it has one root: an in-process adapter returns objects, and the runner called their methods. The owner ruled (2026-10-15): read everything the parser returns into plain built-in values once, inside the guard; a dict subclass read both through its methods and by what it holds, a disagreement failing in words; str, int and datetime subclasses as plain values; floats by value; any exception from the parser's code caught inside the guard, the runner's own `CorpusIncomplete` included; the twin and the wording mended; a property test that nothing but plain built-ins leaves the guard. **What changed.** A new module, `gpconf/plain.py`, holds one reading per kind of value: None, bool, int, float, str, bytes and Decimal as they are, a subclass of int, float, str, bytes or Decimal as the value it holds, read by the base type past any method of its own, a bytearray or memoryview as the bytes it holds; any other integer type (numpy's) through `operator.index`; any other binary floating type (numpy's `float16`, `float32`, `float64`, `longdouble`) as the float of its value, so that a `float32` mean motion is compared as the value it holds, not as the short text it prints, and fails at the relative 1e-12 a float is held to; a datetime, date or timedelta built again from the fields it holds, read by the base type's descriptors, a `datetime.timezone` from the offset and the name it holds, and a timezone of the adapter's own as the fixed offset it gives; a list or tuple element by element, a subclass of either by what it holds and through its own iteration, which must agree; a record, a dict by what it holds, a dict subclass by what it holds and through its own `keys()` and `[]`, which must agree, and any other mapping through its `keys()` and `[]` (the bounds of this rule are the owner's ruling on the boundary's third reading, below); a transparent proxy that says it is a record, an integer (any `numbers.Integral`) or a datetime as one, read through its own methods; a key that is a str subclass as its text, a key that is not text left out; anything else as its `str()`. The guard (`_Guarded`) reads every return through it, `parse()`'s answer, every hook's answer, `write_tle`'s lines and any attribute it is asked for, all before the guard is left; a property is read inside the guard too. The reading is not meant to raise at all, since a raise inside the guard is the parser's refusal: a record that disagrees with itself or holds a field twice, or an entry that is no record, travels on as the runner's own `Problem`, which `as_records` words. An exception the parser's code raises, from `parse()` or while its answer is read, is turned inside the guard into the runner's `ParserRaised` of the same name and message (or `Unsupported`), so no method of the parser's exception runs later and its `CorpusIncomplete` is no longer the runner's; where no check takes one, the case fails as `parser-raised` in its words. `run_case` keeps a net for an exit raised outside every guard, which nothing should now reach. **What it closes**, against the readings: second reading 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 and third reading 1, 3, 4 and 5 are closed; second reading 3, the record type that hides `_refused` from `keys()`, and third reading 2, the record type that shows names it does not hold, now fail in words, as the owner ruled, where D-334 and D-330 passed them: a record that holds one thing and shows another has no one answer. **The adversarial adapters** are in `tests/adversarial/test_answers_071.py`: `TheReviewersSecondReading`, its dict-subclass test now the two-reading rule (a type that hides `_refused`, one that doubles a value it holds, one that holds its fields under keys of its own, one whose `keys()` exits, against plain dicts and a dict subclass that agrees with itself), its list and tuple twin made exact and compared item by item; and `TheReviewersThirdReading`, one test per finding with its twin: text from objects whose comparisons lie, a datetime subclass whose `strftime()` lies, the input's epoch inside a `UserString` or an object of its own, hook answers whose comparisons lie, the runner's `CorpusIncomplete` raised from `parse()` and from a value, a float subclass whose `__repr__` and `__float__` give the right value while it holds another, and a binary32 value registered as a `numbers.Real`, against the plain wrong values (which fail) and the honest ones (which pass). On the runner before this entry all of them together give 23 failures and 6 errors across their subtests, with the final test file [tested]. The property tests gain two (`PlainBoundary`): whatever an adapter returns, built from lying subclasses of str, int, float, Decimal, datetime, list and dict, objects of its own and nesting, the reading holds nothing but plain built-in values and `Problem`; and a plain value reads as itself. CI checks that twenty-four properties ran, D-336's three and `RealWorldTypes` among them. **The boundary's own reading.** A fresh reviewer, given the model, read this change and found: (1) an escape it made: the reading turned a refusal reason of bytes, a set or an object into its `str()`, a non-empty reason, so a corrupt record was credited as refused with a reason, where D-144 counts a reason that is not a string as a drop; now a reason counts only when the adapter gave text, and bytes stay bytes; (2) a false fail it made: `write_tle` answering bytes, a generator, an iterator or a map read as `str()`; now its answer has a reading of its own (`plain.lines`), a str or bytes block as it is and any other iterable read in full, inside the guard; (3) a false fail it made: a type registered as `numbers.Integral` without `__index__`, or as `numbers.Real` without `__float__`, raised inside the reading, which read as the parser raising; now `int()` or the text is used, and a huge integer or a deep nest no longer raises (the comparison of two readings no longer turns an int into text, and a value nested more than 32 levels deep is not read further); (4) a false fail it made: a property raising `Unsupported` read as the parser raising it; now it answers `Unsupported` when called, as from inside the call; (5) older, the same root as the owner's ruling: a list subclass whose own iteration shows other records than it holds, on an answer or on the provider's empty answer, and a dict subclass honest through `keys()` and `[]` but not through `get()` or `items()`, passed; the ruling's reason, a record that holds one thing and shows another has no one answer, is the same for these faces, so a list or tuple subclass is now read by what it holds and through its own iteration, and a dict subclass through `items()` and `get()` as well, each disagreement failing in words; (6) wording: the model quoted with the owner's punctuation, `--cmd` said to be no sandbox (it runs as the user and could read the expected values; it cannot patch the runner or hand it objects), the second reading's item 3 listed where it belongs, the contract texts and the changelog brought up to what the code does, the claim that the reading never raises withdrawn, a class whose metaclass makes up a `__name__` named by its own, a Ctrl-C passed through the exit's reading; (7) older: the writer case read "-753 of 0 records correct" when no output could be read as lines, and three items passed on nothing written; now such output counts in the checksum item and the items that checked nothing read `not-exercised`. Outside the model, not changed: an adapter whose `__class__` claims to be the runner's guard, and gc of objects the adapter made. Each has a test in `TheBoundarysFirstReading`, with its twin; on the first form of this change they give 15 failures and 1 error, with the final test file [tested]. **numpy, measured** with the repository's numpy 2.5.3 [tested]: `float16`, `float32`, `float64` and `longdouble` read as Python floats, numpy's integers as ints, `numpy.str_` as text; a mean motion returned as `float64` or `longdouble` passes the three cases that need no data, one returned as `float32` fails them, and D-321's `float64` test passes. **The boundary's second reading**, by another fresh reviewer, of the mend: every finding of the first closed, and: (1) an escape older than this mend, present in the change's first form: a `datetime.timezone` left the guard as it was, holding a timedelta and a str subclass of the parser's own, and a property's `AttributeError` left it as the parser's own exception; their methods ran after the guard, in the words of a failing item, and one that raised the runner's own `ParserExit` was swallowed by `run_case`'s `except ParserExit: pass`, so the case stopped early and read pass on what had passed so far, or the run ended through `CorpusIncomplete`; now a timezone is built again from the offset and name it holds, a property's `AttributeError` becomes the runner's own with its text read inside the guard, and a `ParserExit` the guard did not count is counted, never swallowed; (2) a false fail the mend made: what a container held was read before its faces, so one that fills itself when first read was judged two-faced, and an answer's records in another order were too, though their order is not graded; now every face is read first and what is held last, and an answer's records are compared in any order; (3) older: a mapping that lists a field twice with one value failed as "a str subclass beside the plain key"; now it is one field, and two values for one field fail in plain words; (4) the writer's words: a two-faced answer read "'Problem' object is not iterable", and with nothing written the checksum item read pass beside two catalog-field items; now the answer's problem is worded and the item reads `not-exercised`, once; (5) wording: the guide's rule said more than the faces compared, so a mapping that is not a dict is now compared through `keys()` and `[]`, `items()` and `get()`, a list subclass through its `len()` and `[]` as well as its iteration, and the guide says which; the test comment that bytes read as text, and two test docstrings; (6) older: the empty-answer check had no fallback to an adapter that is itself callable, and a refusal's `_input` given as bytes was quoted as its `repr`; both mended. Outside the model and mended for the cost: honest nested subclasses were read once per face at every level, an exponential reading; faces that hand back the very same objects are now read once. Each has a test in `TheBoundarysSecondReading`, with its twin; on the mend that reading read they give 10 failures across their subtests, with the final test file, the cost's among them: that test does not end there and was stopped by hand (ten nested levels already take 2.26 s there, against well under one here) [tested]; and the property `PlainBoundary` now generates bytes, fixed-offset and named timezones and timezones holding the parser's own subclasses. **The boundary's third reading**, by another fresh reviewer, of the second mend, found: (1) two false fails that mend made, a list subclass whose `[]` looks a record up by catalog number and a mapping registered with `Mapping.register` that has `keys()` and `[]` but no `items()` or `get()`, each failing three cases as the parser raising; (2) older: containers with storage of their own that are no dict, list or tuple subclass (a `deque` or `UserList` subclass, a dict subclass behind `MappingProxyType`, `ChainMap` or `UserDict`), whose other faces nothing compared, so the extended rule would want them too; (3) older: transparent proxies (the wrapt `ObjectProxy` and lazy-object-proxy pattern), which `isinstance()` sees as what they wrap and `type()` does not, failing every case that reads records, catalog numbers or epochs behind one; (4) the writer's words: a writer that wrote three records with a wrong catalog field and declined the rest had only the all-or-none item for the field, which said nothing of the three; (5) the runner's own `Problem` shown in words, "A0000 -> Problem('...')"; (6) a capability declaration whose value is a false one of the adapter's own type (numpy's `bool_` pattern) read as true, so a dropped record read as dropped silently by an adapter that reports refusals; (7) wording, stale counts and twins in this entry. Every route it tried through the faces the runner reads was closed. **The owner's ruling (2026-10-15): bounded.** A dict, list or tuple subclass has its storage compared with what it shows, a dict subclass's `keys()` and `[]`, a list's or tuple's own iteration; every other container is read through one defined face and converted to plain values; the `[]` and `len()` and the `items()` and `get()` extensions are reverted; the limit is stated in `docs/ADAPTERS.md` and here; proxies are honoured through `isinstance()` in the fallback paths only, records, integers and datetimes, read through the proxy's own methods inside the guard. **D-343 (2026-10-17) — 0.8.0, 2a: an id the input holds more than once is compared copy by copy with the input's record each copy matches, and the item says so (D-317's withdrawn note, done as it said it should be).** D-311 stated a limit: where a live file holds an id twice with records that differ, every copy a parser returns is compared with the one record the oracle keeps for that id, so a correct parser fails there; D-317 withdrew a note meant to excuse it after four readings found three smaller forms of it unsound, and kept for 0.7.1 the right size: "matching each returned copy to one of the input's records, so that the runner knows which values are the input's". The 0.8.0 plan's 2a, in the owner's order. **What changed** (`gpconf/runner.py`). The oracle keeps every record of an id the input holds more than once (`_oracle_by_id`: the first record, with all of them under `_copies`), from the frozen records or from the reference reader's reading of live bytes, where it kept the last alone; `compare_values` compares each returned copy with one of the input's records (`_match_copies`: first, a copy that gives both its element set number and its revolution is paired with the one record of that ordinal, if it is free and the copy fails nothing against it, a lookup each; the copies left are paired with the records left at the least cost, a failure weighing more than any number of values within tolerance: exhaustively up to seven of each, up to 10,000 pairs least cost first and, where that leaves a failure, by augmenting paths over the pairs that fail nothing, so that a pairing failing nothing is found wherever one exists, and beyond 10,000 in epoch order, a stated limit (where two of those records share an epoch, or lie within the tolerance of each other, and differ, a correct parser that returns them in another order than the input's can fail; a wrong parser never passes); every record is paired with a copy while copies last, and a copy beyond them, the surplus D-311 fails, goes to the record it matches best, among those of its ordinal, or all of them, or, past the cap, the first), each failure naming the copy and the record ("copy 2 of 2, against the input's record 2 of 2"); and the values item says, passing or failing, "the input holds 1 id more than once with records that differ (e.g. id 25544, 2 records): each copy returned is compared with the input's record it matches (D-343)". **D-361 (2026-10-16) — Trusted Publishing: `.github/workflows/publish.yml` builds the release from its tag the way the maintainer does, publishes nothing that is not byte for byte the maintainer's build, and the maintainer's hashes travel in the annotated tag's message (0.8.0, item 8; lane B, numbered at the merge).** The owner's plan (`docs/PLAN.md`, "publishing with provenance") and ruling (the PyPI and GitHub setup is the owner's). **What the workflow does.** On a pushed tag `v*`, a build job (`contents: read`, the checkout's credentials not kept) checks out the tag and, before setup-python and the toolchain from PyPI run, fetches the tag object itself (`actions/checkout` may leave a lightweight ref), stops unless the tag is annotated, names the commit the run checked out (`GITHUB_SHA` peeled to a commit, so either reading of it holds [inferred: it names the commit on a tag push; not settled here, so both are handled]) and that commit is on `main`, and records the tag object; it then builds the sdist and the wheel from `git archive` of the commit with `tools/stage_package.py`, Python 3.14.6, build 1.6.1, setuptools 84.0.0, packaging 26.3 and pyproject_hooks 1.3.3 (the maintainer's toolchain, D-203, D-259) and `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` the commit's committer time; and `tools/release_hashes.py check` passes only when the tag is `v<version>` (the version of `[project]`, read with `tomllib` where Python has it, as the build reads it), the build made exactly `gpconf-<version>-py3-none-any.whl` and `gpconf-<version>.tar.gz`, the tag's message holds exactly one well-formed line `<64 lowercase hex>  <file name>` for each and no other line with a SHA-256 in it, and each file hashes to its line; otherwise the job fails, and the runner's files are kept for 14 days as an artifact no job downloads. A publishing job, in the environment `pypi` (the owner approves each deployment; deployments only from tags `v*`), holds `id-token: write` and nothing else and runs no build tool; its own steps install nothing and check nothing out: it downloads the two files, fetches the tag again by itself, logs the tag object, its commit, the object the build job read and `github.event.after`, stops, saying why, unless the tag is still the object the build job read and, on a push, one the push event names (the tag object [inferred] or, if GitHub gives the commit, the commit), and runs the tag's own `release_hashes.py`, in Python's isolated mode, on the downloaded files against the tag's own message; then `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish` uploads them by OIDC with PEP 740 attestations. That action's definition is pinned by commit; the container image it pulls is named by a registry tag after that commit, not by a digest (read in its `create-docker-action.py` at the pinned commit), so the pin covers the definition, not the image. Run by hand on a tag, the same build and checks publish to TestPyPI only (environment `testpypi`); run by hand on a branch, nothing builds. No configured secret is read; the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` carries `contents: read` in the build job and no scope in the publishing jobs. **What it rests on.** The workflow holds what it publishes to what the tag's message names; who may write the tag is GitHub's to enforce (a tag ruleset; today the owner alone has write access), and which run is approved is the owner's. With write access to `v*` tags and a compromised build job together, nothing in the file stops a re-made tag: re-making it is a push, which starts a run of its own in which the tag, the event and the build job agree; the event check stops only the first run's re-made tag, and only where the event names the tag object; and the object the build job read reaches the publishing job as a job output, delivered when the build job ends, after the toolchain ran, which a compromised toolchain might forge [inferred]. What the tag-object check gives is a stop, in words, when the tag changes between an honest build and the approval. So the handoff has the owner approve only a lone waiting run whose build log names the tag object and commit of the owner's own tag. Actions pinned by commit (D-269), every pin a commit that an upstream tag of the action's own repository names, looked up read-only on 2026-10-16 (`gh api` GET): `actions/upload-artifact` v7.0.2 `cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9`, `actions/download-artifact` v8.0.2 `9000827ccba6bdab643e8b6fd33ac0654aef8333`, `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish` v1.14.2 `dc37677b2e1c63e2034f94d8a5b11f265b73ba33` (tag object `a892a5a6`), and the commits CI already pins, `actions/checkout` `fbc6f399` (v5.1.0, which `v5` names that day) and `actions/setup-python` `ece7cb06` (v6.3.0, `v6` that day); publish.yml names the exact release beside each. **Where the hashes travel: the annotated tag's message.** The maintainer builds from an archive of the commit to be tagged, before tagging, writes the message with `release_hashes.py message`, and tags with it; the workflow reads it back with `git for-each-ref --format=%(contents)`. A hash file in the tree cannot work as simply: the epoch is the tagged commit's own time, so a file committed in that commit would have to hold the hashes of a build that needs the commit to exist first (and the file must then stay out of the sdist, which `stage_package.py` would do, since it stages named paths only). **Checked** [tested, 2026-10-16]: v0.7.0, built again on this machine from the public clone's tag with the release build environment and epoch 1792023858, gives PyPI's two hashes (D-328), and `release_hashes.py check` passes with them in a message, fails (exit 1) with one digit changed and refuses (exit 2) the tag `v0.7.1`; and the workflow itself, every `run:` block executed as written by bash with `-eo pipefail` against a scratch repository made from this branch's export, the `uses:` steps stood in for and the publish action replaced by a stub that uploads nothing, in twelve scenarios: a pushed tag reaches PyPI and not TestPyPI, a run by hand on the tag TestPyPI and not PyPI, a run on `main` builds nothing; a wrong hash, a lightweight tag, a tag off `main`, a tag moved after the push, a tag not naming the version and a tag re-made before the build each stop the build job; a wheel changed after the build job's check, as a compromised build job could, is stopped by the publishing job's own check, and so is the same with the tag re-made after the build to name the changed files, at the tag object (a compromise that reaches the files and not the build job's outputs); and the publishing job's check alone, against a tag re-made before the build with a compromised build's files, stops when the push event names the pushed tag object and passes when it names the re-made object, the commit or nothing, the limits. 34 tests in `tests/test_release_hashes.py`: the check on folders made in the test, the message through a real `git tag -a`, the version readers, the workflows read as text (every action pinned by a full commit id with its version named, the exact release in publish.yml; publish.yml's shape held exactly: its three jobs and no other, each job's whole condition, its permissions, one publish step in each publishing job after the check, the one `repository-url`, no `write-all`, `packages-dir` or secret; the tag read before setup-python), and the publishing step itself run by bash against a scratch repository, passing and stopping where it should; the wrong forms the two readings built, five of the workflow and three of the step's guards, are kept as cases the tests must catch. The owner's setup and the release's new order (build, a Linux build of the same commit, then the tag) are in the private handoff. [untested until a first run on GitHub: the actions themselves, the publish action's image, PyPI's acceptance of the token, the environment's approval, what `GITHUB_SHA` and `github.event.after` hold on an annotated tag push, and whether the Linux build matches the maintainer's macOS build at 0.8.0; it did at 0.6.1 (D-259) and was not tried at 0.7.0, so the handoff puts a Linux build of the commit before the tag.] **Read before commit by a separate reviewer** (the owner's instruction for a release path), which found no escape within the model, no wrong event and no permission held that is not needed, and twelve findings, each answered: (1) the approval exists only if the environment does, with its protections, before the first tag, since GitHub creates a missing one unprotected, while the owner's list put the PyPI publisher first: the handoff now creates and protects the environments first and checks them before the tag; (2) the publishing job held the tag only to the commit, so write access to the tag and a compromised build job together could re-make it: it now holds it to the tag object the build job read and, on a push, to the event's, which stops less than that (the second reading, below; "What it rests on" says what), and the tag ruleset is required before the first release, no longer optional; (3) the publish action's image is not covered by its pin: said above; (4) the Linux build was last shown to match at 0.6.1: a Linux build of the commit before the tag; (5) the tests checked each job's condition anywhere in the file, so a swap of the two publishing jobs' conditions, or PyPI's widened to a run by hand, passed: each job's whole condition is read in its own text, and both forms are kept as cases; (6) the pins named moving major tags: the exact releases, looked up, are named; (7) "installs nothing" was said of the whole job, and "no secret" of the token too: worded as above; (8) the diagnostic artifact was named as if never published, and is kept on refusals too: renamed `runner-build-not-published`, the handoff saying it is downloadable as any artifact of a public repository is; (9) the version was read by a pattern stricter than the build (a comment after it, single quotes, another table's `version` first): `[project].version` by `tomllib`, a pattern scoped to `[project]` before Python 3.11, both held to the same forms; (10) the publishing job's guards stopped without a word: each says why; (11) the check now runs in Python's isolated mode; (12) this entry's number appears in five exported files (publish.yml, `tools/release_hashes.py`, the tests' docstring, `PUBLIC_ALLOWLIST.txt`, `CHANGELOG.md`), each to change at the renumbering. **A second reading**, limited to the mends, found no escape, false stop, permission or wrong event they made, and six things, each answered: the binding of (2) described as protecting more than it does (reworded above, and the handoff's approval made a lone run whose build log names the owner's tag object and commit); six wrong forms the 30 tests then let through (a fourth job publishing by hand with `write-all`, an upload of another folder, a second publish step, the event guard deleted or made always true, the tag guard taking an empty value), now caught, the step itself run under bash; "before any third-party code" loose, `actions/checkout` running first (now "before setup-python and the toolchain"); the handoff's step reading a log that does not exist before the approval (a log line added, the step reworded); two edges of the version reader, a `project` that is no table (an AttributeError, exit 1) and a version with a line break (refused later), now refused at once; and the owner's list in the plan still in the old order (corrected there). Both reports are copied whole in the private handoff. Alternatives: the hashes in a file of the tree (above); in a repository or environment variable the owner sets per release (mutable, outside the repository's record, one more manual step each release); as inputs of a run by hand (the tag push would no longer be the trigger); checked only in the build job, its outputs carried to the publishing job (the build job runs a toolchain installed from PyPI, which could rewrite both the files and the outputs); installing the toolchain with `--require-hashes` (its hashes cannot be had here without a download; with the publishing job's own check a compromised toolchain can stop a release, not change one, and pinning by hash is left to the owner); GitHub's own build-provenance attestations (`actions/attest-build-provenance`, which needs `attestations: write`; PyPI's PEP 740 attestations are what the plan names); a check in the publishing job that the environment is protected (it would need another permission in the job that holds the token; the handoff's check before the tag does it); a concurrency group (it would hold a TestPyPI rehearsal behind the waiting PyPI deployment, and PyPI refuses a second upload of a file name).

**D-362 (2026-10-16) — G1's synthetic two-file set: the adversarial routes of D-318 run without provider files, so they run in a clone, an export and public CI (0.8.0, item 4; lane B, numbered at the merge).** D-318's four adversarial adapters needed the provider's `decaying.csv` and `decaying.tle` and skipped everywhere else; so did the one route of D-319 that needs a single TLE/OMM set. Now `tests/adversarial/test_hardening.py` writes, at test time and into a temporary data folder, a synthetic two-file set from the frozen values of `fixtures/bstar-and-derivative-forms/expected.json`, which the export ships unscrubbed: `decaying.csv` with the set's 82 records in CelesTrak's columns and order, `decaying.tle` with the 79 whose catalog number is below 100000, rendered by the corpus's writer as CelesTrak renders (BSTAR and the second derivative rounded to five digits, the eccentricity truncated to seven), CR LF line ends, each with a `.meta.json` beside it saying it is synthetic, written by the test, from the frozen values. No provider byte is read, copied or shipped, no data file is committed, and no case, `expected.json` or manifest is touched. The D-318 routes (the reference adapter with one file of the pair; a parser that drops every TLE record with both present; a parser with no TLE reader; and its twin, unsupported for that one file) are one set of tests run twice: on the provider's files where they are on disk, as before, and on the synthetic set always, with one more test that holds the set to its source: the reference reader reads back every frozen value from the CSV and, from the TLE, every field as the case froze the provider's printing of it, and the reference adapter fails nothing, its count comparison reading "TLE has 79 records, OMM has 79 ids below 100000 and 3 at or above". D-319's route for one set, BSTAR padded in the OMM file only, fails the file as `parse` with no internal error on the synthetic set, and its twin passes. **Measured** [tested, 2026-10-16]: with the provider files (this checkout) all 23 tests of the module run, none skipped; in a public export of the same tree the six provider-file tests skip by name and the five synthetic ones run and pass; and with D-318's two branches removed from a scratch copy of the runner, the synthetic routes fail where they must, the reference adapter failing the half set ("['bstar-and-derivative-forms'] != []") and the parser with no TLE reader failing the comparison ("'fail' != 'skip'"), while the twin routes pass, so the synthetic set exercises the fix and does not merely run. Not covered by it: the routes of D-319 on the two pairing cases, which read several provider files each across three fixtures; they still run only where those files are. Alternatives: a committed synthetic data file (it would need its own allowlist line and label, for files the test can write from values the export already holds, as `test_strict_files_080.py` does); running the synthetic set only where the provider files are absent (the maintainer's runs would then never check the set itself; running it always costs about a second); synthetic pairs for the pairing cases (beyond a two-file set; listed).

The guide is lane A's file, so the two adapters are left as they are and their part is kept as a patch in the private handoff, with the lines of the guide it moves, for the merge. **How it was measured.** The change was written and measured at 03:53Z with mypy 2.4.0 in a scratch environment, which lost most of its files at 04:05Z, before the gate could run; the lane's rule was to stop rather than install, and the change was kept as a patch. On the owner's word (2026-10-16), mypy 2.4.0 was installed into a dedicated environment outside /tmp and Dropbox, used by this lane alone (with its dependencies as pip resolved them, `ast_serialize` 0.13.0 where the cleared environment had 0.12.1); it reproduced the baseline at the lane's head error for error (78, the same 78 lines), and the full patch error for error (53, the same lines as at 03:53Z). The owner's ruling: fix in 0.8.0 finding 1 (missing and duplicate records fail in `check-tle --against`, the secondary fields staying information per D-095), finding 8 (`utf-8-sig`, `object_name` insensitive to trailing blanks), finding 7 (control characters escaped in printed text), finding 2's visible note, and finding 4's Alpha-5 vectors only ("a decoder must read the whole field"); the catalog-id and epoch vectors (-5, day 000, hour 24, a valid 2024-366), finding 2's verdict, and findings 3, 5 and 6 to 0.8.1 as listed known limitations; stop and bring the owner the library and the vector if a new Alpha-5 vector moves a published verdict; credit the review in the changelog as a blind review. **What changed**. (1) `check-tle --against`: `load_against` returns `Against`, the source's records by id with `held`, how many records carry each id; `source_coverage` reads every written record of every file given: an id the format can carry written fewer times than the source holds it, none at all included, fails (`not_written`, each as id, written, held), an id written more often fails (`written_more`), and an id the TLE format cannot carry, written by none, is information (`refusal_correct`), a refusal being its correct output; a record written as a six-digit number from column 3 fails on its own and counts as written (`written_id`); a source record without a catalog number is counted (`without_id`) and noted, no written record being held to it; the command prints them, the summary line counts the failures, the exit code is 1 on any, and `--json` carries them as `source`. An id the source holds more than once (a history) is not compared: its records' round trip is not made, each is noted "not compared: source holds N copies (per-epoch pairing comes in 0.8.1)", the ids are listed (`not_compared`, id and copies, information), and the coverage still counts them (which copies were written is not checked: the same copy written twice passes, with the note); before, each written copy was compared with the source's last record of the id, so a correct file written from a history failed on the other copies (older, found by this entry's reading; the owner's ruling, 2026-10-27: "don't ship a false fail", not compared and said so for 0.8.0, a known limitation, per-epoch pairing in 0.8.1). A file whose records each passed on their own, with two of the source's three left out, passed with exit 0. (2) The Alpha-5 decode vectors gain five fields a decoder must reject, each with its reason: `A12B4` (a letter after the first character), `A1-34` (a sign), `A12.4` (a point), `A1 34` (a blank), `1234A` (a letter last); the case's expected values, its check text and the manifest regenerated. A decoder that read the first two characters and took any other as 0 passed. (3) A command's standard output (`--cmd`, `--vectors-cmd`, `--write-cmd`) is decoded as `utf-8-sig`, so a byte-order mark before the JSON or the lines is read past; any other text before it still fails.
